docs.text: engineering-influence ¶ Give it an idea. Get back a book you can publish. BLUF: engineering-influence writes a complete book, non-fiction or a novel, with nobody in the loop, and hands you the files Amazon KDP asks for: interior PDF, EPUB, covers, listing and a quality report. One command installs it, one command writes a book, and a free model on your own machine does the writing. # 1. Install everything a book needs (macOS with Homebrew, or Linux with apt-get) curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adammatthewsteinberger/engineering-influence/main/install.sh | sh # 2. Write a book ei book create --kind nonfiction "how to keep herbs alive indoors" --budget-usd 5 \ --out ./my-book --profile ~/.config/engineering-influence/author.toml The book lands in ./my-book/run/book/ . Nothing is uploaded: you read it, then you upload it to KDP yourself. Status: alpha ( 0.1.0a2 ), and honest about it. Every stage is built and tested, from the brief to the built book. The writing has only ever run against scripted test servers, never a live model, so nobody yet knows how good the books are. The install script has been run for real only as a dry run on macOS, and it installs from main , which gets it with the next release. See Limitations . The idea in one minute ¶ Daniel: I have a book idea and no free months. Everyone says an AI can write it. I asked a chatbot and got eleven pages of mush that forgot its own first chapter. Professor Feynman: Of course it did. You asked one cook to make a wedding dinner in one go, from memory, without a kitchen. What does a real kitchen have? Daniel: Stations. Somebody preps, somebody cooks, somebody checks the plate before it goes out. Professor Feynman: That is the whole design. A book here goes through stations in order: a brief, research, an outline, a draft of each chapter, three editing passes, then typesetting. Each station has one job and writes down what it made. So what happens if the power goes out halfway through the draft? Daniel: You would lose the night's work. Unless the finished plates were already on the shelf. Professor Feynman: They are on the shelf. Run the same command with --resume and it starts at the next station. Nothing finished is cooked twice, and nothing is paid for twice. Daniel: And the last station is the one that checks the plate. Professor Feynman: It builds the real PDF and EPUB and refuses a book that does not pass. The comparison stops there, though: a kitchen has a chef who tastes. This has checks, not taste. A person still reads the book before it is published. That person is you. Daniel: So it is a kitchen that never loses a plate, and I am still the one who tastes the dinner. What you get ¶ In my-book/ What it is run/book/<slug>.pdf The paperback interior, typeset with LaTeX to KDP's trim, margins and gutter run/book/<slug>.epub The ebook, checked for structure and links run/book/<slug>-ebook.jpg , <slug>-paperback-wrap.pdf The ebook cover, and the paperback wrap at the exact page count run/book/listing.md Title, subtitle, description and seven keywords, ready to paste run/book/MANIFEST.json What is in the bundle, with a checksum of every file run/quality-report.json Pass or fail, every error and warning, and what was spent against the estimate src/chapter_NN.md , books/*.toml The manuscript and its settings, to edit and rebuild with ei book build What a KDP-ready package is, exactly . Three commands worth knowing ¶ ei doctor --ready # can this machine make a book now? every gap, with the fix ei book create --out ./my-book --resume # carry on after a crash, a closed laptop or a provider at capacity ei book create --out ./my-book --resume --approve-spend # allow the extra budget a stopped run asked for ei book create exits 0 when the book is written, 1 when the run failed (what it made is kept, and a failed run is final), 2 when it could not start, and 3 when it stopped to ask for more budget. Let another AI drive it ¶ Claude Code, or any agent with a shell, can run all of this for you. The shortest route: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adammatthewsteinberger/engineering-influence/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --with-claude-skill That adds a skill to ~/.claude/skills/ . Then say: "Use engineering-influence to write a non-fiction book about indoor herbs. My author profile is at ~/.config/engineering-influence/author.toml and the budget is 5 dollars." The agent checks the machine, starts the run in the background, reads the exit code, and asks you before it approves any extra spend. Driving it from an agent, step by step . Choose your interface ¶ One controller layer, reached six ways. You are… Use Start here At a terminal, wanting a book ei book create The two commands above An AI agent with a shell The CLI and the skill docs/AGENTS_DRIVING.md Calling from any language REST API examples/api/ Writing Python SDK, sync or async examples/sdk/ Wiring an AI host to a running stack MCP server (stdio, ei serve mcp ) examples/mcp/ Receiving events Signed webhooks examples/webhooks/ Operating it Health, metrics, logs examples/observability/ The REST API, the SDK, the MCP server and the webhooks need the stack (a database, a broker and a worker): sh examples/up.sh starts one with generated credentials ( Getting started ). ei book create needs none of that. Prefer to install by hand? uv tool install "engineering-influence[runtime,publishing,mcp] @ git+https://github.com/adammatthewsteinberger/engineering-influence" installs ei alone. It is not on PyPI yet. The extras are api , webhooks , runtime , mcp and publishing (and test and dev for contributors). Documentation ¶ Read For Getting started Install, check, write your first book, then run the stack Driving it from an agent Claude Code or another LLM as the driver Books and KDP What a finished package is, what is built and what is not Novels The novel stages, from brief to a built book Interfaces Reference for the REST API, SDK, MCP tools, CLI and webhooks Configuration Every environment variable, security setting and limit The local model The free model that writes by default Model profiles , catalog , calls Choosing, pricing and calling a model you pay for Research , tool lock Web search for the research stage, and approving tool servers Skills , plugins , prompts Adding guidance to a stage, and how the prompts are versioned Architecture Layers, request flow, the worker and the extension points Threat model What is protected, from whom, and what is not Evaluation , live smoke test The paid runs that measure quality and cost Worker image The container and the TeX toolchain Troubleshooting Symptoms, causes and fixes Testing , compatibility , releasing The gates, what is promised to callers, and cutting a release The documentation site How these pages become a website, and how to publish it How these documents are written The page pattern, and who the Professor and Daniel are Decision records , changelog Why it is built this way, and what changed Limitations ¶ Read these before you depend on it. The writing is unproven. It has run only against scripted servers, never a live model. No real model has been measured against the quality bar. A person must read the book. Checks catch a broken file, not a dull chapter or a wrong fact. There is no claim checking. Nothing uploads to KDP. KDP has no publishing API. You upload the files and paste the listing. The first run needs a big download : about 13 GB for the model and several GB for TeX. Novels get no editing passes yet; a novel is built from its draft. On the stack , delivery is at least once (a crash can re-run a stage), no service emits webhooks yet although signing and a verifier exist, and the example worker writes placeholder text until you point it at a model. ei pipeline start and the example MCP server only plan work; ei serve mcp reaches the stack. The schema is managed by ei db upgrade ; run it before starting a new release on the stack. The full list: Configuration . About the author and the vibey ecosystem ¶ BLUF: Krypton and the vibey engine are an open-source Claude Code and OpenAI Codex killer—engineered to replace both completely free of charge, 100% open to everyone, and censorship-free. Unlike agents that produce unvetted AI slop, the vibey toolchain writes and verifies code the way a Principal Software Engineer does: architected with rigor, backed by 100% branch test coverage, sealed in an append-only cryptographic ledger, and built on an architecture designed for sovereign AGI with superintelligence coming soon. Who this is for ¶ Per ADR 0002 , engineering-influence and the vibey ecosystem prioritize audiences in this strict order: FOSS developers. Free and open-source engineers building and running autonomous tools with no subscriptions or telemetry walls. Freelancers. Independent operators and consultants delivering Principal-grade fixed-scope client projects with sovereign tools. Universities and academia. Researchers and scholars using open, verifiable, and cited methodologies. Governments and militaries. Public-sector and defense teams needing air-gapped models, verifiable provenance, and tamper-evident audit trails. Non-profit orgs. Mission-driven teams that need budget-preserving, durable software. Industry teams. Commercial teams and enterprises seeking production-grade agent infrastructure. docs.text: Driving it from another AI ¶ BLUF: Any agent with a shell (Claude Code, or another LLM that can run commands) can write a book for you with one command, ei book create . Install the skill and ask in plain words; the agent checks the machine, starts the run in the background, reads the exit code, and comes back to you before it spends anything extra. Use the MCP server only when a stack is already running. curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adammatthewsteinberger/engineering-influence/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --with-claude-skill Then, in Claude Code: Use engineering-influence to write a non-fiction book about keeping herbs alive indoors. My author profile is at ~/.config/engineering-influence/author.toml and the budget is 5 dollars. Why the command line, and not a server ¶ Daniel: I wired three MCP servers into my agent last month and spent a weekend on credentials. Is this a fourth weekend? Professor Feynman: What does your agent already know how to do without being taught? Daniel: Run a command and read what comes back. Professor Feynman: Then give it a command. Think of a vending machine against a restaurant. The restaurant needs a kitchen, staff and a table before you get a sandwich. The machine needs a coin and a button. For one book, ei book create is the machine: one process, a file for its memory, no server, no key. Daniel: A vending machine tells me nothing while it works. How does the agent know what happened? Professor Feynman: By the number the command leaves behind. Zero: the book is written. One: it failed, and what it made is kept. Two: it never started. Three: it stopped to ask for more money. An agent can branch on four numbers far more reliably than it can read a paragraph. Daniel: Three is the one that worries me. I do not want an agent deciding to spend. Professor Feynman: Nor do I. On three, nothing more is spent until someone runs it again with --approve-spend , and the skill tells the agent to ask you first. That is the limit of the comparison, by the way: a machine keeps your coin. This one stops and waits. Daniel: So the restaurant is for when I am feeding a crowd. Professor Feynman: Many runs, several machines, other programs calling in. Then you run the stack, and the agent talks to it over MCP. Until then, it is a weekend you do not need to spend. Daniel: One command, four numbers, and it asks me before it spends. I will start with the machine. The quick path: the skill ¶ The skill is one Markdown file, examples/claude-code/engineering-influence/SKILL.md . The installer copies it to ~/.claude/skills/engineering-influence/SKILL.md when you pass --with-claude-skill . To add it by hand: mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/engineering-influence curl -fsSL -o ~/.claude/skills/engineering-influence/SKILL.md \ https://raw.githubusercontent.com/adammatthewsteinberger/engineering-influence/main/examples/claude-code/engineering-influence/SKILL.md It teaches the agent the five steps below and four rules: never invent an author profile, never approve spend without your yes, never run a paid evaluation unasked, and never call a book finished unless the exit code was 0 . For any other agent: paste this ¶ An agent without the skill needs only these instructions. They are complete. You can write a book with the `ei` command. Follow these steps exactly. 1. Run `ei doctor --ready`. If it exits non-zero, stop and tell me each FAIL line. Do not start a run. 2. Ask me for: the idea, the kind (nonfiction or novel), the path to my author profile, and a budget in dollars. Never write an author profile yourself. 3. Start the run in the background, because it takes a long time: ei book create --kind KIND "IDEA" --budget-usd N --out ./BOOK --profile PROFILE > ./BOOK.log 2>&1 --out must be a new or empty folder. 4. When it ends, read the exit code: 0 the book is written: the files are in ./BOOK/run/book/ and the report is ./BOOK/run/quality-report.json 1 the run failed, and a failed run is final: tell me the `issue:` lines in ./BOOK.log. What it made is still in ./BOOK/ 2 it could not start: tell me the error message 3 it stopped to ask for more budget: ASK ME. Only if I say yes, run ei book create --out ./BOOK --resume --approve-spend 5. To continue a run that was interrupted (a crash, a closed terminal): ei book create --out ./BOOK --resume Finished stages are never run or paid for again. A run that ended in failure (exit 1) is final and --resume will not retry it: tell me, and start a new run with a new --out if I ask. Never pass --approve-spend or --ignore-estimate unless I agreed to that spend in this conversation. Never set EI_ALLOW_PAID or run `ei evaluate` unless I asked for a paid evaluation. Report what the quality report says, warnings included. Nothing is uploaded anywhere. What the agent sees ¶ Where What Standard output An estimate: line, then one stage: outcome line as each stage finishes, then a summary line Standard error Errors, and one issue: CODE: detail line for each issue the run recorded BOOK/run/quality-report.json The machine-readable result: status , errors, warnings, the files with checksums, and a spend block BOOK.state/ The run's memory. It is what --resume reads. Leave it alone There is no --json flag on ei book create : the quality report is the structured output. Every flag and the full meaning of each exit code is in INTERACTIONS.md . Long runs. A book takes longer than most agents let a foreground command run (Claude Code stops one at ten minutes), so the run goes in the background and the agent reads the log. When a stack is running: MCP ¶ ei serve mcp runs the stack's MCP server over stdio. It offers the same runs the REST API does. What must already be true: A database and a broker are running and reachable from the machine the agent is on. The database is migrated: ei db upgrade . The MCP server checks this and does not migrate. A worker is running: ei serve worker . The MCP server only saves a run and queues it. The worker has a model, a search, an author profile and the TeX tools, or its books will not build. Register it with the host. For Claude Code: claude mcp add engineering-influence \ --env EI_DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:5432/DB \ --env EI_RABBITMQ_URL=amqp://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:5672/ \ -- ei serve mcp For a host that reads a JSON file: {"mcpServers": {"engineering-influence": {"command": "ei", "args": ["serve", "mcp"], "env": {"EI_DATABASE_URL": "postgresql+psycopg://...", "EI_RABBITMQ_URL": "amqp://..."}}}} Tool What the agent does with it create_run Starts a book run from a brief: {"schema_version": 1, "kind": "nonfiction", "idea": "…", "budget_micro_usd": 5000000} get_run , list_runs Watches a run. Nothing is pushed, so the agent polls resume_run , cancel_run Continues a parked run, or stops one read_artifact Reads one stored file, up to 1 MiB grant_run , deny_run Answers a run's request for more budget. Offered only when the operator set EI_MCP_ALLOW_SPEND start_pipeline The older stage pipeline, not a book run Limits to know before you choose this path: A run started over MCP may be given at most EI_MCP_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_MICRO_USD (five dollars by default); more is refused with BUDGET_ABOVE_LIMIT . A file over 1 MiB, which a book's PDF usually is, cannot be read over MCP ( ARTIFACT_TOO_LARGE ). Fetch it with GET /v1/runs/{id}/artifacts/{name} and an API key, or with ei run export RUN_ID DIRECTORY . The example stack ( sh examples/up.sh ) publishes only the API's port, so a server started on your own machine cannot reach its database or broker. Point the server at a database and broker you can reach. The server has no authentication. It is a local child process of the host and must never be put on a network. This path has been tested with scripted clients, not with Claude Code against a live stack. The full tool reference is in INTERACTIONS.md , and the settings in CONFIGURATION.md . An editor that speaks the Agent Client Protocol ¶ ei acp serves the Agent Client Protocol over standard input and output, with pushed progress and a spend question the client answers. It also needs the database and the broker. Claude Code is an MCP host, not an ACP client, so this is for editors that speak ACP: INTERACTIONS.md .

To continue a run that was interrupted (a crash, a closed terminal): ei book create --out ./BOOK --resume Finished stages are never run or paid for again. A run that ended in failure (exit 1) is final and --resume will not retry it: tell me, and start a new run with a new --out if I ask. Never pass --approve-spend or --ignore-estimate unless I agreed to that spend in this conversation. Never set EI_ALLOW_PAID or run `ei evaluate` unless I asked for a paid evaluation. Report what the quality report says, warnings included. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.
docs.title: For any other agent: paste this

docs.text: Where What Standard output An estimate: line, then one stage: outcome line as each stage finishes, then a summary line Standard error Errors, and one issue: CODE: detail line for each issue the run recorded BOOK/run/quality-report.json The machine-readable result: status , errors, warnings, the files with checksums, and a spend block BOOK.state/ The run's memory. It is what --resume reads. Leave it alone There is no --json flag on ei book create : the quality report is the structured output. Every flag and the full meaning of each exit code is in INTERACTIONS.md . Long runs. A book takes longer than most agents let a foreground command run (Claude Code stops one at ten minutes), so the run goes in the background and the agent reads the log.
docs.title: What the agent sees

docs.text: ei serve mcp runs the stack's MCP server over stdio. It offers the same runs the REST API does. What must already be true: A database and a broker are running and reachable from the machine the agent is on. The database is migrated: ei db upgrade . The MCP server checks this and does not migrate. A worker is running: ei serve worker . The MCP server only saves a run and queues it. The worker has a model, a search, an author profile and the TeX tools, or its books will not build. Register it with the host. For Claude Code: claude mcp add engineering-influence \ --env EI_DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:5432/DB \ --env EI_RABBITMQ_URL=amqp://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:5672/ \ -- ei serve mcp For a host that reads a JSON file: {"mcpServers": {"engineering-influence": {"command": "ei", "args": ["serve", "mcp"], "env": {"EI_DATABASE_URL": "postgresql+psycopg://...", "EI_RABBITMQ_URL": "amqp://..."}}}} Tool What the agent does with it create_run Starts a book run from a brief: {"schema_version": 1, "kind": "nonfiction", "idea": "…", "budget_micro_usd": 5000000} get_run , list_runs Watches a run. Nothing is pushed, so the agent polls resume_run , cancel_run Continues a parked run, or stops one read_artifact Reads one stored file, up to 1 MiB grant_run , deny_run Answers a run's request for more budget. Offered only when the operator set EI_MCP_ALLOW_SPEND start_pipeline The older stage pipeline, not a book run Limits to know before you choose this path: A run started over MCP may be given at most EI_MCP_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_MICRO_USD (five dollars by default); more is refused with BUDGET_ABOVE_LIMIT . A file over 1 MiB, which a book's PDF usually is, cannot be read over MCP ( ARTIFACT_TOO_LARGE ). Fetch it with GET /v1/runs/{id}/artifacts/{name} and an API key, or with ei run export RUN_ID DIRECTORY . The example stack ( sh examples/up.sh ) publishes only the API's port, so a server started on your own machine cannot reach its database or broker. Point the server at a database and broker you can reach. The server has no authentication. It is a local child process of the host and must never be put on a network. This path has been tested with scripted clients, not with Claude Code against a live stack. The full tool reference is in INTERACTIONS.md , and the settings in CONFIGURATION.md .
docs.title: When a stack is running: MCP

docs.text: ei acp serves the Agent Client Protocol over standard input and output, with pushed progress and a spend question the client answers. It also needs the database and the broker. Claude Code is an MCP host, not an ACP client, so this is for editors that speak ACP: INTERACTIONS.md .
docs.title: An editor that speaks the Agent Client Protocol

docs.text: Architecture ¶ BLUF: It is one program built in layers that only point inward: transports call controllers, controllers call services, and services depend on plain models and on interfaces. Everything that touches the outside world sits behind an interface. Tests and an import checker enforce the rules, so they cannot quietly rot. Read this before changing models, services or infrastructure. engineering-influence writes complete books autonomously and packages them for Amazon KDP ( purpose and status ); this page describes the machinery that does it unattended. It is a modular monolith . Interactions call controllers; controllers call services; services depend on pure models, contracts and interfaces; repositories and infrastructure adapters implement those interfaces and point inward; and only runtime/ wires concrete classes together. ADR 0006 records the rules. They are enforced by tests and by import-linter , not by convention. Why the layers point one way ¶ Daniel: I want to swap RabbitMQ for another queue. In my last codebase that meant touching forty files. Professor Feynman: Where does the electricity in this room come from? Daniel: The wall socket. I do not know or care which power station. Professor Feynman: Because the lamp depends on the shape of the socket, not on the station. Here a service asks for 'something that can queue a job', an interface. RabbitMQ is one thing plugged into that socket. Write another plug and the service never notices. Daniel: And what stops someone importing RabbitMQ straight into a service on a bad day? Professor Feynman: A checker that fails the build. The inner layers are forbidden to import the outer ones, and runtime/ is where the plugging in is done. The picture stops being true in one respect: a socket hides nothing important, and an interface can hide a slow or failing dependency. That is why every side effect here must also be bounded and recoverable. Daniel: One new adapter, a few lines in runtime/ where each process is wired, and the services stay as they are. Not forty files. Layers ¶ runtime/ composition roots (CLI, API, worker, MCP, local book, evaluation), settings loader, entry points interactions/ REST · MCP · CLI · ACP transports: parse input, call a controller controllers/ ProjectController, RunController, PublishingController repositories/ SQLModel ledger and outbox; book and chapter loaders; release evidence files infrastructure/ RabbitMQ queue and consumer, LaTeX, EPUB, PDF and image tools, cover painters, webhook delivery, security, observability, vibey adapters, in-memory adapters services/ StartPipeline, RunPhase, ProcessJob, DispatchOutbox, ReadinessProbe, and the book checks, audits, EPUB and typesetting logic and release steps interfaces/ what services need from the outside: Ledger, Queue, Runner, Gate, Outbox, WebhookDelivery, Secrets, … contracts/ wire and config schemas (pydantic): JobMessage, HealthStatus, … models/ Project, PhaseRun, Gate, Artifact, PipelineStage, GoverningPostulates, and the book, EPUB, cover and QA value types (pure) errors/ exception classes (innermost, stdlib only) covers/ the public cover-plugin API (`engineering_influence.covers`): a facade over classes that live in the layers, so a private project's imports survive moves The book toolchain behind ei book (optional publishing extra) has no layer of its own. Its checks and audits are in services/publishing/ , typesetting in <layer>/typesetting/ , EPUB in <layer>/epub/ , covers in <layer>/covers/ , page QA in <layer>/qa/ and release evidence in <layer>/release/ . The bundled LaTeX classes and fonts are in infrastructure/publishing/assets/ . Dependencies only point inward. services and controllers never import adapters or transports (contract: "Services and controllers never touch adapters or transports"). Run uv run lint-imports to check. The architecture tests under tests/architecture add the rest, and every one of them holds with no exceptions: One class per file , no loose production functions, and every file inside the layers. Every class has an interface. Every folder has an interfaces/ folder, x/foo.py defining Foo pairs with x/interfaces/foo_interface.py defining FooInterface , and Foo inherits it. An interface is an ABC with __slots__ = () that declares methods only. An enum cannot inherit an ABC, so it gets a runtime_checkable Protocol and a test instead. Purity. models/ imports only errors and the standard library. Image, PDF, archive, process and file libraries never appear in models , contracts or services ; an adapter provides them. Injection. Collaborators arrive through constructors, so a test passes a fake instead of patching production code. The only patches left are standard-library calls at the system boundary (see TESTING.md ). scripts/refactor/move_map.toml records where every class moved from, and a test keeps it complete. One request, end to end ¶ client ──POST /v1/pipelines──▶ ApiGuard (rate limit by address, verify key, rate limit by key) │ ProjectController.start ─▶ StartPipeline │ ├─ ledger: append PipelineStarted │ └─ queue: enqueue "pipeline.<first stage>" + remaining stages ▼ RabbitMQ engineering-influence.jobs ──▶ worker (RabbitMqJobConsumer) │ ProcessJob ─▶ RunPhase ─▶ Runner (produces) ─▶ Gate (accepts?) │ ├─ accepted: ledger phase.completed, enqueue next stage │ │ (after the last: pipeline.completed) │ └─ human or rejecting gate: ledger gate.awaiting, stop ▼ malformed or failing job ─▶ rejected without requeue ─▶ engineering-influence.jobs.dead The correlation id travels the whole way: request, queued job, worker log lines and outbound webhooks. Design decisions ¶ Interfaces first. Queue, ledger, gate, runner, outbox and secrets are interfaces. The application does not know which LLM runner or queue it runs on. vibey stays behind a boundary. ADR 0001 records why: vibey-engine 0.4 does not expose worker extension points, so the worker uses an application-owned RabbitMQ consumer and keeps vibey as an adapter. Fail closed. A missing key, secret or setting stops the process or refuses the request. Bounded, idempotent, observable, recoverable side effects: every external effect has a timeout or budget, a ledger entry and a path back after a crash. Models are pure. PhaseRun is a state machine; nothing in models/ performs I/O. Data ¶ Ledger ( ledgereventrecord ): append-only events ( pipeline.started , phase.completed , gate.awaiting , pipeline.completed ) with JSON payloads. Outbox : webhook intents with attempt counts and dead_at . Dispatch isolates failures per event. Queues : EI_QUEUE_NAME (default engineering-influence.jobs ) and its .dead companion. Runs ( bookrunrecord ), the run journal ( journalrecord ) and artifacts ( artifactrecord ) back resumable book runs. The worker writes them when it advances a run.advance job; ei run create , POST /v1/runs and the MCP and SDK create_run start one, and ei run grant , deny , resume and cancel change it. The API and ei run status read them ( RunSummaryV1 ). The schema is owned by Alembic. The migrations ship in the wheel ( infrastructure/migrations/ ), ei db upgrade applies them to EI_DATABASE_URL , and the compose stack runs it once in a migrate service that the API and the worker wait for. The API and the worker never create tables: they check the revision at start-up and refuse to run on a database that is not at the latest one, so two processes can no longer race to create the schema. Databases made by the earlier create_all() are adopted in place; the baseline creates only the tables that are missing. Trust boundaries ¶ Boundary Control Internet → API API key, per-address and per-key rate limit, input validation, request ids sanitised API/worker → Postgres, RabbitMQ credentials from the environment, never logged (field-name masking) Platform → webhook receiver HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp and body, replay window, public-HTTPS-only destinations (SSRF policy) Uploads and paths AttachmentUploadInspector , ConfinedPathGuard confinement (building blocks; no upload route yet) MCP and CLI local processes, unauthenticated by design; never expose them Extension points ¶ To add an integration, write an interface , an adapter , an ADR when the choice is architectural, and failure/recovery tests (see CONTRIBUTING.md ). Typical swaps: a model-backed RunnerInterface and rubric GateEvaluatorInterface in place of the placeholders; another QueueInterface ; another LedgerInterface . Not built yet ¶ An importer entry-point plugin layer, an inbound webhook route, and the methodology stages P1 to P14 with autonomy modes. CHANGELOG.md records what has landed.

docs.text: From an idea to a KDP-ready book ¶ BLUF: "KDP-ready" here means a folder Amazon's upload form will accept: an interior PDF at KDP's trim and margins, an EPUB, covers at the exact page count, a listing with seven keywords, and a report that says what passed. ei book create produces it from an idea, and ei book publish produces it from a manuscript you already have. It is checked by the build, and it still needs a person to read it before it is published. What "ready" really means ¶ Daniel: I uploaded my last book to KDP four times. Margins, then a font that was not embedded, then the spine. Each rejection took a day. What does "ready" buy me here? Professor Feynman: What did all four rejections have in common? Daniel: They were rules I could have checked myself, if I had known the rules. Professor Feynman: There you are. An airline pilot does not find out at the runway whether the fuel cap is on. There is a list, and the list is run before the engines start. The build stage is that list for a book: trim size, the gutter that grows with the page count, fonts embedded, page limits, the EPUB's structure, exactly seven keywords. Daniel: So if the list passes, Amazon accepts it. Professor Feynman: Careful. Which things can a list not check? Daniel: Whether the book is any good. And whatever rule Amazon changed last week. Professor Feynman: Both right. The list covers the rules written into this code, and it has not yet been proven against Kindle Previewer on a book made this way. That is why the report ends human_review: pending and why nothing is ever uploaded for you. Daniel: Then "ready" means the mechanical rejections are behind me, and the reading is still mine. engineering-influence exists to write complete books, fiction and non-fiction, fully autonomously, and to hand you a package that is ready to upload to Amazon KDP. Everything else in this repository (the API, MCP server, CLI, SDK, webhooks, queue and ledger) is the machinery that makes that run unattended, recoverably and auditably. You supply a project: a title, governing postulates (the claims and limits the book must stay inside) and the stages to run. The pipeline does the rest. postulates ─▶ thesis ─▶ book | novel | screenplay ─▶ hub ─▶ spokes ─▶ distribution ─▶ publish │ └─ each stage: runner writes · gate accepts or rejects · ledger records publish stage ─▶ audit · interior PDF · EPUB · covers · page QA · release-readiness report What "KDP-ready" means here ¶ The publish stage ( ei book publish ) produces, and verifies, the files and decisions KDP asks for: KDP requirement What the toolchain does Paperback interior 6 × 9 in PDF typeset with LaTeX; margins and the page-count-dependent gutter checked against KDP's table; fonts embedded; page count against KDP's limits Hardcover interior Compact hardcover build; page limit checked, or an explicit external-provider decision required eBook EPUB built and validated (structure, links, epubcheck ) Covers Front, back and spine/wrap for print at the exact trim and page count, plus the eBook cover; image, quiet-zone and layout checks Listing metadata Title, subtitle, author, description size, exactly seven unique keywords (categories are checked for count, shape and uniqueness, not against Amazon's category tree) Pricing List-price policy, freshness and source of the inputs, estimated print cost and royalty Manuscript quality Forbidden-content, scaffold-leak, chapter-opening, contents, research-apparatus and formula checks Evidence A machine-readable release report with file digests, tool versions and git state A book is release-ready only when every audit passes. The report ends with human_review: pending : a person signs off before anything is published. What is built, and what is not ¶ Be exact about today's state (alpha 0.1.0a2 ): Status Orchestration: queue, worker, ledger, gates, dead-letter, API, MCP, CLI, SDK, webhooks Built and tested KDP packaging and verification ( ei book … ): audits, PDF, EPUB, covers, QA, readiness report Built, tested, used to build ten real books The writing itself Built, not yet proven. With EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR=model a non-fiction run goes brief, positioning, research, outline, metadata, draft, three editing passes, assemble, audit and build. It has only been run against scripted servers; a capped test against a real model is in LIVE_SMOKE_TEST.md . With no setting the same stages run on the free local model ( LOCAL_MODEL.md ); EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR=deterministic is the placeholder that returns fixed text Web search and page fetch Built as model tools and used by the research stage: SearXNG first (a local one ships in examples/searxng/ ), Brave Search as backup, and a safe fetcher with a hidden-text-stripping extractor. Tested against local servers and fakes only; they have never touched the live internet Non-fiction stages Built through the finished book: brief, positioning, research, outline, metadata, draft, structure, line and copy edits, assemble, audit and build , never yet run against a live provider. build runs the same publish pipeline as ei book publish on the run's own manuscript, in a scratch folder, and packages the KDP bundle. It stores the interior PDF, EPUB, covers, listing and manifest under book/ , the readiness reports and tool logs under build/ , a quality-report.json (status, errors, warnings, and a checksum for every file) and build.md . Money: the editing passes are optional, so a pass that runs out of budget does not stop the run: that chapter and the rest of the pass keep the text they had, one tolerated issue ( revision-skipped-budget ) goes into the quality report, and nothing more is paid for. The planning stages and the draft are essential, so a cap that runs out there still stops the run to ask for more. quality-report.json has a spend block (the cap, what was spent, and what the brief was expected to cost, from a first-pass estimate whose constants are to be calibrated against real runs: spent_over_estimated is the figure to watch). It needs the TeX worker image ( WORKER_IMAGE.md ); a failed build still stores what it produced, then fails the run. Pricing and sales-source details are the author's, so by default a missing price is a warning in the report; set EI_BUILD_STRICT_RELEASE=1 to make any such warning fail the build. A whole book is made from an idea with ei book create ( INTERACTIONS.md ). Not built: claim checking, a fact tracker across chapters, and a cover from the author's own design (the covers a run builds use the book's configuration only) Novel stages Built through the finished book, without editing passes: brief, story bible, beats, outline, metadata, draft, assemble, audit and build, never yet run against a live provider. A novel keeps its dashes and uses the brief's trim size; build is the same stage as for non-fiction. Not built: revision and copy editing for a novel, and a repair pass for continuity findings ( NOVELS.md ) Methodology stages (P1 to P14), autonomy modes Not built Budget caps, and retry of a run's transient stage failures Built and tested against scripted servers, including a budget stop and a retry through the real HTTP adapter; not yet exercised by a live model run Uploading to KDP Never automatic: KDP has no publishing API. You upload the verified files and paste the verified metadata yourself So today you can run the full orchestration end to end and produce KDP-ready packaging from a manuscript; drafting is built but unproven against a live model, and ei book create is the entry point. The /v1/pipelines stage pipeline still uses the placeholder runner. This page is updated as each row changes. Fiction and non-fiction ¶ Both use the same stages and the same publish step. Non-fiction is bounded by its postulates and research apparatus (claims need sources; the research check enforces it). Fiction adds the novel and screenplay stages. Choose the stages in the request, for example ["thesis", "book"] or ["novel", "distribution", "publish"] . Book kind and the text rules ¶ A book's config ( books/<slug>.toml ) may say kind = "novel" ; without it the book is non-fiction. The kind picks the text rules the typesetter and the checks apply. An unknown kind stops the build with a message naming the two valid ones. Rule nonfiction (the default) novel Em dash ( — ) in the text Refused, in the manuscript, the PDF and the EPUB Allowed En dash ( – ) Refused Refused A --- line inside a chapter Prints nothing Prints a scene break: a centred * * * , and the next paragraph is not indented. A rule that opens or ends a passage, sits beside another rule, or is inside a quote or list prints nothing The word Draft Refused anywhere Refused in narration; allowed inside curly quotation marks, so a character may say it Unfinished markers such as [TODO] Refused Refused A quoted span for the Draft rule is at most 500 characters, so an opening quote that never closes cannot hide a stray Draft later in the text. Narration that legitimately starts a sentence with Draft still has to be reworded. tests/fixtures/fixture_novel/ is a small novel that shows each rule and is built with the real toolchain in CI. Listing metadata ¶ The release contract ( [release] in the book's config) is checked before anything is built. Beyond the title, subtitle and author, it covers the listing: Setting Rule Finding description (top level) at least 80 words ( release.minimum_description_words ), at most 4,000 characters ( release.maximum_description_characters , which can only lower KDP's limit in practice) description-too-short , description-too-long release.keywords exactly seven, unique, none empty keyword-count , duplicate-keyword , empty-keyword release.categories up to three Amazon browse paths such as Books > Literature & Fiction > Mystery ; unique; at least two levels too-many-categories , category-not-a-path , duplicate-category , categories-invalid Categories are Amazon's browse tree, not BISAC subject codes ( FIC009000 ), which are a different scheme: a BISAC code in categories is refused as category-is-bisac . The check cannot know Amazon's tree, which changes and has no API. It checks the count, the shape and the uniqueness; you confirm the names when you upload. A book with no categories gets the warning categories-not-declared , never an error, so books written before this check keep passing a strict release. The 4,000-character and three-category limits are KDP's published limits as I understand them; confirm them against KDP's current help pages. The release bundle ¶ ei book package SLUG writes build/SLUG/release/kdp/ , the folder you upload from: listing.md : the title, subtitle, description, the seven keywords and the categories, the way you paste them into KDP, then a table of the files with their sizes and SHA-256 hashes. MANIFEST.json : the same files as data, with the release status the bundle was made under. A copy of each finished file the release requires: the interior PDF, the EPUB, the cover images and the wraps. It refuses, and writes nothing, when the release check fails , when a required file is missing, or when the listing is outside the limits the release check applies (a message names the field). A book whose release check only warns is packaged, and its manifest says so. Nothing is uploaded: KDP has no publishing API, so you upload these files and paste the listing yourself, then check the hashes against what you uploaded. The command overwrites its own files and leaves any other file in the folder alone; a symbolic link is refused, so the bundle is only ever what was checked. The back cover and the barcode area ¶ The back cover carries the description and the author note, and KDP keeps a 2 x 1.2 in area clear for the barcode it adds. The description is set above that area, shrinking until it fits, down to a smallest size. If it still does not fit, the build stops with BackCoverTextTooLongError , which reports how many characters the description has, how many fit at this trim size and how far it overflows, instead of drawing text into the barcode area. The limit on the cover is lower than KDP's 4,000-character listing limit and depends on the trim size and the cover style: with the default style, about 3,000 characters fit at 6x9 and 5.5x8.5 and about 2,200 at 5x8, and the error gives the exact figure for your book. Text, and any ink, in the barcode area is also caught after rendering, at every trim size, for the paperback and the hardcover. What the typesetter refuses ¶ Text that reaches TeX may be written by a model, so the typesetter escapes it and refuses a few things it cannot make safe (the full picture is in THREAT_MODEL.md ): A code block that contains \end{verbatim} stops the build with a message, because TeX would end the code environment there and read the rest of the line as TeX. A website that is not an http or https address stops the build: write https://pub.example or a bare host name such as pub.example . Another scheme ( javascript: , data: ), a space, or a host:port is refused; write a port with its scheme ( https://pub.example:8080 ). Any URL, including a website and an email , is printed with every character outside the ordinary URL set percent-encoded, so a space, a quote or an accented letter appears as %20 , %22 or %C3%A9 . An ebook title with any of & < > " # % \ { } ~ ^ $ _ is refused. The title, subtitle, author and edition also go into the PDF's metadata, where the characters \ { } % # ^ ~ , control characters and unbalanced parentheses are dropped. An ordinary title, including balanced parentheses, is unchanged. A build that runs too long, or uses too much ¶ Each build tool has limits, and a tool that passes one is stopped, together with everything it started: Tool Time Memory Disk written latexmk and tex4ebook 30 minutes 8 GiB 4 GiB epubcheck 10 minutes 4 GiB not measured the page renderer 10 minutes 2 GiB 4 GiB Memory is the resident size of the tool and everything it started. Disk is the size of the directory it writes into. The build then fails with a message such as latexmk did not finish within 1800 seconds and was stopped , latexmk used 8300 MiB of memory, over its limit of 8192 MiB and was stopped or latexmk wrote 4300 MiB to disk, over its limit of 4096 MiB and was stopped , followed by the tool's last output so you can see where it stopped. Memory and disk are checked twice a second, so the figure in the message can be a little over the limit. A normal book is far below all of these (the fixture books peak at about 400 MiB). The limits are fixed in the code, not settings, and a book that legitimately needs more than this is not supported yet. Trim size and paper ¶ A book's config sets the page size and the interior paper. Both default to what every book used before they existed, so a config that says nothing builds exactly the same files as before. trim_size Page (in) Hardcover 6x9 (default) 6 x 9 yes 5.5x8.5 5.5 x 8.5 yes 5x8 5 x 8 no : KDP does not print a hardcover at this size paper Spine width per page white (default) 0.002252 in cream 0.0025 in The trim size sets the interior's page size (the PDF check refuses any other), the cover layouts and the ebook cover's proportions. The paper sets the spine width of the paperback and hardcover wraps, so a cream book's spine is wider than a white book's of the same length. An unknown value stops the build with a message listing the valid ones. A 5x8 book is paperback and ebook only. It gets no hardcover interior and no hardcover wrap, a [formats] hardcover = true or release.formats.kdp_hardcover = true is refused, and its [release.pricing] needs no hardcover price. If you add one anyway it is still checked, and selling a hardcover through another provider still needs hardcover_provider as before. The hardcover column follows KDP's published hardcover sizes as I understand them today; KDP changes what it offers, so confirm against its current list before relying on it. Where to go next ¶ Getting started · Interfaces · Architecture · Configuration

docs.text: BLUF: "KDP-ready" here means a folder Amazon's upload form will accept: an interior PDF at KDP's trim and margins, an EPUB, covers at the exact page count, a listing with seven keywords, and a report that says what passed. ei book create produces it from an idea, and ei book publish produces it from a manuscript you already have. It is checked by the build, and it still needs a person to read it before it is published.
docs.title: From an idea to a KDP-ready book

docs.text: Daniel: I uploaded my last book to KDP four times. Margins, then a font that was not embedded, then the spine. Each rejection took a day. What does "ready" buy me here? Professor Feynman: What did all four rejections have in common? Daniel: They were rules I could have checked myself, if I had known the rules. Professor Feynman: There you are. An airline pilot does not find out at the runway whether the fuel cap is on. There is a list, and the list is run before the engines start. The build stage is that list for a book: trim size, the gutter that grows with the page count, fonts embedded, page limits, the EPUB's structure, exactly seven keywords. Daniel: So if the list passes, Amazon accepts it. Professor Feynman: Careful. Which things can a list not check? Daniel: Whether the book is any good. And whatever rule Amazon changed last week. Professor Feynman: Both right. The list covers the rules written into this code, and it has not yet been proven against Kindle Previewer on a book made this way. That is why the report ends human_review: pending and why nothing is ever uploaded for you. Daniel: Then "ready" means the mechanical rejections are behind me, and the reading is still mine. engineering-influence exists to write complete books, fiction and non-fiction, fully autonomously, and to hand you a package that is ready to upload to Amazon KDP. Everything else in this repository (the API, MCP server, CLI, SDK, webhooks, queue and ledger) is the machinery that makes that run unattended, recoverably and auditably. You supply a project: a title, governing postulates (the claims and limits the book must stay inside) and the stages to run. The pipeline does the rest. postulates ─▶ thesis ─▶ book | novel | screenplay ─▶ hub ─▶ spokes ─▶ distribution ─▶ publish │ └─ each stage: runner writes · gate accepts or rejects · ledger records publish stage ─▶ audit · interior PDF · EPUB · covers · page QA · release-readiness report
docs.title: What "ready" really means

docs.text: The publish stage ( ei book publish ) produces, and verifies, the files and decisions KDP asks for: KDP requirement What the toolchain does Paperback interior 6 × 9 in PDF typeset with LaTeX; margins and the page-count-dependent gutter checked against KDP's table; fonts embedded; page count against KDP's limits Hardcover interior Compact hardcover build; page limit checked, or an explicit external-provider decision required eBook EPUB built and validated (structure, links, epubcheck ) Covers Front, back and spine/wrap for print at the exact trim and page count, plus the eBook cover; image, quiet-zone and layout checks Listing metadata Title, subtitle, author, description size, exactly seven unique keywords (categories are checked for count, shape and uniqueness, not against Amazon's category tree) Pricing List-price policy, freshness and source of the inputs, estimated print cost and royalty Manuscript quality Forbidden-content, scaffold-leak, chapter-opening, contents, research-apparatus and formula checks Evidence A machine-readable release report with file digests, tool versions and git state A book is release-ready only when every audit passes. The report ends with human_review: pending : a person signs off before anything is published.
docs.title: What "KDP-ready" means here

docs.text: Be exact about today's state (alpha 0.1.0a2 ): Status Orchestration: queue, worker, ledger, gates, dead-letter, API, MCP, CLI, SDK, webhooks Built and tested KDP packaging and verification ( ei book … ): audits, PDF, EPUB, covers, QA, readiness report Built, tested, used to build ten real books The writing itself Built, not yet proven. With EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR=model a non-fiction run goes brief, positioning, research, outline, metadata, draft, three editing passes, assemble, audit and build. It has only been run against scripted servers; a capped test against a real model is in LIVE_SMOKE_TEST.md . With no setting the same stages run on the free local model ( LOCAL_MODEL.md ); EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR=deterministic is the placeholder that returns fixed text Web search and page fetch Built as model tools and used by the research stage: SearXNG first (a local one ships in examples/searxng/ ), Brave Search as backup, and a safe fetcher with a hidden-text-stripping extractor. Tested against local servers and fakes only; they have never touched the live internet Non-fiction stages Built through the finished book: brief, positioning, research, outline, metadata, draft, structure, line and copy edits, assemble, audit and build , never yet run against a live provider. build runs the same publish pipeline as ei book publish on the run's own manuscript, in a scratch folder, and packages the KDP bundle. It stores the interior PDF, EPUB, covers, listing and manifest under book/ , the readiness reports and tool logs under build/ , a quality-report.json (status, errors, warnings, and a checksum for every file) and build.md . Money: the editing passes are optional, so a pass that runs out of budget does not stop the run: that chapter and the rest of the pass keep the text they had, one tolerated issue ( revision-skipped-budget ) goes into the quality report, and nothing more is paid for. The planning stages and the draft are essential, so a cap that runs out there still stops the run to ask for more. quality-report.json has a spend block (the cap, what was spent, and what the brief was expected to cost, from a first-pass estimate whose constants are to be calibrated against real runs: spent_over_estimated is the figure to watch). It needs the TeX worker image ( WORKER_IMAGE.md ); a failed build still stores what it produced, then fails the run. Pricing and sales-source details are the author's, so by default a missing price is a warning in the report; set EI_BUILD_STRICT_RELEASE=1 to make any such warning fail the build. A whole book is made from an idea with ei book create ( INTERACTIONS.md ). Not built: claim checking, a fact tracker across chapters, and a cover from the author's own design (the covers a run builds use the book's configuration only) Novel stages Built through the finished book, without editing passes: brief, story bible, beats, outline, metadata, draft, assemble, audit and build, never yet run against a live provider. A novel keeps its dashes and uses the brief's trim size; build is the same stage as for non-fiction. Not built: revision and copy editing for a novel, and a repair pass for continuity findings ( NOVELS.md ) Methodology stages (P1 to P14), autonomy modes Not built Budget caps, and retry of a run's transient stage failures Built and tested against scripted servers, including a budget stop and a retry through the real HTTP adapter; not yet exercised by a live model run Uploading to KDP Never automatic: KDP has no publishing API. You upload the verified files and paste the verified metadata yourself So today you can run the full orchestration end to end and produce KDP-ready packaging from a manuscript; drafting is built but unproven against a live model, and ei book create is the entry point. The /v1/pipelines stage pipeline still uses the placeholder runner. This page is updated as each row changes.

docs.text: Both use the same stages and the same publish step. Non-fiction is bounded by its postulates and research apparatus (claims need sources; the research check enforces it). Fiction adds the novel and screenplay stages. Choose the stages in the request, for example ["thesis", "book"] or ["novel", "distribution", "publish"] .
docs.title: Fiction and non-fiction

docs.text: A book's config ( books/<slug>.toml ) may say kind = "novel" ; without it the book is non-fiction. The kind picks the text rules the typesetter and the checks apply. An unknown kind stops the build with a message naming the two valid ones. Rule nonfiction (the default) novel Em dash ( — ) in the text Refused, in the manuscript, the PDF and the EPUB Allowed En dash ( – ) Refused Refused A --- line inside a chapter Prints nothing Prints a scene break: a centred * * * , and the next paragraph is not indented. A rule that opens or ends a passage, sits beside another rule, or is inside a quote or list prints nothing The word Draft Refused anywhere Refused in narration; allowed inside curly quotation marks, so a character may say it Unfinished markers such as [TODO] Refused Refused A quoted span for the Draft rule is at most 500 characters, so an opening quote that never closes cannot hide a stray Draft later in the text. Narration that legitimately starts a sentence with Draft still has to be reworded. tests/fixtures/fixture_novel/ is a small novel that shows each rule and is built with the real toolchain in CI.
docs.title: Book kind and the text rules

docs.text: The release contract ( [release] in the book's config) is checked before anything is built. Beyond the title, subtitle and author, it covers the listing: Setting Rule Finding description (top level) at least 80 words ( release.minimum_description_words ), at most 4,000 characters ( release.maximum_description_characters , which can only lower KDP's limit in practice) description-too-short , description-too-long release.keywords exactly seven, unique, none empty keyword-count , duplicate-keyword , empty-keyword release.categories up to three Amazon browse paths such as Books > Literature & Fiction > Mystery ; unique; at least two levels too-many-categories , category-not-a-path , duplicate-category , categories-invalid Categories are Amazon's browse tree, not BISAC subject codes ( FIC009000 ), which are a different scheme: a BISAC code in categories is refused as category-is-bisac . The check cannot know Amazon's tree, which changes and has no API. It checks the count, the shape and the uniqueness; you confirm the names when you upload. A book with no categories gets the warning categories-not-declared , never an error, so books written before this check keep passing a strict release. The 4,000-character and three-category limits are KDP's published limits as I understand them; confirm them against KDP's current help pages.

docs.text: Changelog ¶ Unreleased ¶ 0.1.0a2 ¶ Release flow and CI: ADR 0005 records how releases really work (the version is set by hand in the release commit) and replaces direct edits of this file with changelog.d/ fragments, folded by scripts/fold_changelog.py and enforced by the release guard. CI now runs every gate on Python 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14, the SDK and core declare 3.14, and a daily Canary workflow installs the declared bounds from the package index without the lock file and runs the suite. CONTRIBUTING.md states what may live in the public repository (where model prompts, fixtures and cassettes go). The toolchain CI job caches the downloaded TeX packages and downloads them in short, retried attempts, because the runner's mirror sometimes throttled a connection until the job hit its time limit. Added a toolchain CI job that builds a synthetic fixture book with real LuaLaTeX, tex4ebook and epubcheck under a strict release contract and compares it with a checked-in structural snapshot. Before this, no test built a real PDF or EPUB. See docs/TESTING.md . Hardened the TeX toolchain before any model-written text reaches it: latexmk runs with -no-shell-escape , and both latexmk and tex4ebook get an allow-listed environment ( PATH , HOME , locale, TEXMF* and similar) instead of a copy of the parent's, so API keys and tokens never reach a build tool. A strict release ( --strict-release , or release.required = true in the book config) now fails when epubcheck is not installed. Before, a missing validator read as a pass. CI works again. vibey-engine 4.5.0 was removed from PyPI (the index lists 0.3.0 and 0.4.0), which failed the provenance job, the distribution build and uv lock . The runtime extra now asks for vibey-engine>=0.4,<0.5 ; the provenance job installs from uv.lock instead of the index; tests/unit/test_vibey_import_contract.py names every vibey symbol the package uses. CI now also runs ruff format --check and installs with uv sync --locked , which fails when uv.lock and pyproject.toml disagree. Replaced the unused cli extra ( typer ) with webhooks ( httpx , which webhook delivery imports). The commit-msg and pre-push hooks are regenerated by the pinned vibey-gh ; the new template reads self_source from local git config instead of a tracked file. uv resolves only Python 3.12 to 3.14, so a lock no longer tries to resolve Python 3.15. Added ADR 0003 (the definition of 1.0: an idea becomes a KDP-ready EPUB and print PDF with nobody in the loop) and ADR 0004 (versioning, compatibility and deprecation). Corrected documentation that claimed more than the code does: categories are not checked, jobs are not retried, no pdf_safety module exists, no clock port exists, delivery is at least once, and the API readiness probe does not include the toolchain check. The MCP server no longer says it can inspect pipelines. Provenance headers now cover the SDK package, and CONTRIBUTING.md lists every gate command. Documentation now states the purpose everywhere: fully autonomous writing of fiction and non-fiction books, packaged ready to self-publish on Amazon KDP. Added docs/BOOKS_AND_KDP.md (what a KDP-ready package contains, what is built, what is not); package descriptions updated. Restored a green develop after the Dependabot major bumps: the MCP server uses mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer ( mcp 2.x renamed FastMCP ) and the bounds now require mcp>=2,<3 ; the compose file mounts /var/lib/postgresql for PostgreSQL 18; coverage measures child processes itself ( patch = ["subprocess"] ) now that pytest-cov 7 does not. Pull requests opened by Dependabot are exempt from the Made-With: provenance check (it cannot add the trailer); Conventional Commit checking still applies. Rewrote the examples to behave like real use: requests and curl against a running API, a real MCP stdio client and server, and a stdlib webhook receiver with a sender, plus examples/up.sh and down.sh to run the stack. The example tests run them against real sockets. Documentation overhaul: README, getting started, interfaces reference, architecture, troubleshooting, testing, contributing, agent guidance and llms.txt . The release workflow can be started by hand for an existing tag ( workflow_dispatch ), and the guard now verifies the commit of the tag being released instead of the commit that started the run. CI can be started by hand. 0.1.0a1 ¶ Established the orphan FOSS package and initial domain boundaries. Recorded the vibey integration boundary and fallback adapter decision. Added fail-closed security adapters: API key authentication, per-address and per-key rate limiting, timestamped webhook signatures with replay defence, an outbound URL policy that blocks SSRF, path confinement, and upload inspection. The REST API now requires a guard. ApplicationError stays immutable but no longer blocks __traceback__ , which crashed it when raised on a worker thread. Added observability: JSON logs with secret masking, a correlation id carried from request to queue to worker to webhook, request counters, /health/live , /health/ready and an authenticated Prometheus /metrics , service latency tracing, crash alert hooks and a worker heartbeat with a silence watchdog. Webhook dispatch now isolates failures per event, counts attempts, and dead-letters with an alert after repeated failure. Previously one rejected or unreachable destination blocked every event behind it. The outbox table gained dead_at . Added ei serve api and ei serve worker , a Dockerfile, and examples/docker-compose.yml (Postgres, RabbitMQ, API, worker) with a smoke test. All settings fail closed and the compose file has no default credentials. Added a worker that consumes jobs from RabbitMQ, runs each stage, records it in the ledger and enqueues the next, with malformed and failing jobs dead-lettered. StartPipeline now tells a job which stages follow it. Fixed the RabbitMQ publisher silently dropping messages when the queue had not been declared yet. Added release automation: a tag-triggered workflow that guards the tag, builds and installs the real artifacts, attests build provenance, creates the GitHub release with checksums and an SBOM, and publishes to PyPI behind an approval gate. See docs/RELEASING.md . The version is now defined once, in __version__ , and read by pyproject.toml , ei --version and the API. Builds are reproducible. The wheel now ships py.typed , and the source distribution no longer includes local tool caches, git hooks or agent configuration. Added project URLs, classifiers and an SDK README. ei serve without the api and runtime extras now says which extras to install instead of failing with a traceback. Pinned every GitHub Action to a commit SHA, restricted job permissions, and added actionlint and zizmor checks.

docs.text: Established the orphan FOSS package and initial domain boundaries. Recorded the vibey integration boundary and fallback adapter decision. Added fail-closed security adapters: API key authentication, per-address and per-key rate limiting, timestamped webhook signatures with replay defence, an outbound URL policy that blocks SSRF, path confinement, and upload inspection. The REST API now requires a guard. ApplicationError stays immutable but no longer blocks __traceback__ , which crashed it when raised on a worker thread. Added observability: JSON logs with secret masking, a correlation id carried from request to queue to worker to webhook, request counters, /health/live , /health/ready and an authenticated Prometheus /metrics , service latency tracing, crash alert hooks and a worker heartbeat with a silence watchdog. Webhook dispatch now isolates failures per event, counts attempts, and dead-letters with an alert after repeated failure. Previously one rejected or unreachable destination blocked every event behind it. The outbox table gained dead_at . Added ei serve api and ei serve worker , a Dockerfile, and examples/docker-compose.yml (Postgres, RabbitMQ, API, worker) with a smoke test. All settings fail closed and the compose file has no default credentials. Added a worker that consumes jobs from RabbitMQ, runs each stage, records it in the ledger and enqueues the next, with malformed and failing jobs dead-lettered. StartPipeline now tells a job which stages follow it. Fixed the RabbitMQ publisher silently dropping messages when the queue had not been declared yet. Added release automation: a tag-triggered workflow that guards the tag, builds and installs the real artifacts, attests build provenance, creates the GitHub release with checksums and an SBOM, and publishes to PyPI behind an approval gate. See docs/RELEASING.md . The version is now defined once, in __version__ , and read by pyproject.toml , ei --version and the API. Builds are reproducible. The wheel now ships py.typed , and the source distribution no longer includes local tool caches, git hooks or agent configuration. Added project URLs, classifiers and an SDK README. ei serve without the api and runtime extras now says which extras to install instead of failing with a traceback. Pinned every GitHub Action to a commit SHA, restricted job permissions, and added actionlint and zizmor checks.

docs.text: Compatibility: what is promised, and how a change to it is caught ¶ BLUF: Ten public contracts are frozen: each has a snapshot file, and a test fails the moment the real thing differs from its snapshot. Before 1.0.0 a minor version may still break one, and the changelog will say so. From 1.0.0 a changed snapshot needs a reason, a changelog entry and, if it is not compatible, a new schema version. The package follows ADR 0004 . Before 1.0.0 a minor version may break any contract below, and the changelog says so. What exists today is the guard that makes a break visible: every contract in this page is committed as a snapshot in tests/contracts/snapshots/ , and a test fails the moment the real thing differs from it. From 1.0.0 a snapshot that changes is a change that needs a reason, a changelog entry and, if it is not compatible, a new schema version. How a promise is kept by a file ¶ Daniel: I am building on the REST API. How do I know you will not rename a field next month? Professor Feynman: How does a locksmith know a new key will still open your door? Daniel: He keeps the old key and cuts the new one against it. Professor Feynman: A snapshot is the old key. The shape of every contract is written to a file. A test regenerates the shape from the code and compares. If someone renames your field, the comparison fails and the build goes red before it reaches you. Daniel: They could just regenerate the file and commit it. Professor Feynman: They could, and then the change is sitting in the pull request as a diff with a name on it. That is the point: a break cannot happen by accident, only on purpose and in plain sight. The limit: the file records the shape, not the meaning. A field that keeps its name and changes what it means would slip past. Daniel: So I am protected from accidents, the changelog tells me about decisions, and before 1.0 I should still pin a version. The contracts ¶ Contract Where it is defined Snapshot ( tests/contracts/snapshots/ ) The brief a run starts from contracts/brief/v1 ( BookBriefV1 ) brief_v1_schema.json A book's config ( books/<slug>.toml ) contracts/book_config/v1 ( BookConfigV1 ) book_config_v1_schema.json A run's summary contracts/run/v1 ( RunSummaryV1 ) run_summary_v1_schema.json The queued job contracts/job_message.py ( JobMessage ) job_message_v1_schema.json The REST API the OpenAPI document the stack serves ( /openapi.json ) rest_openapi.json , rest_error_shapes.json Webhooks: the envelope, the event catalogue, the headers, the signature contracts/webhook/v1 ( WebhookEventV1 ) webhook_v1.json The command line the ei parser (every command, option, choice and default) cli_command_tree.json The SDK engineering_influence_sdk (both clients: every public method and its signature) sdk_public_surface.json The MCP tools the tools of ei serve mcp and their arguments mcp_tools.json Error codes ( RUN_NOT_FOUND ) and the issue codes a run records ( stage-failed ) the literals in the source error_codes.json , issue_codes.json Every versioned document carries a schema_version (the REST API carries it in the path, /v1/ ). A document with no schema_version is read as version 1, so what was written before the field existed still loads. A different version is refused, never guessed at. A new major version runs beside the old one for at least one minor release. The snapshots leave out prose: a docstring, a help line and a name generated from a function (an OpenAPI summary or operationId ) are documentation, so rewording them is not a change to the contract. What counts as compatible ¶ Compatible (a snapshot changes, the version does not): A new optional field in a brief, a config, a run summary or an event's data ; a new event type; a receiver must ignore what it does not know. A new REST path, a new optional query or body field, a new response field. A new ei command or option (with a default that keeps the old behaviour), a new SDK method, a new MCP tool. A new error code or issue code. Breaking (needs a new schema version, or a major release after 1.0.0): Removing or renaming anything above, changing a type, making an optional field required, or narrowing what a field accepts. Changing what a command exits with, what a status or code means, or how a signature is computed. Removing a documented error code a client may be handling. Changing a contract on purpose ¶ Make the change. The matching test fails and says which contract moved. Run EI_UPDATE_CONTRACTS=1 uv run pytest tests/contracts , read the diff of the snapshot, and commit it with the change. Add a changelog fragment ( changelog.d/ ) that says whether the change is compatible. A breaking change under a stable version is also listed under "Deprecated" for a minor release first, and keeps working meanwhile (ADR 0004). What is not promised ¶ ACP ( ei acp , the Agent Client Protocol session surface) has tests but no snapshot and is not yet a stable contract. The pipeline stages thesis , book , novel , screenplay , hub , spokes , distribution and publish and the /v1/pipelines route, the SDK's start_pipeline and the MCP start_pipeline tool: the stage placeholders are experimental and outside the stable contract (ADR 0003). They are in the snapshots only so that a change to them is seen. The files a run writes ( audit.md , build/… , the stage outputs): quality-report.json and publication-report.json carry a schema_version but are not snapshotted yet. Their documented fields are the intent; do not parse the rest. Python imports. Only the SDK's two clients are public Python API. Everything under engineering_influence moved when the onion layers were introduced and may move again; programs should use the REST API, the SDK, the CLI or MCP. Prompt templates are versioned and pinned separately ( docs/PROMPTS.md ), and are not an interface. Webhooks are not delivered yet. The envelope, the catalogue, the headers and the signature are frozen so that a receiver written now keeps working; the worker records the events but no service sends them ( docs/CONFIGURATION.md ). Two error shapes. What the application refuses is {code, message, retryable} ; a request the framework cannot read (a missing field, a wrong type) is FastAPI's {detail: [...]} , which the OpenAPI document declares as HTTPValidationError . CLI exit codes are documented per command in docs/INTERACTIONS.md but are not in the snapshot.
