docs.text: Configuration ¶ BLUF: Settings come from environment variables, a few files those variables name, and command-line flags. Every security setting fails closed: a missing or weak value stops the process instead of opening it. To write one book you need only an author profile. To run the stack you need a database URL, a broker URL and API keys. Every EI_* variable the code reads is in one index on this page. Book configuration is intentionally separate from author profile configuration. The public package accepts a project title, slug, governing postulates and the stages to run. Target formats and an autonomy policy are planned, not accepted yet. Private books repositories may add a profile that fills the governing-postulates slot without changing the public domain model. The book config, the brief and the run summary schemas are versioned under contracts/ and frozen by snapshot tests ( COMPATIBILITY.md ). Why a missing setting stops everything ¶ Daniel: I left the API keys blank to try it quickly and the server refused to start. Most tools just run open in that case. Why so strict? Professor Feynman: What does a shop do when the lock on the front door is broken? Daniel: A careless one props the door open. A careful one stays shut until the lock is fixed. Professor Feynman: That is fail closed. An unset key could mean 'I forgot' or 'I want no security', and a program cannot tell which. So this one assumes you forgot, and stays shut. It also tells you which variable is wrong, and never prints the value. Daniel: Annoying on day one. Professor Feynman: And it is the reason there is no day when you discover the door was open all along. The picture has a limit: a closed shop loses customers, and a stopped worker loses time. So a setting that is merely optional, like the log level, has a default instead. Daniel: Required things stop the process, optional things have defaults, and the error names the variable. I will look mine up in the index. Security settings ¶ Every security control fails closed: a missing or weak setting stops the service instead of opening it. Setting Meaning EI_API_KEYS Comma-separated API keys, each at least 24 characters. Required: the REST API cannot be built without a guard, and the guard cannot be built without a key. Rate limits TokenBucketRateLimiter(burst, per_second) . A client address is limited before its key is compared, then each key has its own budget. Webhook secret Passed to WebhookDelivery.deliver and WebhookSigner ; read it with EnvSecretProvider().require(name) so an absent secret raises SECRET_MISSING (HTTP 503). Webhook tolerance SignedRequestVerifier(tolerance_seconds=300) : deliveries older or newer than this are refused. Clients send the key as Authorization: Bearer <key> (what the SDK does) or X-API-Key: <key> . Webhook signature (v1) ¶ X-Engineering-Influence-Signature: v1=<hex> is HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<timestamp>." + body) , and X-Engineering-Influence-Timestamp carries the Unix time. Verify the raw bytes, not re-serialised JSON. A receiver must check the signature, the timestamp window and replays, in that order: SignedRequestVerifier does. Outbound destinations ¶ WebhookDelivery requires an OutboundUrlPolicyInterface . PublicHttpsUrlPolicy allows only https URLs without embedded credentials whose every resolved address is publicly routable, which blocks loopback, private ranges and cloud metadata addresses. It resolves the name when called, so webhook delivery is still open to DNS rebinding ; route deliveries to untrusted URLs through an egress proxy as well. fetch_url and remote MCP servers do not have this gap: they go through PublicHttpsUrlPinner , which resolves once and connects to the address it checked. Not covered yet ¶ No upload or inbound-webhook HTTP route exists, so AttachmentUploadInspector and SignedRequestVerifier are building blocks that no endpoint uses yet. The MCP server (stdio) and the CLI are local processes and are not authenticated; do not expose them on a network. Request body size limits, TLS termination, and API key rotation are deployment concerns for the reverse proxy and are not implemented here. AttachmentUploadInspector and ConfinedPathGuard exist but no route uses them yet, because the service accepts no uploads. Observability ¶ Wire these adapters in the process entry point. Nothing is global except what vibey_bootstrap itself keeps (counters, latency statistics, alert state). Concern Use JSON logs JsonLoggingConfigurator(level).configure() : one JSON line per record on stderr, secrets masked, correlation_id on every line. Safe to call twice. Correlation ContextVarCorrelation plus CorrelatingQueue(queue, correlation) on the API side and CorrelatedPhaseHandler(handler, correlation) on the worker side. Request metrics ApiObservability(readiness, metrics, correlation) passed to ApiApplication . Health ReadinessProbe((TcpHealthCheck("postgres", host, 5432), TcpHealthCheck("rabbitmq", host, 5672))) . ToolchainHealthCheck() exists but the API does not add it, since the runtime image has no TeX. Service spans TracedStartPipeline , TracedRunPhase , TracedDispatchOutbox wrap the services. Crash alerts ProcessCrashHooks().install() , once per process. Worker liveness WorkerHeartbeat(metrics, alerts).start() , .record_progress() per job, .stop() . Endpoints ¶ Path Auth Purpose GET /health/live none Always {"status": "alive"} while the process runs. GET /health/ready none 200 {"status": "ready"} or 503 {"status": "unavailable"} . It never names the failing dependency; that is in /metrics and the logs. GET /metrics API key Prometheus text format. Give the scraper a bearer token. Correlation ¶ Every request gets one id. It is the trace id of an inbound traceparent , else a well-formed X-Request-ID (8 to 64 characters of A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ - ), else a new random one. Anything else is replaced, never echoed, because the id lands in every log line. The id is returned in X-Request-ID , copied into each queued job's correlation_id (and a traceparent when it is a 32-hex trace id), restored by the worker, and sent on outbound webhooks as X-Request-ID and traceparent . Alerts and dead letters ¶ A webhook that fails is retried on every dispatch and counted. After max_attempts (default 5) it is dead-lettered, which stops retries, increments webhook.dead_lettered and raises an error alert. One bad event never blocks the events behind it. vibey_bootstrap sends only CRITICAL alerts at once, holds ERROR and WARN in a digest that nothing here drains, and only records alerts when no recipients are configured. So BootstrapAlertDispatcher always writes the alert to the log first, at its own level. Alert on those log lines ( message starting with alert: , fields alert_severity and dedup_key ) rather than relying on mail. The outbox table gained a dead_at column before migrations existed. ei db upgrade adopts an existing table as it is and does not add the column, so recreate any database created before that change. What the observability does not tell you ¶ Log masking is by field name. A secret written into the message text itself is not masked, so pass values as extra fields. Counters and latencies are per process. Scrape every replica. ToolchainHealthCheck and TcpHealthCheck check presence and reachability, not that the dependency is healthy. There is no LLM-runner health check and no alert on budget exhaustion; a budget stop shows as a run awaiting consent. ei serve api and ei serve worker build this wiring for you. If you embed the application in your own process, wire the adapters above yourself. Running the stack ¶ ei serve api and ei serve worker read their settings from the environment. A missing or invalid value prints which variable is wrong and exits with status 2; it never prints a traceback, which could carry a connection string. Variable Needed by Meaning EI_DATABASE_URL both SQLAlchemy URL, for example postgresql+psycopg://user:pw@host:5432/db . Required. EI_RABBITMQ_URL both amqp://user:pw@host:5672/ . Required. EI_API_KEYS API Comma-separated keys, each at least 24 characters. Required: with none, the API will not start. EI_QUEUE_NAME both Job queue name. Default engineering-influence.jobs ; the dead-letter queue is that name plus .dead . EI_HOST , EI_PORT API Default 127.0.0.1 and 8000 . A bare run is never reachable from the network. EI_LOG_LEVEL both DEBUG to CRITICAL . Default INFO . EI_RATE_BURST , EI_RATE_PER_SECOND API Token-bucket limits, default 30 and 10. EI_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_MICRO_USD API, ei run , MCP, ACP The most any one run may be given, in micro-dollars, at its start and after every grant. Not set by default (no ceiling). A bigger brief, or a grant that would take a cap over it, is refused with BUDGET_ABOVE_LIMIT (HTTP 422) before anything is saved or queued. EI_MAX_OUTSTANDING_BUDGET_MICRO_USD API, ei run , MCP, ACP The most unspent budget all runs may hold together : each unfinished run's cap less what it has spent (a parked or waiting run still counts; a completed, failed or cancelled one does not). Not set by default. A new run or a grant that would take the total over it is refused with OUTSTANDING_BUDGET_EXCEEDED (422). A client that starts many runs, or is granted more again and again, runs out of room instead of out of money. A check and the save that follows it are one locked step, so many requests at once to one API or MCP process cannot each pass against the same total; two processes (the API and a command line, say) each hold their own lock, so across processes it is a check with a window of a few milliseconds. ei book create runs on your own machine and is not held to it. EI_MCP_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_MICRO_USD MCP server The most a run started over MCP may be given, in micro-dollars (default 5,000,000, five dollars). A bigger brief is refused with BUDGET_ABOVE_LIMIT . It bounds one run, not how many an agent starts. EI_MCP_ALLOW_SPEND MCP server 1 , true or yes lets ei serve mcp offer grant_run and deny_run , so an agent can answer a run's request for more budget. Off by default: an agent can then start, watch, resume, cancel and read runs, but cannot raise a run's cap. Every variable, and where it is described ¶ A test ( tests/unit/test_docs_match_code.py ) fails when the code reads an EI_* variable that is not in this index, or when this index names one nothing uses. The two compose only rows are read by Docker Compose, not by the program. Variable For Described in EI_ALLOW_PAID lets ei evaluate spend money; without it the command refuses EVALUATION.md BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY (not an EI_ variable) a Brave Search key, the backup search RESEARCH.md EI_API_KEYS the API's keys Security settings EI_API_PORT (compose only) the host port the API is published on, default 8000 examples/.env.example , TROUBLESHOOTING.md EI_AUTHOR_PROFILE the author's own details file; a run reads it only when this names it The author profile EI_BUILD_STRICT_RELEASE makes any release warning fail a run's build stage Limits to know EI_DATABASE_URL the database Running the stack EI_EVAL_JUDGE_PROFILE the model profile that judges books in ei evaluate EVALUATION.md EI_HOST , EI_PORT where the API listens Running the stack EI_LOCAL_MODEL , EI_LOCAL_URL the free local model's name and address LOCAL_MODEL.md EI_LOG_LEVEL log verbosity Running the stack EI_MAX_OUTSTANDING_BUDGET_MICRO_USD the most unspent budget all runs may hold together Running the stack EI_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_MICRO_USD the most any one run may be given Running the stack EI_MCP_ALLOW_SPEND lets ei serve mcp offer grant_run and deny_run Running the stack EI_MCP_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_MICRO_USD the most a run started over MCP may be given Running the stack EI_MODEL_CATALOG , EI_MODEL_PROFILES the model price list and the profiles file MODEL_PROFILES.md EI_PLUGIN_LOCK the plugin lock file The plugin lock EI_QUEUE_NAME the job queue's name Running the stack EI_RABBITMQ_URL the broker Running the stack EI_RATE_BURST , EI_RATE_PER_SECOND the API's rate limit Running the stack EI_SEARXNG_PORT (compose only) the host port of the local search container, default 8888 A free local web search EI_SEARXNG_URL the SearXNG address the research stage searches through A free local web search EI_SKILL_LOCK the skill lock file The skill lock EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR what writes a run's stages: local , model or deterministic Limits to know EI_STAGE_MODEL_PROFILE the profile the model executor uses MODEL_PROFILES.md EI_TOOL_LOCK the tool lock file The tool lock cp examples/.env.example examples/.env # fill in the three blank values docker compose -f examples/docker-compose.yml --env-file examples/.env up -d --build --wait The database schema is created by ei db upgrade , which reads EI_DATABASE_URL and is safe to run again. The compose file runs it once in a migrate service that the API and the worker wait for. Outside compose, run it yourself before starting either process; they check the schema revision at start-up and exit with the database schema is not at the latest revision if it is not current. Upgrade before you roll out a new release, then start the new processes. examples/compose_smoke.sh does all of this with throwaway credentials, runs a two-stage pipeline, checks that a malformed message is dead-lettered, and tears the stack down. It needs Docker and curl . The compose file has no default credentials and refuses to start without them. Ports are published on 127.0.0.1 only, and the containers run as a non-root user with a read-only filesystem and no capabilities. What the worker does ¶ For each pipeline.<stage> job it runs the phase, appends phase.completed to the ledger, and enqueues the next stage, or appends pipeline.completed after the last. A human gate, or an automatic gate that rejects, appends gate.awaiting and stops the pipeline there. For each run.advance job (payload {run_id, stage, attempt} ) it advances a book run one stage: it executes the run's current stage, saves the run, and queues the next stage. Redelivered messages are safe. A message for a stage the run already passed is skipped, a transient failure re-queues the stage with the next attempt up to three, running out of credit parks the run on its stage, and any other failure ends the run with a blocking issue. Every change to the run is a compare-and-swap, so two overlapping deliveries cannot overwrite each other. The worker routes by the prefix before the first dot: pipeline.* and run.* are handled, and any other kind is dead-lettered. A run that parks for lack of credit stays parked: further run.advance messages for it are skipped until ei run resume RUN_ID moves it back to running and queues its stage. ei run cancel RUN_ID ends a run for good; a stage already executing is not interrupted, but its result cannot be stored, so the run stays cancelled and nothing more is queued. Both commands change the same stored run the worker does, through the same compare-and-swap, and refuse a run that is already completed or failed. A job that is malformed, or that fails, is rejected without requeue and lands in the .dead queue, with an alert for failures. Nothing retries it automatically: inspect it and republish it by hand. Stopping the worker finishes the job in flight first. A failed run carries one blocking issue that says why: stage-failed (a failure that cannot be retried), retries-exhausted (three transient failures in a row) or budget-exceeded (the journal holds more than the cap). Limits to know ¶ A run starts from ei run create BRIEF.TOML . It saves the run and queues its first stage on the broker, and the worker does the stages, as resume does. A run can also be started with POST /v1/runs , the SDK's create_run , the MCP create_run tool, or ei book create (in one process); ei run runs lists them. The worker's default is a free local model. EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR is local unless set: an open-source model ( gpt-oss:20b , Apache 2.0) on this machine through Ollama, no key, no cost, and a SearXNG at http://127.0.0.1:8888 for research. Nothing is contacted when the worker starts; LOCAL_MODEL.md says how to set it up and check it ( ei doctor --local ) and how to point at another model ( EI_LOCAL_MODEL , EI_LOCAL_URL ). deterministic is the offline placeholder, which writes <stage>.md from the brief's idea at no cost and calls no model; the example compose stack uses it because a container cannot reach the host's 127.0.0.1 . With EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR=model a model of your own does the stages instead, and the worker refuses to start unless EI_STAGE_MODEL_PROFILE (a profile's name), EI_MODEL_PROFILES and EI_MODEL_CATALOG (the files ei doctor --models checks, see MODEL_PROFILES.md ) are set, the profile exists, a price is in force today, and its key is available. A profile file being present never switches it on, because this spends money. Non-fiction and novel runs have stages from the brief to a built book ( BOOKS_AND_KDP.md ). An answer that is refused, cut off or empty stops the run, and so does an outline that cannot be read as numbered chapters ( OUTLINE_INVALID ; see PROMPTS.md ). Nothing has been run against a live provider. EI_EVAL_JUDGE_PROFILE (required by ei evaluate ): the name of the profile, in EI_MODEL_PROFILES , of the model that scores the evaluation's books. It is named separately; nothing stops you naming the writer's own profile, so do not. ei evaluate refuses to start without it ( EVALUATION_JUDGE_REQUIRED ) and spends only when EI_ALLOW_PAID=1 ( EVALUATION.md ). EI_BUILD_STRICT_RELEASE (optional, default off): 1 , true or yes makes a run's build stage build a strict release, so any readiness warning (for example a missing price or its source and date) fails the run. Off, those are warnings in the run's quality-report.json . The build needs the TeX worker image ( WORKER_IMAGE.md ). Web search for the research stage. The research stage gives the model two tools, web_search and fetch_url , so a model-backed run needs a search. Set EI_SEARXNG_URL to a SearXNG instance (free; examples/searxng/ runs one locally, see below) and it is tried first. Set BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY and Brave is the backup: it is asked only when SearXNG fails, is refused, is rate-limited or finds nothing, so a query reaches Brave only then. With only one of the two set, that one is the search. With neither, the process stops at start ( STAGE_SEARCH_NOT_CONFIGURED ) before anything is spent. A search sends the query to the instance (which sends it on to its engines) or to Brave. fetch_url reads public https pages only. Neither search adapter has been run against a live service, and nothing here has touched the live internet. Retries are immediate. A transient failure is re-queued with no delay, because the queue port has none yet. The runner and gate are placeholders. DeterministicRunner returns a fixed line of text and NonEmptyArtifactGate accepts anything non-blank. They let the whole pipeline run offline; a model-backed runner and rubric gates implement the same interfaces. Delivery is at least once. A worker that dies between writing the ledger and acknowledging the job runs it again and records the stage twice. Nothing resolves a human gate yet. There is no endpoint for it, so a pipeline that reaches one stays parked. No webhook is emitted. The outbox, signing and dispatch exist, but no service creates outbox intents, and the worker does not run the dispatcher. The read API covers book runs only. GET /v1/runs/{id} and ei run status show a run; pipeline progress is still visible only in the ledger table and the logs. The base images are tags, not digests , and the worker has no container healthcheck; it logs a heartbeat and raises a critical alert if it stalls. A free local web search (SearXNG) ¶ examples/searxng/ runs SearXNG on your machine, so the research stage can search without an account or a key. It is published on 127.0.0.1 only, refuses to start without a secret, and its settings.yml turns on the json format the adapter asks for (without it SearXNG answers 403). export SEARXNG_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" docker compose -f examples/searxng/docker-compose.yml up -d --wait export EI_SEARXNG_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8888 What is and is not checked: the compose file is validated by docker compose config and its settings are pinned by tests, and it has been started once by hand: the container went healthy and the adapter ran against it for real (queries, validation, and the 403 a default instance gives when json is not enabled). That is not run by the project's tests or CI. The image is pinned by digest to the build it was tested with (2026-11-21), so it does not get SearXNG updates until someone moves the digest: pull a newer image, check a search works against it, then replace the digest in the compose file. SearXNG passes your queries to the public search engines it is set to use, and those engines can throttle or block a local instance, which is what the Brave backup is for. The port is EI_SEARXNG_PORT (default 8888). Check that it answers with ei doctor --search (one real search per provider; see RESEARCH.md ). The tool lock (third-party tool servers) ¶ ei tools add , list and verify read and write one lock file: --lock PATH , else EI_TOOL_LOCK , else ei-tools.lock.toml in the current directory. add and verify start the server's code , so run them only on servers you mean to run. Each server is started with a bare environment (see TOOL_LOCK.md ) and, for one look, at most two minutes, 2 GiB of memory and 1 GiB of disk . These are fixed in the command, not settings. A remote server ( add --url ) is contacted, not started: it is held to https and a public address, with a 30-second request limit, and its token is the variable named by --bearer-env , read from the environment when the connection is made. A run reads a lock only when EI_TOOL_LOCK names it (the file in the current directory is not read). Its servers are then started and verified when the stage executor is built, a changed one stops the process ( TOOL_LOCK_MISMATCH ), a named file that does not exist is TOOL_LOCK_MISSING , and a stage is offered only the locked tools the lock grants it ( ei tools grant ). For the life of the process each server may use four hours, 2 GiB of memory and 1 GiB of disk. See TOOL_LOCK.md . The skill lock (installed prompt text) ¶ ei skills add , enable , disable , remove , list and verify read and write one lock file: --lock PATH , else EI_SKILL_LOCK , else ei-skills.lock.toml in the current directory, with the skill files in a skills/ folder beside it. Nothing here starts a process or opens a connection; a skill is text. A run reads a skill lock only when EI_SKILL_LOCK names it (the file in the current directory is not read). Each skill enabled for some stage is read and hashed once when the stage executor is built, before any tool server is started: a skill that changed is SKILL_LOCK_MISMATCH , a named file that does not exist is SKILL_LOCK_MISSING , and a stage's prompt carries only the skills the lock enables for it. A file is at most 64 KiB, a part at most 8,000 characters, and a stage at most four skills; these are fixed in the code, not settings. See SKILLS.md . The plugin lock (installed bundles) ¶ ei plugins show , add , list , verify and remove read and write the plugin lock: --lock PATH , else EI_PLUGIN_LOCK , else ei-plugins.lock.toml in the current directory, with the bundles kept in a plugins/ folder beside it. add , verify and remove also use the skill lock ( --skill-lock , else EI_SKILL_LOCK , else ei-skills.lock.toml ). Nothing here starts a process or opens a connection. A run never reads the plugin lock. It is a record for verify and remove ; what a run may do is in the tool lock and the skill lock. A bundle is at most 512 KiB, with at most 16 servers and 16 skills; these are fixed in the code, not settings. See PLUGINS.md . ei plugins search INDEX and fetch INDEX NAME take an index that is a file on disk or an https:// address . They are the only commands that can use a network, only for an https:// address, with no setting for a proxy or a credential. An index may be up to 512 KiB and list 500 plugins, a download is at most 512 KiB, and a request has 30 seconds; these are fixed in the code. Downloading needs the runtime extra ( pip install 'engineering-influence[runtime]' ), which a local index file does not. A run never contacts a marketplace. The author profile (your own details) ¶ A book's title page, copyright page and about-the-author page need things only the author can say. They go in a small TOML file you keep yourself, outside this repository, and a run reads it only when EI_AUTHOR_PROFILE names it (a file in the current directory is not read). The assemble stage writes it into the book's config; it is never sent to a model. author = "Ann Author" # required publisher = "Pub House" # required edition = "First Edition" # required; has to say "Edition" author_bio = "Ann writes." # required; paragraphs allowed year = 2031 # optional website = "https://pub.example" # optional email = "ann@pub.example" # optional isbn = "978-0-0000-0000-0" # optional ebook_isbn = "978-0-0000-0001-7" # optional dedication = "For you." # optional copyright_notes = "Notes." # optional also_by = ["Earlier Book"] # optional, at most 20 [pricing] # optional; needed for a strict release verified_on = "2026-11-19" # the day you checked the prices (an ISO date) source_url = "https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G201834170" # a page that shows the print costs ebook = 4.99 paperback = 12.99 hardcover = 22.99 # optional; a price here makes the book a KDP hardcover too The prices are yours: a run never invents them. They go into the book's [release.pricing] , which is what a strict release checks ( EI_BUILD_STRICT_RELEASE , or --strict-release on ei book create ). Without a [pricing] table a missing price is a warning in the run's quality-report.json , and a strict release fails. Any other key is refused, a missing file stops the process at start ( AUTHOR_PROFILE_MISSING ), and a bad one stops it with the reason ( AUTHOR_PROFILE_INVALID ). The file is at most 64 KiB. A one-line field is at most 200 characters with no space at either end; author_bio , dedication and copyright_notes are at most 4,000; year is 1000 to 9999; email has an @ and no space; an ISBN is digits and hyphens ending in a digit or X ; also_by has at most 20 titles; and no field may hold a control or invisible character. [pricing] needs verified_on (an ISO date), source_url (http or https), and ebook and paperback above zero; hardcover is optional. Without a profile the assembled book loads but does not build, and the build says which of these is missing. Em and en dashes are refused in non-fiction when the book is built, and the profile is not rewritten, so leave them out of your own text.
docs.title: Configuration

docs.text: BLUF: Settings come from environment variables, a few files those variables name, and command-line flags. Every security setting fails closed: a missing or weak value stops the process instead of opening it. To write one book you need only an author profile. To run the stack you need a database URL, a broker URL and API keys. Every EI_* variable the code reads is in one index on this page. Book configuration is intentionally separate from author profile configuration. The public package accepts a project title, slug, governing postulates and the stages to run. Target formats and an autonomy policy are planned, not accepted yet. Private books repositories may add a profile that fills the governing-postulates slot without changing the public domain model. The book config, the brief and the run summary schemas are versioned under contracts/ and frozen by snapshot tests ( COMPATIBILITY.md ).
docs.title: Configuration

docs.text: Daniel: I left the API keys blank to try it quickly and the server refused to start. Most tools just run open in that case. Why so strict? Professor Feynman: What does a shop do when the lock on the front door is broken? Daniel: A careless one props the door open. A careful one stays shut until the lock is fixed. Professor Feynman: That is fail closed. An unset key could mean 'I forgot' or 'I want no security', and a program cannot tell which. So this one assumes you forgot, and stays shut. It also tells you which variable is wrong, and never prints the value. Daniel: Annoying on day one. Professor Feynman: And it is the reason there is no day when you discover the door was open all along. The picture has a limit: a closed shop loses customers, and a stopped worker loses time. So a setting that is merely optional, like the log level, has a default instead. Daniel: Required things stop the process, optional things have defaults, and the error names the variable. I will look mine up in the index.
docs.title: Why a missing setting stops everything

docs.text: Every security control fails closed: a missing or weak setting stops the service instead of opening it. Setting Meaning EI_API_KEYS Comma-separated API keys, each at least 24 characters. Required: the REST API cannot be built without a guard, and the guard cannot be built without a key. Rate limits TokenBucketRateLimiter(burst, per_second) . A client address is limited before its key is compared, then each key has its own budget. Webhook secret Passed to WebhookDelivery.deliver and WebhookSigner ; read it with EnvSecretProvider().require(name) so an absent secret raises SECRET_MISSING (HTTP 503). Webhook tolerance SignedRequestVerifier(tolerance_seconds=300) : deliveries older or newer than this are refused. Clients send the key as Authorization: Bearer <key> (what the SDK does) or X-API-Key: <key> .
docs.title: Security settings

docs.text: X-Engineering-Influence-Signature: v1=<hex> is HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<timestamp>." + body) , and X-Engineering-Influence-Timestamp carries the Unix time. Verify the raw bytes, not re-serialised JSON. A receiver must check the signature, the timestamp window and replays, in that order: SignedRequestVerifier does.
docs.title: Webhook signature (v1)

docs.text: WebhookDelivery requires an OutboundUrlPolicyInterface . PublicHttpsUrlPolicy allows only https URLs without embedded credentials whose every resolved address is publicly routable, which blocks loopback, private ranges and cloud metadata addresses. It resolves the name when called, so webhook delivery is still open to DNS rebinding ; route deliveries to untrusted URLs through an egress proxy as well. fetch_url and remote MCP servers do not have this gap: they go through PublicHttpsUrlPinner , which resolves once and connects to the address it checked.
docs.title: Outbound destinations

docs.text: No upload or inbound-webhook HTTP route exists, so AttachmentUploadInspector and SignedRequestVerifier are building blocks that no endpoint uses yet. The MCP server (stdio) and the CLI are local processes and are not authenticated; do not expose them on a network. Request body size limits, TLS termination, and API key rotation are deployment concerns for the reverse proxy and are not implemented here. AttachmentUploadInspector and ConfinedPathGuard exist but no route uses them yet, because the service accepts no uploads.
docs.title: Not covered yet

docs.text: Wire these adapters in the process entry point. Nothing is global except what vibey_bootstrap itself keeps (counters, latency statistics, alert state). Concern Use JSON logs JsonLoggingConfigurator(level).configure() : one JSON line per record on stderr, secrets masked, correlation_id on every line. Safe to call twice. Correlation ContextVarCorrelation plus CorrelatingQueue(queue, correlation) on the API side and CorrelatedPhaseHandler(handler, correlation) on the worker side. Request metrics ApiObservability(readiness, metrics, correlation) passed to ApiApplication . Health ReadinessProbe((TcpHealthCheck("postgres", host, 5432), TcpHealthCheck("rabbitmq", host, 5672))) . ToolchainHealthCheck() exists but the API does not add it, since the runtime image has no TeX. Service spans TracedStartPipeline , TracedRunPhase , TracedDispatchOutbox wrap the services. Crash alerts ProcessCrashHooks().install() , once per process. Worker liveness WorkerHeartbeat(metrics, alerts).start() , .record_progress() per job, .stop() .
docs.title: Observability

docs.text: Path Auth Purpose GET /health/live none Always {"status": "alive"} while the process runs. GET /health/ready none 200 {"status": "ready"} or 503 {"status": "unavailable"} . It never names the failing dependency; that is in /metrics and the logs. GET /metrics API key Prometheus text format. Give the scraper a bearer token.
docs.title: Endpoints

docs.text: Every request gets one id. It is the trace id of an inbound traceparent , else a well-formed X-Request-ID (8 to 64 characters of A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ - ), else a new random one. Anything else is replaced, never echoed, because the id lands in every log line. The id is returned in X-Request-ID , copied into each queued job's correlation_id (and a traceparent when it is a 32-hex trace id), restored by the worker, and sent on outbound webhooks as X-Request-ID and traceparent .
docs.title: Correlation

docs.text: A webhook that fails is retried on every dispatch and counted. After max_attempts (default 5) it is dead-lettered, which stops retries, increments webhook.dead_lettered and raises an error alert. One bad event never blocks the events behind it. vibey_bootstrap sends only CRITICAL alerts at once, holds ERROR and WARN in a digest that nothing here drains, and only records alerts when no recipients are configured. So BootstrapAlertDispatcher always writes the alert to the log first, at its own level. Alert on those log lines ( message starting with alert: , fields alert_severity and dedup_key ) rather than relying on mail. The outbox table gained a dead_at column before migrations existed. ei db upgrade adopts an existing table as it is and does not add the column, so recreate any database created before that change.
docs.title: Alerts and dead letters

docs.text: Log masking is by field name. A secret written into the message text itself is not masked, so pass values as extra fields. Counters and latencies are per process. Scrape every replica. ToolchainHealthCheck and TcpHealthCheck check presence and reachability, not that the dependency is healthy. There is no LLM-runner health check and no alert on budget exhaustion; a budget stop shows as a run awaiting consent. ei serve api and ei serve worker build this wiring for you. If you embed the application in your own process, wire the adapters above yourself.
docs.title: What the observability does not tell you

docs.text: ei serve api and ei serve worker read their settings from the environment. A missing or invalid value prints which variable is wrong and exits with status 2; it never prints a traceback, which could carry a connection string. Variable Needed by Meaning EI_DATABASE_URL both SQLAlchemy URL, for example postgresql+psycopg://user:pw@host:5432/db . Required. EI_RABBITMQ_URL both amqp://user:pw@host:5672/ . Required. EI_API_KEYS API Comma-separated keys, each at least 24 characters. Required: with none, the API will not start. EI_QUEUE_NAME both Job queue name. Default engineering-influence.jobs ; the dead-letter queue is that name plus .dead . EI_HOST , EI_PORT API Default 127.0.0.1 and 8000 . A bare run is never reachable from the network. EI_LOG_LEVEL both DEBUG to CRITICAL . Default INFO . EI_RATE_BURST , EI_RATE_PER_SECOND API Token-bucket limits, default 30 and 10. EI_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_MICRO_USD API, ei run , MCP, ACP The most any one run may be given, in micro-dollars, at its start and after every grant. Not set by default (no ceiling). A bigger brief, or a grant that would take a cap over it, is refused with BUDGET_ABOVE_LIMIT (HTTP 422) before anything is saved or queued. EI_MAX_OUTSTANDING_BUDGET_MICRO_USD API, ei run , MCP, ACP The most unspent budget all runs may hold together : each unfinished run's cap less what it has spent (a parked or waiting run still counts; a completed, failed or cancelled one does not). Not set by default. A new run or a grant that would take the total over it is refused with OUTSTANDING_BUDGET_EXCEEDED (422). A client that starts many runs, or is granted more again and again, runs out of room instead of out of money. A check and the save that follows it are one locked step, so many requests at once to one API or MCP process cannot each pass against the same total; two processes (the API and a command line, say) each hold their own lock, so across processes it is a check with a window of a few milliseconds. ei book create runs on your own machine and is not held to it. EI_MCP_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_MICRO_USD MCP server The most a run started over MCP may be given, in micro-dollars (default 5,000,000, five dollars). A bigger brief is refused with BUDGET_ABOVE_LIMIT . It bounds one run, not how many an agent starts. EI_MCP_ALLOW_SPEND MCP server 1 , true or yes lets ei serve mcp offer grant_run and deny_run , so an agent can answer a run's request for more budget. Off by default: an agent can then start, watch, resume, cancel and read runs, but cannot raise a run's cap.
docs.title: Running the stack

docs.text: A test ( tests/unit/test_docs_match_code.py ) fails when the code reads an EI_* variable that is not in this index, or when this index names one nothing uses. The two compose only rows are read by Docker Compose, not by the program. Variable For Described in EI_ALLOW_PAID lets ei evaluate spend money; without it the command refuses EVALUATION.md BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY (not an EI_ variable) a Brave Search key, the backup search RESEARCH.md EI_API_KEYS the API's keys Security settings EI_API_PORT (compose only) the host port the API is published on, default 8000 examples/.env.example , TROUBLESHOOTING.md EI_AUTHOR_PROFILE the author's own details file; a run reads it only when this names it The author profile EI_BUILD_STRICT_RELEASE makes any release warning fail a run's build stage Limits to know EI_DATABASE_URL the database Running the stack EI_EVAL_JUDGE_PROFILE the model profile that judges books in ei evaluate EVALUATION.md EI_HOST , EI_PORT where the API listens Running the stack EI_LOCAL_MODEL , EI_LOCAL_URL the free local model's name and address LOCAL_MODEL.md EI_LOG_LEVEL log verbosity Running the stack EI_MAX_OUTSTANDING_BUDGET_MICRO_USD the most unspent budget all runs may hold together Running the stack EI_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_MICRO_USD the most any one run may be given Running the stack EI_MCP_ALLOW_SPEND lets ei serve mcp offer grant_run and deny_run Running the stack EI_MCP_MAX_RUN_BUDGET_MICRO_USD the most a run started over MCP may be given Running the stack EI_MODEL_CATALOG , EI_MODEL_PROFILES the model price list and the profiles file MODEL_PROFILES.md EI_PLUGIN_LOCK the plugin lock file The plugin lock EI_QUEUE_NAME the job queue's name Running the stack EI_RABBITMQ_URL the broker Running the stack EI_RATE_BURST , EI_RATE_PER_SECOND the API's rate limit Running the stack EI_SEARXNG_PORT (compose only) the host port of the local search container, default 8888 A free local web search EI_SEARXNG_URL the SearXNG address the research stage searches through A free local web search EI_SKILL_LOCK the skill lock file The skill lock EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR what writes a run's stages: local , model or deterministic Limits to know EI_STAGE_MODEL_PROFILE the profile the model executor uses MODEL_PROFILES.md EI_TOOL_LOCK the tool lock file The tool lock cp examples/.env.example examples/.env # fill in the three blank values docker compose -f examples/docker-compose.yml --env-file examples/.env up -d --build --wait The database schema is created by ei db upgrade , which reads EI_DATABASE_URL and is safe to run again. The compose file runs it once in a migrate service that the API and the worker wait for. Outside compose, run it yourself before starting either process; they check the schema revision at start-up and exit with the database schema is not at the latest revision if it is not current. Upgrade before you roll out a new release, then start the new processes. examples/compose_smoke.sh does all of this with throwaway credentials, runs a two-stage pipeline, checks that a malformed message is dead-lettered, and tears the stack down. It needs Docker and curl . The compose file has no default credentials and refuses to start without them. Ports are published on 127.0.0.1 only, and the containers run as a non-root user with a read-only filesystem and no capabilities.
docs.title: Every variable, and where it is described

docs.text: For each pipeline.<stage> job it runs the phase, appends phase.completed to the ledger, and enqueues the next stage, or appends pipeline.completed after the last. A human gate, or an automatic gate that rejects, appends gate.awaiting and stops the pipeline there. For each run.advance job (payload {run_id, stage, attempt} ) it advances a book run one stage: it executes the run's current stage, saves the run, and queues the next stage. Redelivered messages are safe. A message for a stage the run already passed is skipped, a transient failure re-queues the stage with the next attempt up to three, running out of credit parks the run on its stage, and any other failure ends the run with a blocking issue. Every change to the run is a compare-and-swap, so two overlapping deliveries cannot overwrite each other. The worker routes by the prefix before the first dot: pipeline.* and run.* are handled, and any other kind is dead-lettered. A run that parks for lack of credit stays parked: further run.advance messages for it are skipped until ei run resume RUN_ID moves it back to running and queues its stage. ei run cancel RUN_ID ends a run for good; a stage already executing is not interrupted, but its result cannot be stored, so the run stays cancelled and nothing more is queued. Both commands change the same stored run the worker does, through the same compare-and-swap, and refuse a run that is already completed or failed. A job that is malformed, or that fails, is rejected without requeue and lands in the .dead queue, with an alert for failures. Nothing retries it automatically: inspect it and republish it by hand. Stopping the worker finishes the job in flight first. A failed run carries one blocking issue that says why: stage-failed (a failure that cannot be retried), retries-exhausted (three transient failures in a row) or budget-exceeded (the journal holds more than the cap).
docs.title: What the worker does

docs.text: A run starts from ei run create BRIEF.TOML . It saves the run and queues its first stage on the broker, and the worker does the stages, as resume does. A run can also be started with POST /v1/runs , the SDK's create_run , the MCP create_run tool, or ei book create (in one process); ei run runs lists them. The worker's default is a free local model. EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR is local unless set: an open-source model ( gpt-oss:20b , Apache 2.0) on this machine through Ollama, no key, no cost, and a SearXNG at http://127.0.0.1:8888 for research. Nothing is contacted when the worker starts; LOCAL_MODEL.md says how to set it up and check it ( ei doctor --local ) and how to point at another model ( EI_LOCAL_MODEL , EI_LOCAL_URL ). deterministic is the offline placeholder, which writes <stage>.md from the brief's idea at no cost and calls no model; the example compose stack uses it because a container cannot reach the host's 127.0.0.1 . With EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR=model a model of your own does the stages instead, and the worker refuses to start unless EI_STAGE_MODEL_PROFILE (a profile's name), EI_MODEL_PROFILES and EI_MODEL_CATALOG (the files ei doctor --models checks, see MODEL_PROFILES.md ) are set, the profile exists, a price is in force today, and its key is available. A profile file being present never switches it on, because this spends money. Non-fiction and novel runs have stages from the brief to a built book ( BOOKS_AND_KDP.md ). An answer that is refused, cut off or empty stops the run, and so does an outline that cannot be read as numbered chapters ( OUTLINE_INVALID ; see PROMPTS.md ). Nothing has been run against a live provider. EI_EVAL_JUDGE_PROFILE (required by ei evaluate ): the name of the profile, in EI_MODEL_PROFILES , of the model that scores the evaluation's books. It is named separately; nothing stops you naming the writer's own profile, so do not. ei evaluate refuses to start without it ( EVALUATION_JUDGE_REQUIRED ) and spends only when EI_ALLOW_PAID=1 ( EVALUATION.md ). EI_BUILD_STRICT_RELEASE (optional, default off): 1 , true or yes makes a run's build stage build a strict release, so any readiness warning (for example a missing price or its source and date) fails the run. Off, those are warnings in the run's quality-report.json . The build needs the TeX worker image ( WORKER_IMAGE.md ). Web search for the research stage. The research stage gives the model two tools, web_search and fetch_url , so a model-backed run needs a search. Set EI_SEARXNG_URL to a SearXNG instance (free; examples/searxng/ runs one locally, see below) and it is tried first. Set BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY and Brave is the backup: it is asked only when SearXNG fails, is refused, is rate-limited or finds nothing, so a query reaches Brave only then. With only one of the two set, that one is the search. With neither, the process stops at start ( STAGE_SEARCH_NOT_CONFIGURED ) before anything is spent. A search sends the query to the instance (which sends it on to its engines) or to Brave. fetch_url reads public https pages only. Neither search adapter has been run against a live service, and nothing here has touched the live internet. Retries are immediate. A transient failure is re-queued with no delay, because the queue port has none yet. The runner and gate are placeholders. DeterministicRunner returns a fixed line of text and NonEmptyArtifactGate accepts anything non-blank. They let the whole pipeline run offline; a model-backed runner and rubric gates implement the same interfaces. Delivery is at least once. A worker that dies between writing the ledger and acknowledging the job runs it again and records the stage twice. Nothing resolves a human gate yet. There is no endpoint for it, so a pipeline that reaches one stays parked. No webhook is emitted. The outbox, signing and dispatch exist, but no service creates outbox intents, and the worker does not run the dispatcher. The read API covers book runs only. GET /v1/runs/{id} and ei run status show a run; pipeline progress is still visible only in the ledger table and the logs. The base images are tags, not digests , and the worker has no container healthcheck; it logs a heartbeat and raises a critical alert if it stalls.
docs.title: Limits to know

docs.text: examples/searxng/ runs SearXNG on your machine, so the research stage can search without an account or a key. It is published on 127.0.0.1 only, refuses to start without a secret, and its settings.yml turns on the json format the adapter asks for (without it SearXNG answers 403). export SEARXNG_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" docker compose -f examples/searxng/docker-compose.yml up -d --wait export EI_SEARXNG_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8888 What is and is not checked: the compose file is validated by docker compose config and its settings are pinned by tests, and it has been started once by hand: the container went healthy and the adapter ran against it for real (queries, validation, and the 403 a default instance gives when json is not enabled). That is not run by the project's tests or CI. The image is pinned by digest to the build it was tested with (2026-11-21), so it does not get SearXNG updates until someone moves the digest: pull a newer image, check a search works against it, then replace the digest in the compose file. SearXNG passes your queries to the public search engines it is set to use, and those engines can throttle or block a local instance, which is what the Brave backup is for. The port is EI_SEARXNG_PORT (default 8888). Check that it answers with ei doctor --search (one real search per provider; see RESEARCH.md ).
docs.title: A free local web search (SearXNG)

docs.text: ei tools add , list and verify read and write one lock file: --lock PATH , else EI_TOOL_LOCK , else ei-tools.lock.toml in the current directory. add and verify start the server's code , so run them only on servers you mean to run. Each server is started with a bare environment (see TOOL_LOCK.md ) and, for one look, at most two minutes, 2 GiB of memory and 1 GiB of disk . These are fixed in the command, not settings. A remote server ( add --url ) is contacted, not started: it is held to https and a public address, with a 30-second request limit, and its token is the variable named by --bearer-env , read from the environment when the connection is made. A run reads a lock only when EI_TOOL_LOCK names it (the file in the current directory is not read). Its servers are then started and verified when the stage executor is built, a changed one stops the process ( TOOL_LOCK_MISMATCH ), a named file that does not exist is TOOL_LOCK_MISSING , and a stage is offered only the locked tools the lock grants it ( ei tools grant ). For the life of the process each server may use four hours, 2 GiB of memory and 1 GiB of disk. See TOOL_LOCK.md .
docs.title: The tool lock (third-party tool servers)

docs.text: ei skills add , enable , disable , remove , list and verify read and write one lock file: --lock PATH , else EI_SKILL_LOCK , else ei-skills.lock.toml in the current directory, with the skill files in a skills/ folder beside it. Nothing here starts a process or opens a connection; a skill is text. A run reads a skill lock only when EI_SKILL_LOCK names it (the file in the current directory is not read). Each skill enabled for some stage is read and hashed once when the stage executor is built, before any tool server is started: a skill that changed is SKILL_LOCK_MISMATCH , a named file that does not exist is SKILL_LOCK_MISSING , and a stage's prompt carries only the skills the lock enables for it. A file is at most 64 KiB, a part at most 8,000 characters, and a stage at most four skills; these are fixed in the code, not settings. See SKILLS.md .
docs.title: The skill lock (installed prompt text)

docs.text: ei plugins show , add , list , verify and remove read and write the plugin lock: --lock PATH , else EI_PLUGIN_LOCK , else ei-plugins.lock.toml in the current directory, with the bundles kept in a plugins/ folder beside it. add , verify and remove also use the skill lock ( --skill-lock , else EI_SKILL_LOCK , else ei-skills.lock.toml ). Nothing here starts a process or opens a connection. A run never reads the plugin lock. It is a record for verify and remove ; what a run may do is in the tool lock and the skill lock. A bundle is at most 512 KiB, with at most 16 servers and 16 skills; these are fixed in the code, not settings. See PLUGINS.md . ei plugins search INDEX and fetch INDEX NAME take an index that is a file on disk or an https:// address . They are the only commands that can use a network, only for an https:// address, with no setting for a proxy or a credential. An index may be up to 512 KiB and list 500 plugins, a download is at most 512 KiB, and a request has 30 seconds; these are fixed in the code. Downloading needs the runtime extra ( pip install 'engineering-influence[runtime]' ), which a local index file does not. A run never contacts a marketplace.
docs.title: The plugin lock (installed bundles)

docs.text: A book's title page, copyright page and about-the-author page need things only the author can say. They go in a small TOML file you keep yourself, outside this repository, and a run reads it only when EI_AUTHOR_PROFILE names it (a file in the current directory is not read). The assemble stage writes it into the book's config; it is never sent to a model. author = "Ann Author" # required publisher = "Pub House" # required edition = "First Edition" # required; has to say "Edition" author_bio = "Ann writes." # required; paragraphs allowed year = 2031 # optional website = "https://pub.example" # optional email = "ann@pub.example" # optional isbn = "978-0-0000-0000-0" # optional ebook_isbn = "978-0-0000-0001-7" # optional dedication = "For you." # optional copyright_notes = "Notes." # optional also_by = ["Earlier Book"] # optional, at most 20 [pricing] # optional; needed for a strict release verified_on = "2026-11-19" # the day you checked the prices (an ISO date) source_url = "https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G201834170" # a page that shows the print costs ebook = 4.99 paperback = 12.99 hardcover = 22.99 # optional; a price here makes the book a KDP hardcover too The prices are yours: a run never invents them. They go into the book's [release.pricing] , which is what a strict release checks ( EI_BUILD_STRICT_RELEASE , or --strict-release on ei book create ). Without a [pricing] table a missing price is a warning in the run's quality-report.json , and a strict release fails. Any other key is refused, a missing file stops the process at start ( AUTHOR_PROFILE_MISSING ), and a bad one stops it with the reason ( AUTHOR_PROFILE_INVALID ). The file is at most 64 KiB. A one-line field is at most 200 characters with no space at either end; author_bio , dedication and copyright_notes are at most 4,000; year is 1000 to 9999; email has an @ and no space; an ISBN is digits and hyphens ending in a digit or X ; also_by has at most 20 titles; and no field may hold a control or invisible character. [pricing] needs verified_on (an ISO date), source_url (http or https), and ebook and paperback above zero; hardcover is optional. Without a profile the assembled book loads but does not build, and the build says which of these is missing. Em and en dashes are refused in non-fiction when the book is built, and the profile is not rewritten, so leave them out of your own text.
docs.title: The author profile (your own details)

docs.text: Contributing ¶ BLUF: Read the code of conduct, set up with one uv sync , and run the gates before you push: ruff, the import rules, bandit, types, pip-audit , a lock check and the full suite at 100% branch coverage. Code is built in layers that only point inward, one class per file, and tests pass fakes instead of patching. This repository holds product code only, never an author's manuscripts or profiles. Thank you for helping. Read CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md first; report security problems privately through SECURITY.md . Why the rules are strict ¶ Daniel: Why one class per file and no patching in tests? It feels like a lot of ceremony for a pull request. Professor Feynman: When you walk into a library, how do you find a book? Daniel: By where it is shelved. If I know the rule I do not have to search. Professor Feynman: Same here. Most rules are shelving rules that a test or a tool enforces, so nobody has to remember them, and a couple are conventions that review holds. One class per file means a class is where its name says. Layers that point inward mean a service never imports a database adapter, so swapping the adapter touches one place. And tests pass fakes instead of patching because a patched test passes even when the real wiring is wrong. Daniel: So the ceremony is what lets a stranger change the code without breaking something they cannot see. Professor Feynman: That is the idea. The limit: rules enforced by a test are only as good as the test, so a new rule needs a test that can fail. Daniel: Follow the shelving, run the gates, and give any new rule a test that can fail. The rules at a glance ¶ Rule How it is enforced One class per file, no loose production functions tests/architecture/test_architecture.py Every class has an interface in a sibling interfaces/ folder tests/architecture Layers point inward only lint-imports and the layer matrix in tests/architecture Models import nothing effectful, only models, errors and the standard library tests/architecture No monkeypatch.setattr of production code outside a short list of system-boundary calls tests/architecture/test_no_patching.py (other ways of patching are not checked) 100% line and branch coverage pytest --cov --cov-fail-under=100 Set up ¶ You need Python 3.12 or newer, uv , and Docker for the smoke test. git clone https://github.com/adammatthewsteinberger/engineering-influence cd engineering-influence uv sync --extra test --extra runtime --extra dev --extra publishing uv run vibey-gh install # commit hooks: add the Made-With trailer, check subjects The checks a pull request must pass ¶ Run them before you push (details in docs/TESTING.md ): uv run ruff check . uv run ruff format --check . uv run lint-imports uv run bandit -q -r src packages uv run mypy --strict src packages uv run pip-audit uv lock --check uv run pytest --cov --cov-branch --cov-fail-under=100 sh examples/compose_smoke.sh # when you touch the runtime, compose file or examples # when you touch persistence, the broker or how runs advance (then: sh tests/integration/stack.sh down) eval "$(sh tests/integration/stack.sh up)" && uv run pytest -m integration tests/integration Coverage is 100% with branches. New code arrives with its tests. The road to 1.0 is ADR 0003 ; the compatibility and deprecation rules are ADR 0004 . Architecture rules ¶ Interactions call controllers, controllers call services, services use models, contracts and interfaces, and adapters implement interfaces ( docs/ARCHITECTURE.md ). The tests enforce: one class per file, no loose production functions; every class implements an interface, and interfaces live in sibling interfaces/ folders; layers point inward only ( lint-imports runs a strict layers contract); only runtime/ composes concrete classes; everything else receives its collaborators (a convention that review holds, not a test); tests pass fakes instead of patching production code. A new external integration needs an interface , an adapter , an ADR when the choice is architectural ( docs/adr/ ), and failure and recovery tests. Every pipeline side effect must be bounded, idempotent, observable and recoverable. What may live in this repository ¶ This repository is public product code. It never holds an author's manuscripts, profiles, covers or built books. The leak-scan CI job rejects any path containing manuscripts/ , living-waters/ , archive/ , prompts/ or chapters/ , a top-level output/ , and any .pdf or .docx file anywhere in history. Prompts the product sends to a model are code. They live in a package folder named templates/ (never prompts/ ), are versioned, are tested, and are written generically, with no author's voice or content in them. How to write and change one: docs/PROMPTS.md . Test fixtures live in tests/fixtures/<name>/ and use original, synthetic text. Built PDFs are never committed; a build is checked by a structural snapshot ( docs/TESTING.md ). Recorded model responses (cassettes) live in tests/cassettes/ and are made only from synthetic briefs. If a legitimate file trips the scan, move the file. Loosening the pattern needs an ADR. Changelog fragments ¶ Do not edit CHANGELOG.md in a pull request. Add changelog.d/<short-slug>.md with one paragraph, the text of one bullet (see changelog.d/README.md and docs/adr/0005-release-flow-and-changelog-fragments.md ). Commits and branches ¶ Branch from develop ; open the pull request against develop . main receives releases. Conventional Commit subjects ( feat: , fix: , docs: , ci: , chore: …). Every commit carries a Made-With: trailer; the installed commit-msg hook adds it. Pull requests Dependabot opens are exempt from that one check. Use your GitHub no-reply address if you want to keep your email out of history. Restructuring commits that only move or rename files are listed in .git-blame-ignore-revs ; GitHub honours it, and locally run git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs . Dependency updates ¶ Dependabot opens pull requests for major versions too. Do not merge on a green title: read the failing job, run the gates above on the branch, and fix the code or the version bound. Past examples: mcp 2 renamed FastMCP ; Postgres 18 moved its data directory; pytest-cov 7 stopped measuring subprocesses. Documentation and examples ¶ Examples in examples/ are run by the test suite and must behave like real use: shell for the CLI, requests or curl for HTTP, a real MCP client for MCP. Keep docs/INTERACTIONS.md and the README in step with any interface change. The documents are also published as a website from the same Markdown ( docs/DOCUMENTATION_SITE.md ); a link that goes nowhere fails the docs check.

docs.text: The documentation site ¶ BLUF: These documents are also published as a website, from the same Markdown, so there is one copy to keep true. scripts/build_docs_site.py assembles the pages, ProperDocs builds them, and the build fails on any link that goes nowhere. It publishes only when you turn it on: set the repository variable PUBLISH_DOCS to true and switch GitHub Pages to "GitHub Actions". The site has no analytics and no tracking, and it has never been published yet. One source, two readers ¶ Daniel: A website means a second copy of every page, and a second copy means two things that disagree. I have been burned by that before. Professor Feynman: What if there were no second copy? Think of a translator at a border. The speaker says one thing, and each listener hears it in their own language. Daniel: So the Markdown is the speaker. Professor Feynman: Yes. On GitHub a link says ../examples , because it is read from inside the repository. On a website that means nothing. So before the build, a script walks every page and translates each link: a link to another page becomes a link between the site's pages, and a link to anything else, an example or a source file, becomes a link to that file on GitHub. Daniel: And if a link points at something that is not there? Professor Feynman: The build stops. Warnings are errors here, so a link that goes nowhere cannot be published. The limit of the picture: the translator can tell that a heading exists, not that the sentence around the link still makes sense. Daniel: One source, a translator, and a build that refuses a broken link. I will edit the Markdown and nothing else. How it fits together ¶ Piece What it does scripts/build_docs_site.py Copies each page into .site-src/ under a clean address ( GETTING_STARTED.md becomes getting-started/ ), rewrites its links, and builds the page that lists the decision records properdocs.yml The site's name, description, address and navigation. A page that is not in the navigation is an error docs-site/site.css The few rules this site adds to the Vibey stylesheet: the scenes, and a readable width The Vibey stylesheet Taken from the locked vibey-engine package at build time, so no copy of it is committed scripts/inject_docs_meta.py Adds each page's description, canonical address and Open Graph and Twitter tags, and the home page's SoftwareApplication description. It adds an image tag only if the site has img/social-preview.png .github/workflows/docs.yml On a pull request, builds strictly and publishes nothing. On develop , builds and, if PUBLISH_DOCS is true , publishes The site shows the develop branch, which documents what is built today. Links to files that are not pages point at develop too, so they match the pages beside them. Build it yourself ¶ uv sync --extra runtime uv run python scripts/build_docs_site.py --out .site-src uv run --with 'properdocs==1.6.7' --with 'properdocs-theme-mkdocs==1.6.7' properdocs build --strict uv run python scripts/inject_docs_meta.py --site-dir site python3 -m http.server --directory site 8000 # then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 .site-src/ and site/ are not committed. Without the runtime extra the site builds with no Vibey stylesheet and says so. Publishing it ¶ In the repository settings, open Pages and set the source to GitHub Actions . Set the repository variable PUBLISH_DOCS to true . Merge to develop , or run the Docs workflow by hand. The site appears at https://adammatthewsteinberger.github.io/engineering-influence/ . The github-pages environment may carry required reviewers, as the upload environments do. What is not verified ¶ The workflow has never run on GitHub, and nothing is published. The build and the metadata step were run locally against ProperDocs 1.6.7, and the pages were looked at in a browser; the deploy step has not been exercised. There is no social preview image yet, so shared links show a title and description and no picture. The site has not been checked with a screen reader, and its colours are the Vibey stylesheet's, not audited here. The home page is the README, whose first screen is written for GitHub and PyPI.

docs.text: The evaluation ¶ BLUF: ei evaluate measures whether a release is good enough: it makes five books, has a separately named judge model score each one against a rubric, and passes only if every book finished, every dimension's mean is at least 3.5 of 5, none has dropped by more than 0.2, and the cost estimate was within 30% of the real cost. It spends real money and refuses to start without EI_ALLOW_PAID=1 . It has never been run against a real model. ADR 0003 defines 1.0 by criteria that can be measured. Two of them are measured by one command, ei evaluate : A5 — the pre-flight cost estimate is within 30% of what the books really cost. A6 — a judge's mean score is at least 3.5 of 5 on every rubric dimension, and no dimension falls by more than 0.2 from the previous release. ei evaluate makes every book of a fixed set with the stack's own pipeline, has a separately configured model score each finished book, and applies the bar. It spends real money , on the writing model and on the judge. Status. The harness is built and tested against scripted models. It has not been run against a real model, so nothing here says the stack clears the bar. The first paid run is what produces the first baseline. Why the judge must be someone else ¶ Daniel: Could the writing model not just rate its own books? It would save a second model. Professor Feynman: Would you let a student mark his own exam? Daniel: No. He would be generous, and he would miss exactly the mistakes he made. Professor Feynman: So the judge is named separately, and the command refuses to start without one. Nothing stops you naming the writer's own profile as the judge, so do not. It gets a fixed rubric with written anchors for 1, 3 and 5, and it must give a reason for every score. Daniel: One strict marker can still have a bad day. Professor Feynman: Which is why the bar is on the mean of each dimension across the books, at 3.5 or more, and why no dimension may fall more than 0.2 below the last release. The second catches a slow slide that a fixed bar would miss. Every book must also finish, and the cost estimate must be within 30%. Here the picture gives out: a human examiner knows the subject. This one reads carefully, and it has not yet been checked against human readers. Daniel: A judge I name separately, a floor on every mean, and no backsliding. And until someone pays for the first run, there is no baseline at all. What is in evaluation/ ¶ File What it is evaluation/set.toml The books made on every release: three non-fiction ideas and two novels, each a short book ( target_words = 10000 ) so a run stays affordable evaluation/rubric.toml The dimensions, the question the judge asks for each, what a 1, a 3 and a 5 look like, which kinds of book each applies to, and the bar ( pass_mean = 3.5 , max_drop = 0.2 ) The rubric's dimensions: Dimension Applies to structure , prose , voice both kinds accuracy , usefulness non-fiction continuity , character , pacing novels The set is the benchmark. Changing an idea changes what is measured, so edit the set only together with a new baseline. The ideas are generic on purpose: this repository holds no author's own material. Running it ¶ EI_ALLOW_PAID=1 \ EI_STAGE_EXECUTOR=model EI_STAGE_MODEL_PROFILE=writer \ EI_EVAL_JUDGE_PROFILE=judge \ EI_MODEL_PROFILES=profiles.toml EI_MODEL_CATALOG=catalog.toml \ EI_AUTHOR_PROFILE=author.toml \ ei evaluate --out eval-out --budget-usd 5 --judge-budget-usd 3 --baseline previous/evaluation.json Also accepted: --profile FILE (the author profile, as an alternative to EI_AUTHOR_PROFILE ), --set FILE (default evaluation/set.toml ), --rubric FILE (default evaluation/rubric.toml ) and --release LABEL (recorded in the report). EI_ALLOW_PAID=1 is required. Without it the command refuses before it reads a file or calls a model. --budget-usd is the most each book may spend; --judge-budget-usd is the most the judge may spend in all . Both are required and have no default. --out must be a new or empty folder, so one evaluation never mixes with another. Each book is made under it ( <case>/ and <case>.state/ ), and evaluation.json is written beside them. --baseline is an earlier evaluation.json . Without one only the pass mark applies; with one a fall of more than 0.2 on any dimension fails. The books are built for real, so the worker needs the TeX toolchain: run it from the worker-tex image ( WORKER_IMAGE.md ). Exit status: 0 the release meets the bar, 1 it does not (every reason is printed and is in the report), 2 the command could not run. The judge ¶ The judge is a different configuration from the writer: EI_EVAL_JUDGE_PROFILE names a profile in the same EI_MODEL_PROFILES file, and the command refuses to start without it. A model that grades its own writing is the least informative judge, and pinning the judge's profile is what makes this release's scores and the last release's the same measurement. It is called once per finished book, with the whole book, using the eval_judge prompt ( PROMPTS.md ). The book is an untrusted blank: a book that tells the judge to score it highly is data, not an instruction. It sees the text only: not the brief, what the run cost, or any earlier score. It answers one JSON object, a whole score from 1 to 5 and a reason for each dimension. An answer that is not exactly the rubric's dimensions with whole scores is refused ( JUDGE_ANSWER_INVALID ) and asked for once more; two refusals stop the evaluation, because scores from a judge that sometimes could not answer would not be comparable. It has a budget of its own, reserved call by call before anything is sent, so it cannot spend past --judge-budget-usd . A call that does not fit is refused ( JUDGE_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED ). A book too long for the judge's window is refused ( JUDGE_INPUT_TOO_LARGE ), not cut: a judge that read half a book scores half a book. The bar ¶ A release meets the bar when none of these is found. Each one that is found is listed in evaluation.json and printed. Every book finished. A book whose run failed, stopped for money or did not build is a failure of the release, not a missing data point: leaving it out would let a pipeline that breaks on hard ideas pass by scoring only the easy ones. Only a finished book is judged. Every dimension's mean reaches the pass mark. The mean is over the books the dimension applies to ( kinds in the rubric). No dimension fell by more than the allowed drop since the baseline. A dimension the baseline had and this evaluation did not measure is a failure. The cost estimate was within 30% of what was spent , over the whole set. Money spent with no estimate recorded is a failure, because the check cannot be made. The report ¶ evaluation.json is stable (the same inputs give the same bytes) and is its own baseline: commit it, and pass it as --baseline to the next release's evaluation. It holds the rubric version and bar, dimension_means , the spend (making, estimated, the estimate's error, judging), the verdict, and for each case the title, the run's status, how many chapters and words, what it cost, and every score with its reason. Read the reasons: a mean says how far, not why. What it does not tell you ¶ It cannot show that a real model clears 3.5. Only a paid run can. A judge is a model. Its scores are comparable from release to release only while the judge's profile and the rubric stay the same; change either and take a new baseline. The estimate's tolerance is measured on five short books. The estimator's constants are first guesses until real runs calibrate them. Five books are a small sample. A pass is evidence, not a guarantee. Nightly ¶ .github/workflows/nightly-eval.yml runs the evaluation each night. It is off until the repository variable RUN_NIGHTLY_EVAL is true , and it runs in the evaluation environment, which holds the model key and whose reviewers approve each run. It has not run yet. The maintainer provides the secrets, the profiles and the committed baseline; see the comments in the workflow.
