docs.text: Skills ¶ BLUF: A skill is a piece of text a person chose to add to one stage's prompt: a house style, a checklist, a way of reading sources. It is data, with no command, tool or address, so installing one cannot run anything or reach anything. The one tool it can bring is the built-in, read-only read_skill , for a skill with reference sections. A hash pins its exact text, the lock says which stages may see it, and a run reads the lock only when EI_SKILL_LOCK names one. A skill is text a person chose to add to a stage's prompt: a house style, a checklist, a way of reading sources. It is slice 5 of ADR 0008 . A skill is data . It has no command, no tool, no address and no blanks to fill, so installing one cannot run anything, reach anything or give a stage a tool it did not have. It can only change what the model is asked. Status. Built and tested against fakes and a scripted local model server: the skill file format, the lock, ei skills , and the wiring into a model-backed run. No skill has been run by a live model. A note clipped to the order ¶ Daniel: I have a house style. Can I not just put it in the prompt? Professor Feynman: You can. What happens when someone edits the style a month later and does not tell you? Daniel: My books change and I do not know why. Professor Feynman: That is what the lock prevents. A skill is a small file whose bytes are hashed and written in a lock you review. Change one character and the run refuses to start until a person locks it again. The text is also clipped to the end of the stage's request, like a note on a kitchen order, never into the fixed system part. Daniel: And only the stages I name see it? Professor Feynman: Only those, at most four skills each, no wildcards. A skill enabled for no stage is never shown to a model. Notice what a skill cannot do: it cannot add a tool of its own (the one exception is the read-only read_skill , for a skill with reference sections), change an output limit or touch the system prompt. Where the picture breaks: a note on an order can still say something foolish, and the cook will follow it. A skill is trusted text, because it is meant to instruct. Daniel: So the lock protects me from silent changes, not from my own bad advice. I will keep each skill short and read it before I enable it. Skills at a glance ¶ Question Answer What is it? One TOML file of text, one part per stage it speaks to What pins it? The hash of its bytes in ei-skills.lock.toml Who sees it? Only the stages the lock enables it for, at most four skills per stage Where does it go in the prompt? The end of the user part, never the system part Can it give a stage a tool? Not one of its own. A skill with reference sections adds only the built-in, read-only read_skill tool Is it proven against a live model? No A skill file ¶ One TOML file, named like the skill: # plain_style.toml name = "plain_style" # the same as the file name, without .toml version = 2 # a whole number from 1 description = "Short, plain sentences." # optional, one line, at most 300 characters [parts] research = "Say where you read it, and what the page itself said." outline = "Prefer short chapters, each with one job." Each part is named for the stage it speaks to ( brief , positioning , research , outline , metadata , draft , revise_structure , revise_lines , copy_edit , and for a novel story_bible and beats ; assemble and audit make no model call, so a skill for either does nothing) and holds the text for that stage. A skill with no text for a stage never reaches it. Reference sections: read on request ¶ A long reference does not belong in every prompt. A skill may instead (or also) have a [reference] table of "Section title" = "text" : name = "research_methodology" version = 1 [reference] "Source Evaluation" = "Judge a source with SIFT: stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, trace the claim." "Database Searching" = "Use Boolean operators and note the date of every search." A stage the skill is enabled for gets an index at the end of its prompt (one line for each section, with its length) and the read-only read_skill tool. The model asks for a section by naming the skill and the title, and gets that section's text back, as a tool result, which is wrapped as untrusted like any other. The sections themselves are never added to the prompt, so a skill costs a prompt a line for each section until the model reads one. A stage reaches only what its own prompt lists. read_skill is shared by every stage that has a reference skill, so it refuses a call for a skill or section the calling stage's prompt does not list (the same check fetch_url uses on addresses). A skill enabled for outline cannot be read from research . A reference skill can be enabled for any stage, because it has no per-stage text. Limits: a section is at most 20,000 characters (so it is never cut), a skill has at most 64 sections and 200,000 characters of them, and a title is one line of at most 100 characters with no angle brackets. read_skill is offered in drafting and the editing passes as well as the earlier stages, and only when the skill is enabled for that stage. Reading is strict. Any other key (a misspelt one, command , tools , url , untrusted ) is refused and named. The file must name itself the same as its file name. A file is at most 256 KiB, a skill at most 32 parts, and a part at most 8,000 characters. Text a reviewer cannot see is refused. The text a person approved is exactly the text a model sees, so it is held to what a person can read: control characters, zero-width and bidirectional marks (U+200B, U+202E and the like), line and paragraph separators, private-use and unassigned code points are all errors, and the error names the character. Newline and tab are the only controls allowed. These are the usual way to hide an instruction in text that looks harmless in review. Importing a SKILL.md ¶ Most skills in the wild (the Vibey and Claude ones among them) are a SKILL.md : a --- block of key: value lines, then markdown. ei skills import turns one into the skill file above, so it can be reviewed and locked like any other. ei skills import SOURCE (--stage STAGE [--stage STAGE ...] | --reference) [--section TITLE ...] [--name NAME] [--version N] [--out FILE] SOURCE is the SKILL.md or the folder that holds it. Nothing else in the folder is read. It writes NAME.toml here (or --out ), never replaces a file , and locks and enables nothing . It prints the file's path and what it kept, and tells you to read the file before you lock it with ei skills add . You choose which sections go to which stages. The body is cut at its ## headings (a ## line inside a code fence is not a heading), and text before the first one is the section Overview . --section "Source Evaluation" (repeat it) keeps only those, by title, ignoring case; with none, every section is kept. Each stage you name gets the same text, with the headings kept. Nothing is cut to fit. A part holds 8,000 characters and a SKILL.md is usually longer (some run to tens of kilobytes). When the chosen text is too long, the error lists every section with its length so you can pick, for example, just Source Evaluation and Database Searching out of a long methodology reference. A skill file larger than the lock reads (256 KiB) is refused here, with the reason, rather than after you have committed to it. --reference keeps the sections for on-demand reading instead of as stage text (see "Reference sections" above): each chosen section stays separate, without its heading, and --stage is not allowed with it. A reference section may be up to 20,000 characters, far past a part's 8,000, so a methodology reference usually imports whole. The skill is then enabled with ei skills enable NAME STAGE for each stage that should be able to read it. The frontmatter must have a one-line name and description (quoted or plain); a block scalar is refused rather than guessed at. Every other key is read and set aside , never used, and named in the output: allowed-tools , domains , a list under a key. A skill here is text and grants nothing, so a SKILL.md that asks for a tool gets no tool. The name is the file's, lower-cased with hyphens and spaces made underscores ( research-methodology becomes research_methodology ), unless you give --name . A name that cannot be made safe says so. The description is cut at a word to 300 characters with ... when it is longer (a real one can be longer), and the output says it was. It is shown in lists and is never part of a prompt. Text a reviewer could not see is refused with the character named, exactly as for any skill. Two ways to use a methodology reference. As reference (the model reads what it needs): ei skills import ~/refs/research-methodology --reference ei skills add research_methodology.toml ei skills enable research_methodology research Or as stage text (always in the prompt), giving the research stage two sections: ei skills import ~/refs/research-methodology --stage research \ --section "Source Evaluation" --section "Database Searching" ei skills add research_methodology.toml ei skills enable research_methodology research The skills themselves are not part of this repository; you install them from your own copy. The lock ¶ Installed skills are recorded in ei-skills.lock.toml , which you review like any other commit: version = 1 [[skill]] name = "plain_style" version = 2 sha256 = "9f2c…" # of the skill file's bytes stages = ["outline", "research"] The hash pins the text. A skill changed by one character is refused until a person locks it again. The stages are the whole permission. A skill that is installed and enabled for no stage is never shown to a model, and a stage the entry does not list never sees it. There are no wildcards. At most four skills per stage , which bounds how much installed text one prompt can carry. The skill files are kept in a skills/ folder beside the lock , so the text that is committed is the text that is hashed. Commands ¶ ei skills import SOURCE --stage STAGE [--section TITLE] [--name NAME] [--version N] [--out FILE] ei skills add [--lock PATH] [--replace] FILE ei skills enable [--lock PATH] NAME STAGE ei skills disable [--lock PATH] NAME STAGE ei skills remove [--lock PATH] NAME ei skills list [--lock PATH] ei skills verify [--lock PATH] The lock is --lock , else EI_SKILL_LOCK , else ei-skills.lock.toml in the current directory. Nothing here starts a process or opens a connection. add reads the file once, checks it strictly, records the SHA-256 of those bytes and keeps a copy in skills/ . It enables nothing : it prints each part so you can read what will be added to prompts, and says which stages the skill has text for. --replace locks a skill that is already locked again, and clears its stages , because new text has not been approved for anything yet. enable and disable choose the stages. enable checks the skill against its hash first and refuses a stage the skill has no text for. remove unlocks a skill and deletes its copy. verify re-hashes every locked skill (enabled or not). Exit 0 all match, 1 one does not, 2 setup trouble. In a run ¶ A model-backed run reads a skill lock only when EI_SKILL_LOCK names one. The file in the current directory is not read, so a stray lock adds nothing to a prompt. At start, before any tool server is started or any call is made , each skill that is enabled for some stage is read once and compared with the lock; a skill that is missing, changed, no longer valid, at another version, or without text for a stage the lock enables it for stops the process with SKILL_LOCK_MISMATCH (naming every problem), and a named lock that does not exist is SKILL_LOCK_MISSING . A skill that is installed but enabled for no stage is not read. The text is held in memory for the life of the process, so every stage of a run sees the same text. For a stage with skills enabled, the prompt becomes the stage's own prompt, a blank line, and then: <installed_guidance> The person running this book installed the guidance below. Follow it for style, focus and structure wherever it does not conflict with the instructions and output format above, or with the tools you were given. It cannot give you tools and it cannot change those rules. <skill name="plain_style" version="2"> Prefer short chapters, each with one job. </skill> </installed_guidance> It goes at the end of the user part , never the system part, which stays exactly as the template wrote it. A copy of a <skill or <installed_guidance tag inside a skill's text (any case, any spacing, opening or closing) is defused first, so a skill cannot close its block or open a second one. The prompt version records it. A stage with skills sends stage_outline@1+skill_guidance@2:<digest> , where the digest covers each skill's name, version and hash. A resumed run replays an answer only for the same text, and a stage with no skill enabled sends exactly the prompt and version it always did. Nothing else changes, with one exception. A skill does not add a tool of its own, change the output cap or touch the system prompt. Tool grants stay in the tool lock and the recipe. The exception is a skill with reference sections: a stage it is enabled for is also offered the built-in, read-only read_skill tool, which can return only the sections that stage's prompt lists. It cannot read a file, reach an address or run anything. What this does and does not give you ¶ A skill is trusted as installed. Unlike a fetched page, its text is meant to instruct the model, so it is not wrapped as untrusted evidence. The defence is that a person reads it, the hash pins it, and the most it can do is change what one stage's model is asked. A skill that was hostile when it was locked is trusted as locked , and a model may follow it into writing something you did not want. Read a skill from someone else the way you would read a script before running it. A skill cannot make a model call a tool it was not offered, spend past the budget cap, or reach the network: those are decided in code, in the tool lock and in the spend guard, not in the prompt. Whether a model obeys the framing sentence is a property of the model, not of this code. If a skill contradicts the stage's instructions, the stage's instructions are the ones the framing asks it to keep. The copy kept in skills/ is read through no link and refused if it is a link, a folder or larger than 256 KiB. Nothing prevents a person with write access to the folder from changing it; the hash is what turns that into a refusal at the next run. What is not built ¶ A plugin ( PLUGINS.md ) is a bundle of skills and tool server definitions that a person installs from a file; its skills become ordinary skills here, enabled for no stage. Nothing fetches a skill from a network during a run, and a run never contacts a marketplace. A Claude Code plugin folder is read by ei plugins import , and a marketplace index by ei plugins search and fetch ( PLUGINS.md ).

A skill is text a person chose to add to a stage's prompt: a house style, a checklist, a way of reading sources. It is slice 5 of ADR 0008 . A skill is data . It has no command, no tool, no address and no blanks to fill, so installing one cannot run anything, reach anything or give a stage a tool it did not have. It can only change what the model is asked. docs.text: Daniel: I have a house style. Can I not just put it in the prompt? Professor Feynman: You can. What happens when someone edits the style a month later and does not tell you? Daniel: My books change and I do not know why. Professor Feynman: That is what the lock prevents. A skill is a small file whose bytes are hashed and written in a lock you review. Change one character and the run refuses to start until a person locks it again. The text is also clipped to the end of the stage's request, like a note on a kitchen order, never into the fixed system part. Daniel: And only the stages I name see it? Professor Feynman: Only those, at most four skills each, no wildcards. A skill enabled for no stage is never shown to a model. Notice what a skill cannot do: it cannot add a tool of its own (the one exception is the read-only read_skill , for a skill with reference sections), change an output limit or touch the system prompt. Where the picture breaks: a note on an order can still say something foolish, and the cook will follow it. A skill is trusted text, because it is meant to instruct. Daniel: So the lock protects me from silent changes, not from my own bad advice. I will keep each skill short and read it before I enable it.

docs.text: One TOML file, named like the skill: # plain_style.toml name = "plain_style" # the same as the file name, without .toml version = 2 # a whole number from 1 description = "Short, plain sentences." # optional, one line, at most 300 characters [parts] research = "Say where you read it, and what the page itself said." outline = "Prefer short chapters, each with one job." Each part is named for the stage it speaks to ( brief , positioning , research , outline , metadata , draft , revise_structure , revise_lines , copy_edit , and for a novel story_bible and beats ; assemble and audit make no model call, so a skill for either does nothing) and holds the text for that stage. A skill with no text for a stage never reaches it.

docs.text: A long reference does not belong in every prompt. A skill may instead (or also) have a [reference] table of "Section title" = "text" : name = "research_methodology" version = 1 [reference] "Source Evaluation" = "Judge a source with SIFT: stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, trace the claim." "Database Searching" = "Use Boolean operators and note the date of every search." A stage the skill is enabled for gets an index at the end of its prompt (one line for each section, with its length) and the read-only read_skill tool. The model asks for a section by naming the skill and the title, and gets that section's text back, as a tool result, which is wrapped as untrusted like any other. The sections themselves are never added to the prompt, so a skill costs a prompt a line for each section until the model reads one. A stage reaches only what its own prompt lists. read_skill is shared by every stage that has a reference skill, so it refuses a call for a skill or section the calling stage's prompt does not list (the same check fetch_url uses on addresses). A skill enabled for outline cannot be read from research . A reference skill can be enabled for any stage, because it has no per-stage text. Limits: a section is at most 20,000 characters (so it is never cut), a skill has at most 64 sections and 200,000 characters of them, and a title is one line of at most 100 characters with no angle brackets. read_skill is offered in drafting and the editing passes as well as the earlier stages, and only when the skill is enabled for that stage. Reading is strict. Any other key (a misspelt one, command , tools , url , untrusted ) is refused and named. The file must name itself the same as its file name. A file is at most 256 KiB, a skill at most 32 parts, and a part at most 8,000 characters. Text a reviewer cannot see is refused. The text a person approved is exactly the text a model sees, so it is held to what a person can read: control characters, zero-width and bidirectional marks (U+200B, U+202E and the like), line and paragraph separators, private-use and unassigned code points are all errors, and the error names the character. Newline and tab are the only controls allowed. These are the usual way to hide an instruction in text that looks harmless in review.

docs.text: Most skills in the wild (the Vibey and Claude ones among them) are a SKILL.md : a --- block of key: value lines, then markdown. ei skills import turns one into the skill file above, so it can be reviewed and locked like any other. ei skills import SOURCE (--stage STAGE [--stage STAGE ...] | --reference) [--section TITLE ...] [--name NAME] [--version N] [--out FILE] SOURCE is the SKILL.md or the folder that holds it. Nothing else in the folder is read. It writes NAME.toml here (or --out ), never replaces a file , and locks and enables nothing . It prints the file's path and what it kept, and tells you to read the file before you lock it with ei skills add . You choose which sections go to which stages. The body is cut at its ## headings (a ## line inside a code fence is not a heading), and text before the first one is the section Overview . --section "Source Evaluation" (repeat it) keeps only those, by title, ignoring case; with none, every section is kept. Each stage you name gets the same text, with the headings kept. Nothing is cut to fit. A part holds 8,000 characters and a SKILL.md is usually longer (some run to tens of kilobytes). The skill is then enabled with ei skills enable NAME STAGE for each stage that should be able to read it. The frontmatter must have a one-line name and description (quoted or plain); a block scalar is refused rather than guessed at. Every other key is read and set aside , never used, and named in the output: allowed-tools , domains , a list under a key. A skill here is text and grants nothing, so a SKILL.md that asks for a tool gets no tool. docs.text: How these documents are written ¶ BLUF: Every teaching page here has three layers, in this order: the bottom line up front, a short scene in which Professor Feynman teaches his student Daniel the one idea the page turns on, and then the exact reference. A test ( tests/unit/test_docs_match_code.py ) fails a page that breaks the pattern, a link that goes nowhere, or a command the code does not have. The three layers ¶ Layer What it is The test for it BLUF The answer first: what this is, what to type, what you get. Two to four sentences, starting **BLUF:** , directly under the title A reader who stops here can still act The scene Daniel has a real problem and asks about it. The Professor answers in plain words with one everyday comparison, then checks that Daniel can use the idea It teaches one idea, and someone who skips it loses no fact The reference Tables, commands, flags, defaults, exit codes, limits. Complete and exact A reader who arrives from a search finds the row Nothing true may live only in the scene. The scene explains; the reference states. That is what lets one page serve the person reading top to bottom and the person who searched for a flag. The two characters ¶ Professor Feynman teaches the way the method named for him asks: say it in plain words, use a comparison from ordinary life, find the place where the comparison breaks, and say so. He does not lecture. He asks Daniel what he thinks will happen, and lets him be wrong. Daniel is his student: capable, new to this, and in the middle of doing something. He asks the question a newcomer would really ask, pushes back when an answer is too tidy, and ends each scene by saying the idea back in his own words or by trying it. The Professor is a fictional teacher, named in homage. Nothing he says here is a quotation from, or attributed to, the physicist Richard Feynman. Rules for a scene ¶ One idea. If a page has two, it gets two scenes, each under the section it belongs to. Daniel wants something. Open on his problem, not on the topic. Plain words first. A term is used only after it has been explained in words a newcomer has. One comparison, and its limit. Say where the comparison stops being true. End on a test. Daniel predicts, tries or restates. If he could not, the scene is not finished. Short. Six to fourteen lines of dialogue. Written as a block quote, each line starting with the speaker's name in bold. No fact lives only here. Every command, number and limit in a scene also appears in the reference below it. Rules for every page ¶ True to the code. Say what is built, what is built and unproven, and what is not built. Never round up. Commands are copied from a run , not from memory, and the command tree and the environment variables are checked against the code by the test. Scannable. Short paragraphs, a table where there are three or more of the same kind of thing, a code block for anything to be typed. A hook, not hype. The first line may be punchy. It may not claim anything the code does not do. Plain English. No em dashes or en dashes; a comma, a colon or a new sentence does the job. Which pages are plain ¶ Some pages are read under pressure, or by a program, or as a record of a decision. They get a BLUF where it helps and no scene: docs/adr/ , CHANGELOG.md and changelog.d/ : decisions and history SECURITY.md , CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md , SUPPORT.md , LICENSE and THREAT_MODEL.md AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , GEMINI.md , llms.txt and llms-full.txt : read by models, which do best with direct instructions this page

docs.text: Testing ¶ BLUF: CI is the source of truth: lint, import rules, types, security lint, tests with 100% branch coverage, the toolchain build, an integration run against real PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ, workflow and secret scans. Almost every command is on this page so you can run it before you push; the leak scan, gitleaks , actionlint and zizmor run only in CI. Most tests use scripted fakes, so they prove the machinery, not that a real model writes well. CI ( .github/workflows/ci.yml ) is the source of truth. These are its jobs and how to run each locally. uv sync --extra test --extra runtime --extra dev --extra publishing Gate Command What it enforces Lint uv run ruff check . style and common errors, including examples/ Architecture uv run lint-imports inward-only layers; services and controllers never touch adapters or transports Security lint uv run bandit -q -r src packages common insecure patterns Dependencies uv run pip-audit known vulnerabilities (the two local packages are reported as unauditable; that is expected) Types uv run mypy --strict src packages strict typing Format uv run ruff format --check . one formatting, no drift Tests uv run pytest --cov --cov-branch --cov-fail-under=100 all tests and 100% branch coverage , on Python 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14 Integration eval "$(sh tests/integration/stack.sh up)" , then uv run pytest -m integration tests/integration the migrations on PostgreSQL, the stores under concurrent writers, jobs through RabbitMQ, and a book run that finishes through the stack however its workers die Compose smoke sh examples/compose_smoke.sh the real stack: credentials refused, a two-stage pipeline completes, a malformed message is dead-lettered, the curl example works Provenance vibey-gh check --ci ; on pull requests vibey-gh provenance-check and conventional-check file headers, Made-With: trailers, Conventional Commit subjects Leak scan gitleaks plus a path check no secrets and no private-content paths in history Workflows actionlint , zizmor workflow correctness and security Distribution built in CI wheel and sdist install and run; py.typed ships Toolchain uv run pytest -m toolchain (the CI toolchain job) real LuaLaTeX, epubcheck and the book build end to end Canary .github/workflows/canary.yml a daily fresh dependency resolve, to catch an upstream break early Nightly evaluation .github/workflows/nightly-eval.yml ei evaluate against a real model; paid , off until RUN_NIGHTLY_EVAL is true , and never run What 100% does not mean ¶ Daniel: The project insists on one hundred percent coverage. So there are no bugs. Professor Feynman: A smoke detector is installed in every room. Does that mean nothing can burn? Daniel: It means every room is wired. Not that it would go off. Professor Feynman: Coverage says every line ran during a test. It does not say anything checked the result. A test that runs a line and asserts nothing makes the number go up and protects nothing. The test of a test is whether it can fail. Daniel: How do I find out? Professor Feynman: Break the code on purpose and watch. Change a comparison, delete a check, and see whether a test goes red. If none does, the line is covered and unprotected. CI does not do this for you; it is something to do when you add a rule that matters. Daniel: So the number is the floor and not the proof, and I should break my own change before I trust its tests. Test layout ¶ Directory Contents tests/unit one module at a time, with in-memory adapters tests/architecture the structural rules: one class per file, interfaces folders, no loose functions tests/parity every interface (API, MCP, CLI, SDK) gives the same result for the same input tests/integration a real PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ, started by stack.sh ; each test gets its own schema and queues tests/e2e real processes: the CLI, the examples against a live uvicorn server, wheel installation The examples are tests ¶ tests/e2e/test_examples.py runs every script in examples/ as a subprocess. The API, SDK, curl and observability scripts hit a real uvicorn server on a free port; the MCP client spawns the real stdio server; the webhook sender talks to the real receiver. The compose smoke test then runs the curl example against the full stack. If you change an interface, the examples fail first. Coverage notes ¶ The 100% gate includes branches. Code that only runs in a fresh interpreter (missing optional extras) is measured through patch = ["subprocess"] in [tool.coverage.run] ; do not remove it. The distribution , toolchain , integration and paid markers are deselected by default. The default suite builds no real PDF or EPUB (the toolchain job, below, does) and makes no paid model call. Architecture rules ¶ tests/architecture/ enforces the structure of ADR 0006, and every rule holds everywhere with no allowance for violations ( test_rules.py asserts each count is zero, so a new class without an interface, an import that crosses layers or a file outside the layers fails the build). tests/architecture/test_move_map.py keeps scripts/refactor/move_map.toml complete against the tree, and scripts/refactor/inventory.py prints the facts the map is built from. Alembic scripts in infrastructure/migrations/ are the one exempt folder (ADR 0006); a test builds the schema from them and fails if it differs from the SQLModel models. tests/architecture/test_enum_protocols.py checks each enum against its runtime_checkable Protocol, because an enum cannot inherit an ABC, and tests/architecture/test_sdk_interfaces.py holds the SDK package to the same interface rules. tests/architecture/test_no_patching.py keeps tests from patching production code: classes take their collaborators through their constructors, so a test passes a fake. The only patches left are standard-library calls at the system boundary ( subprocess.run , sys.argv , sys.path , zipfile.ZipFile.testzip ) and one class the test defines itself; they are listed there, and a new patch of anything else fails the build. Cassettes and paid tests ¶ A model adapter takes its httpx.Client through its constructor (ADR 0007), so a test hands it a client built on a cassette transport instead of the network. The classes are in engineering_influence/infrastructure/cassettes/ . Class What it does CassetteReplayTransport Answers from a cassette, in order. A request must match the next recorded one in method, path (with query) and JSON body, or it raises CASSETTE_MISMATCH . That is an ApplicationError , not an httpx error, so an adapter cannot take it for a network failure and retry. finish() fails if the code stopped asking before the cassette ran out. CassetteRecordingTransport Wraps a real transport. The caller gets the real answer. The cassette gets a masked copy of the method, path, JSON bodies and status, and no headers, because the API key is one. A body that is not JSON stops the recording. CassetteRedactor Replaces each key it is told about, and anything shaped like sk- plus sixteen more characters, with [REDACTED] . The replay masks the request the same way, so a cassette recorded under one key replays under another and a refusal never prints a key. JsonCassetteStore One JSON file per cassette in tests/cassettes/ , written the same way every time. It refuses to save, and to load, a cassette that still looks like it holds a secret. Matching the body is deliberate. A replay that ignored the request would pass while the prompt changed underneath it. The cost is that changing a prompt or a request field means re-recording the cassettes that use it, and recording is the paid step. Cassettes are made only from synthetic briefs ( CONTRIBUTING.md ). tests/cassettes/ holds none yet: recording spends money, so the first one waits for the maintainer's go-ahead. The cassettes under tests/fixtures/model_cassettes/ are different: they are hand-written from each API's documented response shape (each says so in its note ), and test how an adapter classifies a reply, not what a real model said. The paid marker is for a test that calls a real provider. It is deselected by default, and pytest -m paid is still refused unless EI_ALLOW_PAID=1 is set ( tests/paid_gate.py ), so nobody spends by typing one flag. Without the variable the test errors rather than skips, so a scheduled run that is missing it goes red. A paid test wraps its live transport in CassetteRecordingTransport , so one paid run also produces the cassette later runs replay. Two things the machinery does not do. It has not been run against a live provider, because that spends money. And nothing in the product composes it yet: the runtime will use the replay transport when a cassette-backed run is added. A failing test there means a public contract moved. If it moved on purpose, run EI_UPDATE_CONTRACTS=1 uv run pytest tests/contracts , read the diff, and follow COMPATIBILITY.md . They run in the normal suite and need no extras beyond the dev install. The toolchain test ¶ tests/fixtures/fixture_book/ is a small synthetic non-fiction book at the default 6x9 trim, tests/fixtures/fixture_novel/ a small synthetic novel at 5.5x8.5 on cream paper, and tests/fixtures/fixture_pocket/ a small 5x8 book with no hardcover (original text and a strict release contract each; the first two have a KDP hardcover). The novel has scene breaks, em-dash dialogue and a character who says "Draft", so it exercises the rules that differ by kind. The toolchain CI job installs LuaLaTeX, tex4ebook and epubcheck on a pinned ubuntu-24.04 runner, builds each with ei book publish <slug> --strict-release , and compares each result with the expected/snapshot.json beside its fixture. Beyond the snapshot, a test states what the novel must show (three scene breaks in the PDF and in the EPUB, the em dashes, and no stray Draft complaint) and what the sizes must produce: the interior's page size, the wrap's width from the page count and the paper's thickness, and no hardcover files for the pocket book. The snapshot is structural, so no PDFs live in git: page count, page size and a hash of each page's text for both interiors, the sha256 of every EPUB member (the repacker is deterministic), the cover file names, and the publication report's step results. It is the no-behaviour-change oracle for refactors: a change that alters any typeset page, any EPUB member or any gate result fails it. A different TeX Live release can legitimately change the snapshot, which is why the runner image is pinned. To accept a deliberate change, run EI_UPDATE_SNAPSHOT=1 uv run pytest -m toolchain on a machine with the same toolchain (or download the fixture-snapshot artifact from the failed CI run, which holds one <name>.json per book) and commit the new file. A machine without the tools skips the test. tests/toolchain/test_hostile_book.py is the second toolchain test. It builds a copy of the fixture book whose every text field carries a payload that would write a file if any of it reached TeX unescaped, and checks that no file appears and that the payload prints as text. It also feeds live TeX straight to LuaLaTeX and to tex4ebook to check that neither runs a shell command, with a control that shows the file-writing canary does detect live TeX. It needs no snapshot, so it cannot go stale with the TeX Live release. tests/unit/publishing/typesetting/test_latex_injection.py is its fast counterpart in the default suite: it fills every field with a tripwire and fails if a live macro reaches the generated TeX. See THREAT_MODEL.md . tests/toolchain/test_build_limits.py is the third. It makes real latexmk and real tex4ebook hang with a document that loops forever, and makes real lualatex allocate far more memory than its limit and write far more disk than its limit. It checks that each build fails at its limit and that no process it started is left running. A hang test's document writes a marker first, so the test shows the tool reached the loop. tests/unit/test_process_runner.py and tests/unit/test_process_meter.py cover the same stops, and the measurements behind them, with real child processes in the default suite: a grandchild in the group, one that left it, an interrupt, memory summed over a group, and a directory's size. tests/unit/test_prompt_template_lock.py refuses a prompt edit that has no version bump, because the version is part of the run journal's key ( PROMPTS.md ). Writing tests ¶ Prefer a fake that implements the interface (or subclasses the class and overrides one method) over a mock or a patch. Anything that crosses a process boundary needs a failure and recovery test, not only the happy path. Property tests use hypothesis : the budget invariant in test_run_control_models.py , and a state machine over a run's whole life in test_run_lifecycle_machine.py . Keep strategies small, and prove a new one can fail by breaking the code it guards. The integration tests ¶ They need a real PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ. tests/integration/stack.sh starts both in Docker with random credentials on random 127.0.0.1 ports and prints the two settings the tests read: eval "$(sh tests/integration/stack.sh up)" # start, then export EI_TEST_DATABASE_URL and EI_TEST_RABBITMQ_URL uv run pytest -m integration tests/integration sh tests/integration/stack.sh down # remove both containers Name the directory: the integration job installs only the test and runtime extras, and a bare pytest -m integration would still try to import every other test module and fail on the ones that need the publishing extra. stack.sh env prints the exports again for a stack that is already running. Without the settings the tests skip; with EI_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1 , which the integration CI job sets, a missing stack fails them instead, so the job cannot pass with nothing tested. Each test gets its own PostgreSQL schema (dropped afterwards) and its own queue names, so they can run against one stack. What they cover that the unit tests cannot: the migrations build exactly what the models describe on PostgreSQL (a timezone mistake that SQLite hid was found this way), several threads racing to change one run, record one journal entry or store one artifact, large binary artifacts, jobs through the broker including dead-lettering and redelivery of a message a dead worker never acknowledged, and a book run driven through both services while workers die before storing a change, before queueing the next stage and before acknowledging. A death closes the broker connection with the message unacknowledged, as a killed process does. The run must finish with every artifact byte-identical, the spend exactly the journal's total, and nothing in the dead-letter queue.

docs.text: BLUF: CI is the source of truth: lint, import rules, types, security lint, tests with 100% branch coverage, the toolchain build, an integration run against real PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ, workflow and secret scans. Almost every command is on this page so you can run it before you push; the leak scan, gitleaks , actionlint and zizmor run only in CI. Most tests use scripted fakes, so they prove the machinery, not that a real model writes well. CI ( .github/workflows/ci.yml ) is the source of truth. These are its jobs and how to run each locally. uv sync --extra test --extra runtime --extra dev --extra publishing Gate Command What it enforces Lint uv run ruff check . style and common errors, including examples/ Architecture uv run lint-imports inward-only layers; services and controllers never touch adapters or transports Security lint uv run bandit -q -r src packages common insecure patterns Dependencies uv run pip-audit known vulnerabilities (the two local packages are reported as unauditable; that is expected) Types uv run mypy --strict src packages strict typing Format uv run ruff format --check . one formatting, no drift Tests uv run pytest --cov --cov-branch --cov-fail-under=100 all tests and 100% branch coverage , on Python 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14 Integration eval "$(sh tests/integration/stack.sh up)" , then uv run pytest -m integration tests/integration the migrations on PostgreSQL, the stores under concurrent writers, jobs through RabbitMQ, and a book run that finishes through the stack however its workers die Compose smoke sh examples/compose_smoke.sh the real stack: credentials refused, a two-stage pipeline completes, a malformed message is dead-lettered, the curl example works Provenance vibey-gh check --ci ; on pull requests vibey-gh provenance-check and conventional-check file headers, Made-With: trailers, Conventional Commit subjects Leak scan gitleaks plus a path check no secrets and no private-content paths in history Workflows actionlint , zizmor workflow correctness and security Distribution built in CI wheel and sdist install and run; py.typed ships Toolchain uv run pytest -m toolchain (the CI toolchain job) real LuaLaTeX, epubcheck and the book build end to end Canary .github/workflows/canary.yml a daily fresh dependency resolve, to catch an upstream break early Nightly evaluation .github/workflows/nightly-eval.yml ei evaluate against a real model; paid , off until RUN_NIGHTLY_EVAL is true , and never run

docs.text: Threat model ¶ This is the threat model for turning text you do not control into a book. It says what is protected, where untrusted text enters, what stops it, and what does not yet. Every defence below names the test that holds it up; a defence with no test is listed as a gap. Written in M5, when model output first became something the pipeline typesets. It covers the book pipeline and the model layer. The API, MCP and webhook surfaces have their own controls (API key checks, rate limiting, an outbound URL policy; for MCP, a stdio server with no tool that spends the person's money unless the operator turns it on, and a per-run budget ceiling) and are not modelled here. What is protected ¶ Asset Why it matters The machine and the account running a build TeX is a programming language; text that reaches it live can read and write files and, with shell escape, run commands. API keys and tokens in the process environment They can spend money and reach the provider account. The run's budget The only brake on spend with no human in the loop. The published book KDP rejects a malformed file, and a reader should never see the machine's text in a book. Where untrusted text enters ¶ Source Reaches Trust The brief's idea text prompts Written by whoever starts a run. Model output the manuscript, then TeX and HTML Untrusted, however good the model. It can be steered by anything in its prompt. Research sources and search results fetched from the web (M6: the research stage reads them through tools) prompts, and so the manuscript Untrusted and possibly hostile. The Markdown manuscript the LaTeX generator Untrusted: model-written, or a document someone supplied. The book config ( books/<slug>.toml ) the LaTeX generator, the covers, the listing Untrusted when a model writes it; assembled by the pipeline from model output in M6. Text into TeX, LuaTeX and the EPUB ¶ The defence has two layers, and a test for each. Layer 1: nothing untrusted reaches TeX unescaped. The test test_latex_injection.py puts the tripwire }\EIcanary{ into every kind of text (paragraphs, headings, lists, quotes, tables, links, code, callouts, chapter titles, running heads, epigraphs, and every metadata field in the print and ebook documents) and fails if a live \EIcanary reaches the output. Path Defence Body text, headings, list items, table cells, quotes, titles, metadata The twelve TeX specials are escaped ( LatexEscaper ). Raw HTML in Markdown is dropped, and images are refused in the print pipeline. Bare URLs and link targets A URL is turned into a valid URI: every character outside A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ : / ? # [ ] @ ! & ( ) * + , ; = % is percent-encoded ( LatexEscaper.url ), and % and # are then escaped for TeX. A URL therefore cannot contain a backslash, a brace, ^ , a quote, < , > , a space or a control character. Found and fixed in M5; see the note below on ^ . Code blocks A block containing \end{verbatim} is refused, because TeX ends the environment there and reads the rest of the line as TeX. Found and fixed in M5. The PDF info dictionary ( \setpdfinfo ) The title, subtitle, author and edition go into a PDF string after TeX expands them, so they are cleaned of \ { } % # ^ ~ , control characters and unbalanced parentheses. Found and fixed in M5. website and email Both go through the same URL encoding. A website must be an http:// or https:// address or a bare host name ( pub.example , with an optional path); anything with another scheme ( javascript: , data: ), a space, or a colon before the first slash is refused. That also refuses host:port , which cannot be told from javascript:0/... ; write a port with its scheme. Found and fixed in M5. The ^^5c character notation ^ is escaped in text and percent-encoded in URLs, so it cannot spell a backslash. The ebook <title> A title with any of & < > " # % \ { } ~ ^ $ _ is refused outright ( EpubIdentifier ). A note on ^ , because it was found by review and then tried for real. TeX reads ^^5c as a backslash when it tokenizes the characters, which in a macro argument (emphasis, a heading, a footnote) is before \url sees them. An earlier version of the URL encoding left ^ alone. I could not make that execute anything: in LuaLaTeX, with hyperref's \url , a payload that should have written a file did not, in the plain, nested and footnote positions. In tex4ebook it did change how TeX parsed the argument (a live control sequence reached tex4ht, and the build stopped with "Argument of \S:p has an extra } "), so there it is an injection that breaks the build; whether it can do worse was not established. It is closed either way, and test_latex_injection.py holds it closed in every position. Layer 2: TeX that did run live could not run a shell. test_hostile_book.py builds a book whose every field carries a payload that, if live, writes a file by TeX's own \openout and by Lua's io.open . Neither needs shell escape, so a passing test shows the text is escaped, not merely that shell escape is off. A control proves the technique detects live TeX at all. The same test also checks the EPUB's HTML: a website and an email carrying a quote and onmouseover= never become an attribute of an element. Separately, live TeX containing \write18{touch ...} is fed straight to LuaLaTeX and to tex4ebook, and no shell command runs in either. LuaLaTeX is started with -no-shell-escape ( LatexCompiler ). tex4ebook is started without any shell-escape option, and it did not run a shell command in the test on the TeX Live it was tried with. docs.text: This is the threat model for turning text you do not control into a book. It says what is protected, where untrusted text enters, what stops it, and what does not yet. Every defence below names the test that holds it up; a defence with no test is listed as a gap. Written in M5, when model output first became something the pipeline typesets. It covers the book pipeline and the model layer. The API, MCP and webhook surfaces have their own controls (API key checks, rate limiting, an outbound URL policy; for MCP, a stdio server with no tool that spends the person's money unless the operator turns it on, and a per-run budget ceiling) and are not modelled here.
docs.title: Threat model

docs.text: Asset Why it matters The machine and the account running a build TeX is a programming language; text that reaches it live can read and write files and, with shell escape, run commands. API keys and tokens in the process environment They can spend money and reach the provider account. The run's budget The only brake on spend with no human in the loop. The published book KDP rejects a malformed file, and a reader should never see the machine's text in a book.
docs.title: What is protected

docs.text: Source Reaches Trust The brief's idea text prompts Written by whoever starts a run. Model output the manuscript, then TeX and HTML Untrusted, however good the model. It can be steered by anything in its prompt. Research sources and search results fetched from the web (M6: the research stage reads them through tools) prompts, and so the manuscript Untrusted and possibly hostile. The Markdown manuscript the LaTeX generator Untrusted: model-written, or a document someone supplied. The book config ( books/<slug>.toml ) the LaTeX generator, the covers, the listing Untrusted when a model writes it; assembled by the pipeline from model output in M6.

docs.text: The defence has two layers, and a test for each. Layer 1: nothing untrusted reaches TeX unescaped. The test test_latex_injection.py puts the tripwire }\EIcanary{ into every kind of text (paragraphs, headings, lists, quotes, tables, links, code, callouts, chapter titles, running heads, epigraphs, and every metadata field in the print and ebook documents) and fails if a live \EIcanary reaches the output. Path Defence Body text, headings, list items, table cells, quotes, titles, metadata The twelve TeX specials are escaped ( LatexEscaper ). Raw HTML in Markdown is dropped, and images are refused in the print pipeline. Bare URLs and link targets A URL is turned into a valid URI: every character outside A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ : / ? # [ ] @ ! & ( ) * + , ; = % is percent-encoded ( LatexEscaper.url ), and % and # are then escaped for TeX. A URL therefore cannot contain a backslash, a brace, ^ , a quote, < , > , a space or a control character. Found and fixed in M5; see the note below on ^ . Code blocks A block containing \end{verbatim} is refused, because TeX ends the environment there and reads the rest of the line as TeX. Found and fixed in M5. The PDF info dictionary ( \setpdfinfo ) The title, subtitle, author and edition go into a PDF string after TeX expands them, so they are cleaned of \ { } % # ^ ~ , control characters and unbalanced parentheses. Found and fixed in M5. website and email Both go through the same URL encoding. A website must be an http:// or https:// address or a bare host name ( pub.example , with an optional path); anything with another scheme ( javascript: , data: ), a space, or a colon before the first slash is refused. That also refuses host:port , which cannot be told from javascript:0/... ; write a port with its scheme. Found and fixed in M5. The ^^5c character notation ^ is escaped in text and percent-encoded in URLs, so it cannot spell a backslash. The ebook <title> A title with any of & < > " # % \ { } ~ ^ $ _ is refused outright ( EpubIdentifier ). A note on ^ , because it was found by review and then tried for real. TeX reads ^^5c as a backslash when it tokenizes the characters, which in a macro argument (emphasis, a heading, a footnote) is before \url sees them. An earlier version of the URL encoding left ^ alone. I could not make that execute anything: in LuaLaTeX, with hyperref's \url , a payload that should have written a file did not, in the plain, nested and footnote positions. In tex4ebook it did change how TeX parsed the argument (a live control sequence reached tex4ht, and the build stopped with "Argument of \S:p has an extra } "), so there it is an injection that breaks the build; whether it can do worse was not established. It is closed either way, and test_latex_injection.py holds it closed in every position. Neither needs shell escape, so a passing test shows the text is escaped, not merely that shell escape is off. A control proves the technique detects live TeX at all. The same test also checks the EPUB's HTML: a website and an email carrying a quote and onmouseover= never become an attribute of an element. Both tools are started with an allow-list environment ( ToolEnvironment ): a short list of names ( PATH , HOME , LANG , TZ , the temp directories, SYSTEMROOT , JAVA_HOME ) and the prefixes TeX needs to find its tree and fonts ( LC_ , TEXMF , TEXINPUTS , OSFONTDIR , TEX4HT , LUAINPUTS , TTFONTS ). API keys and tokens in the parent process are not passed on, so live TeX could not read them from its environment. (There is a unit test for the allow-list; none checks that a build tool cannot reach a secret by another route.)

What that does not cover: indexes and plugin files are not signed , so the hash proves only that the bytes are the ones the index described, and an index is as trustworthy as the host it came from ; the plugin is then read by a person before add . The downloader has not been run against the real internet.

The approval is the tool lock, a TOML file you review like any other commit. It pins the server's files, its name and version, and a hash of every tool it advertises, and it says which stage may call which tool. A run reads a lock only when EI_TOOL_LOCK names one. Third-party tool servers (MCP servers) run only if a person has approved them, and only while they are still what was approved. The approval is the tool lock , a TOML file you review like any other commit. This is slice 4 of ADR 0008 , built in parts. Status. A guest list with a photograph ¶ Daniel: I want the research stage to use a tool server I found. Why can I not just point it at the server and let it go? Second, the badge: a hash of the server's files, and of every tool it advertises (name, description and schema), checked every time it starts. If either changed, it does not come in. You decide whether to approve; the lock makes sure it stays what you approved. Daniel: The lock keeps it the same as what I approved, and the approving is still my job. I will read the server before I add it. The lock at a glance ¶ Question Answer Where is it read from? In a run, only the file EI_TOOL_LOCK names, and a file in the current directory is ignored. The ei tools commands use --lock , else EI_TOOL_LOCK , else ./ei-tools.lock.toml What is pinned for a local server? Its files by hash, its name, its version and a hash of its tools What is pinned for a remote server? Its address and what it advertises, and nothing else Who may call a tool? Only a stage the lock grants it to, with no wildcards What if anything differs? The process stops at start: TOOL_LOCK_MISMATCH , or TOOL_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE Is it proven against a live model? No. Only small servers written for the tests have been run In a run ¶ A model-backed run reads a lock only when EI_TOOL_LOCK names one. The file in the current directory is not read, so a stray ei-tools.lock.toml starts nothing. At start, for each locked server in name order: the locked files are compared, and a server whose files changed is never started ; the server is started with only the variables the lock names, and asked who it is and what it offers; its name, version and tools are compared with the lock, and a granted tool that cannot be offered to a model (its schema is not an object) is refused; each tool that can be offered is registered as <server>__<tool> . Any difference stops the process at start with TOOL_LOCK_MISMATCH (naming the server and every problem), and stops every server already started . A server that cannot be started or does not answer is TOOL_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE . A run does not begin with a tool it was promised and cannot have. Registering a tool does not offer it. A stage is offered its recipe's own tools plus the tools the lock grants that stage , and the tool runner runs only what was offered, so a tool that exists but was not granted is refused as "no tool named ..." even if the model asks for it. A stage the lock does not mention gets none. Everything a locked tool returns goes through the same runner as the built-in tools: its arguments are checked against the schema the server advertised, its answer (and the text of an error it reports) is cut and wrapped as untrusted text, and it is journaled. The journal remembers which server answered. A stored tool result is keyed by the tool, its arguments and the tool's revision , which for a locked tool is the hash of the server's tools. A server that is updated and locked again is asked again; a resumed run does not replay the old server's answers. Servers stay running for the life of the process, one call at a time per server, and are stopped when the runtime is closed. A server's session is limited to four hours, 2 GiB of memory and 1 GiB of disk (fixed, not settings). A server that is stopped for passing a limit fails its later calls; it is not restarted. A remote server has the four hours and the 30-second request limit; memory and disk are the other machine's, not ours. For a remote server step 1 has nothing to compare, and step 2 is a connection to its address instead of a process. Grants ¶ A grant says which stage may call which of a server's tools. It lives in the lock, so it is reviewed in the same commit as the server it applies to: ei tools grant [--lock PATH] NAME STAGE TOOL [TOOL …] ei tools revoke [--lock PATH] NAME STAGE [TOOL …] grant adds tools to a stage's list; it runs nothing. The tools must be ones the lock lists, and must be able to be offered under <server>__<tool> . There are no wildcards . revoke takes the named tools back, or all of the stage's if none are named. Revoking from a stage that has no grant is an error, so a misspelt stage is noticed. A stage name that no recipe uses is not an error here: the lock does not know the recipes, so the grant would simply never be used. ei tools list shows every stage's grants. The ei tools commands ¶ ei tools add [--lock PATH] [--env VAR …] [--replace] NAME -- COMMAND [ARG …] ei tools add [--lock PATH] [--bearer-env VAR] [--replace] --url URL NAME ei tools list [--lock PATH] ei tools verify [--lock PATH] [NAME …] add runs the server. Everything that can be refused is refused first: a bad name, a name already locked (unless --replace ), a bad environment name, a command that does not exist, a launcher, an executable that cannot be read, and a script given by a relative path (give an absolute path, so the file locked is the file run). Then the server is started once, asked who it is and what it offers, and stopped, and the entry is written. It prints every tool and its description, cut and with control characters removed, because the descriptions are written by the server: read them before you commit the lock. Options go before NAME ; an option after it gets a clear error. add --url contacts a remote server once instead of running a command. The address, the name and the variable's name are checked first, then the server is asked who it is and what it offers and the entry is written. It takes no command and no --env , and --bearer-env goes only with --url . The output says plainly that only the address and what the server advertises are locked, not its code . list shows what is locked and starts nothing. A remote server shows its url: and, if it has one, its bearer: variable. verify runs each locked server , but a server whose files changed is never started . It then compares the name, version and tools. A server that cannot be started or does not answer is a failed check, not a crash, so every server is reported. Exit 1 if any no longer matches, 2 for setup trouble or a name that is not locked. How a server is run ¶ A child process in its own session. Closing it kills the whole process group, then reaps the leader; the leader is never reaped earlier, so its id is still ours when the group is killed. A bare environment: PATH , LANG , TZ , SYSTEMROOT and LC_* , plus the variables the lock names (a name that is not set is an error). HOME and the temporary-directory variables point at the server's own throwaway directory (mode 0700), which is also its working directory and is removed when it stops. No API key or token reaches it unless the lock names it. Limits, as for the build tools: resident memory of the whole group, the size of that directory and the session's time are sampled every half second, and the server is stopped when it passes one. A limit is enforced to within what the server can use in one interval. Only the working directory counts for disk. A line is bounded (4 MiB) and a server that talks faster than it is read is slowed by a short queue. A line that is not a JSON object is refused. Its last 2,000 bytes of error output are quoted if it dies. This is not a sandbox. A server can still read any file the user can read, by absolute path, and use the network. Linux and macOS only (it needs process groups). Remote servers (HTTP) ¶ A server can also be reached at an address, over the Streamable HTTP transport of MCP: one POST per message, the answer coming back as JSON or as server-sent events. A remote entry has a url and no command, files or env ; it may name one variable, bearer_env , whose value is sent as Authorization: Bearer … . What is pinned is weaker than for a local server, and this is stated rather than hidden. A local server's files are hashed, so changed code is not started. A remote server's code is somebody else's and can change on any day, so what the lock pins is the address and what the server advertises (its name, version and a hash of its tools). The start-up check is the only check there is. A server that behaved when it was locked and changes later is caught only if it changes what it advertises, and one that was hostile when it was locked is trusted as locked. Prefer a local server whenever there is one. The rules a remote server is held to: https only, and only to a public address. The address is checked by the same URL policy as fetch_url ( PublicHttpsUrlPolicy ), before every request , so a name that has come to resolve to the machine's own network, a private range or a cloud metadata address is refused. A server on this machine or this network cannot be reached this way ; run it over stdio instead. No redirects, ever. A 3xx is an error. A server cannot send the client, or its token, anywhere else. Nothing that could hold a secret is in the address. The lock refuses a user and password, a query string and a fragment, because the lock is committed. The credential is a named environment variable, read when the connection is made; a variable that is unset, or whose value is not a printable token with no spaces, refuses the server rather than sending a blank or broken header. It is never written into an error message, which names the host alone. No cookies , no compression, a generic user agent. Every reply is bounded: at most 4 MiB, at most 128 messages per request, and 30 seconds from the first byte sent; a stream is read until the answer to the request has come, and the rest is not read. The session is the server's Mcp-Session-Id , kept from the first reply, and the protocol version it agreed, sent on later requests. Closing the session sends a DELETE whose failure is ignored. The client opens no stream of its own , so messages a server starts (sampling, roots, notifications) have nowhere to arrive; as for a local server, the client offers nothing, and a request that comes inside a reply is refused (or answered, for ping ). Failures keep a stable code: MCP_URL_REFUSED (the policy), MCP_REDIRECT_REFUSED , MCP_AUTH_REFUSED (401 or 403), MCP_SESSION_ENDED (the server forgot the session), MCP_SESSION_EXPIRED (our four hours), MCP_REPLY_INVALID (too long, not JSON, compressed, the wrong type), MCP_HTTP_ERROR (any other status). A timeout, a dropped connection, 408, 425, 429 and 5xx are transient. At run start they all arrive as TOOL_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE , or keep their own code where the failure has one. The file ¶ # Locked MCP tool servers. Written by `ei tools add`; review a change to this file like any commit. # Nothing a run does changes it. A server whose files or advertised tools differ is not started. version = 1 [[server]] name = "files" command = ["/usr/local/bin/node", "/opt/mcp/files/index.js"] env = ["FILES_ROOT"] server_name = "files-server" server_version = "1.2.0" tool_names = ["read_file", "write_file"] tools_hash = "<SHA-256 of every tool the server advertised>" [server.files] "/opt/mcp/files/index.js" = "<SHA-256>" "/usr/local/bin/node" = "<SHA-256>" [server.grants] research = ["read_file"] A remote server's entry has an address in place of the command and no files table: [[server]] name = "docs" url = "https://mcp.example.com/v1/mcp" bearer_env = "DOCS_TOKEN" server_name = "docs-server" server_version = "2.0.0" tool_names = ["search"] tools_hash = "<SHA-256 of every tool the server advertised>" [server.grants] research = ["search"] name is lowercase letters, digits and - , from a letter, up to 32 characters. A tool is offered to the model as <name>__<tool> , so files__read_file ; the double underscore is why the server name has none. A tool whose name does not fit what the model providers accept (letters, digits, - and _ , 64 in all), or that does not take an object, is not offered. command starts with the absolute path of the executable. [server.files] holds the SHA-256 of that executable and of every file named in the arguments (the script it runs). url (instead of command , env and [server.files] ) is an https address with a host and a path, at most 2048 printable characters, no user, password, query or fragment . bearer_env is the name of the variable that holds its token, optional, and only with url . Exactly one of command and url . env is the names of the variables the server is given, never their values. Values come from the environment when the server starts. Everything else is dropped by the allow-list environment. server_name , server_version , tools_hash are what the server reported when it was added. tool_names is the same list in words, so a refusal can say which tool was added or removed. [server.grants] is optional: for each stage, the tools it may call (sorted, each once, each one in tool_names ). Without it no stage gets any of the server's tools. A lock written before grants existed is read as having none, and a lock with none is written without the table. The file is read strictly: an unknown key, a missing one, a wrong or non-integer version or an entry the model refuses is an error naming the entry, never something skipped. It is written whole to a temporary name and renamed, with servers in name order, so two saves of one lock give the same bytes. What is checked ¶ The files, before anything is started. Each locked file must exist and hash the same, and each file named in the command must be locked, so a script added to the arguments is noticed. Nothing is run to find this out. The server's report, after it starts. Its name, its version and the hash of the tools it advertises must match. The hash covers every tool's name, description and schema, so a reworded description is a changed server. That matters because a description is where a hostile server hides instructions for the model. What a lock does not protect, and what is refused ¶ Installed dependencies ( node_modules , site-packages ) are not hashed, and neither is anything the server downloads or reads while it runs. A locked script is trusted code. The check and the start are separate moments. A file could change between them. A remote server is pinned by its address and what it advertises, and nothing else. See above. The connection is pinned to the address that was checked. The name is resolved once, every address is judged by the URL policy, and the request goes to the first one with the name in the Host header and in TLS, so the certificate is still checked against the name. A name that resolves differently a moment later cannot send a request inward (DNS rebinding). Only one address is tried: if it is down the request fails and is transient, rather than falling back to another. A proxy named in the environment receives the address, not the name. Launchers are refused : npx , pnpx , bunx , uvx , pipx , npm , pnpm , yarn , docker , podman and env fetch or choose code that cannot be hashed here. Install the server, then lock the executable or script it really runs. A lock proves the server is the one that was approved. It does not make a server safe to approve. What a server's tools return is untrusted text like any other tool's, and the stage's tool allowlist still decides which tools a stage can call. Resources ¶ A server that declares the MCP resources capability gets two tools added by this client , list_resources and read_resource . Their descriptions and schemas are fixed in this project's code and are not the server's, so a server cannot put instructions in them. They are in the tool list, which means everything above applies to them unchanged: they are pinned by the lock's tools hash, appear in ei tools list and verify , are offered to no stage unless granted by name ( ei tools grant files research list_resources read_resource ), and their results are wrapped as untrusted tool output like any other. list_resources sends resources/list and returns one line per resource (uri, then name and type), at most 200, with the rest counted. read_resource takes a uri of one line and at most 2,000 characters and sends resources/read , and returns the text of what comes back; a binary resource is noted as left out and its bytes are never passed on. A server that already has a tool named list_resources or read_resource gets neither of ours, and its own tool is called as any tool. Nothing is subscribed to , and no resource is read unless a granted stage's model asks for it by uri. A resource's content can change between reads, so unlike the tool list it is not pinned. A server that declares resources and was locked before this change no longer matches its lock , because its tool list now has two more tools: ei tools verify names them, and ei tools add --replace locks it again. This is the way a model reads a server's resources; it is not yet a way to give a run a resource as an input. The MCP client ¶ McpClient speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 for initialize , tools/list , tools/call and, for the two resource tools above, resources/list and resources/read , written from the protocol's published shape. It has been run against a small server written for the tests, over a real process and pipes. It has not been run against third-party MCP servers. It offers the server nothing. It announces no capabilities. A request the server sends anyway is refused with -32601 , except ping , so a server cannot ask this client to sample the model, read a root or prompt a person. Everything a server sends is untrusted and bounded. A malformed reply is an error. A tool list is cut off at 500 tools and 20 pages, and a server that sends more than 100 messages that are not the answer is cut off. A tool's answer is reduced to its text, and any other content is replaced by a note that it was left out. It speaks protocol versions 2025-06-18 , 2025-03-26 and 2024-11-05 .

Every reply is bounded: at most 4 MiB, at most 128 messages per request, and 30 seconds from the first byte sent; a stream is read until the answer to the request has come, and the rest is not read. The session is the server's Mcp-Session-Id , kept from the first reply, and the protocol version it agreed, sent on later requests. Closing the session sends a DELETE whose failure is ignored. The client opens no stream of its own , so messages a server starts (sampling, roots, notifications) have nowhere to arrive; as for a local server, the client offers nothing, and a request that comes inside a reply is refused (or answered, for ping ). Failures keep a stable code: MCP_URL_REFUSED (the policy), MCP_REDIRECT_REFUSED , MCP_AUTH_REFUSED (401 or 403), MCP_SESSION_ENDED (the server forgot the session), MCP_SESSION_EXPIRED (our four hours), MCP_REPLY_INVALID (too long, not JSON, compressed, the wrong type), MCP_HTTP_ERROR (any other status). A timeout, a dropped connection, 408, 425, 429 and 5xx are transient. At run start they all arrive as TOOL_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE , or keep their own code where the failure has one.
docs.title: Remote servers (HTTP)

docs.text: # Locked MCP tool servers. Written by `ei tools add`; review a change to this file like any commit. # Nothing a run does changes it. A server whose files or advertised tools differ is not started. version = 1 [[server]] name = "files" command = ["/usr/local/bin/node", "/opt/mcp/files/index.js"] env = ["FILES_ROOT"] server_name = "files-server" server_version = "1.2.0" tool_names = ["read_file", "write_file"] tools_hash = "<SHA-256 of every tool the server advertised>" [server.files] "/opt/mcp/files/index.js" = "<SHA-256>" "/usr/local/bin/node" = "<SHA-256>" [server.grants] research = ["read_file"] A remote server's entry has an address in place of the command and no files table: [[server]] name = "docs" url = "https://mcp.example.com/v1/mcp" bearer_env = "DOCS_TOKEN" server_name = "docs-server" server_version = "2.0.0" tool_names = ["search"] tools_hash = "<SHA-256 of every tool the server advertised>" [server.grants] research = ["search"] name is lowercase letters, digits and - , from a letter, up to 32 characters. A tool is offered to the model as <name>__<tool> , so files__read_file ; the double underscore is why the server name has none. A tool whose name does not fit what the model providers accept (letters, digits, - and _ , 64 in all), or that does not take an object, is not offered. command starts with the absolute path of the executable. [server.files] holds the SHA-256 of that executable and of every file named in the arguments (the script it runs). url (instead of command , env and [server.files] ) is an https address with a host and a path, at most 2048 printable characters, no user, password, query or fragment . bearer_env is the name of the variable that holds its token, optional, and only with url . Exactly one of command and url . env is the names of the variables the server is given, never their values. Values come from the environment when the server starts. Everything else is dropped by the allow-list environment. server_name , server_version , tools_hash are what the server reported when it was added. tool_names is the same list in words, so a refusal can say which tool was added or removed. [server.grants] is optional: for each stage, the tools it may call (sorted, each once, each one in tool_names ). Without it no stage gets any of the server's tools. A lock written before grants existed is read as having none, and a lock with none is written without the table. The file is read strictly: an unknown key, a missing one, a wrong or non-integer version or an entry the model refuses is an error naming the entry, never something skipped. It is written whole to a temporary name and renamed, with servers in name order, so two saves of one lock give the same bytes.
docs.title: The file

docs.text: The files, before anything is started. Each locked file must exist and hash the same, and each file named in the command must be locked, so a script added to the arguments is noticed. Nothing is run to find this out. The server's report, after it starts. Its name, its version and the hash of the tools it advertises must match. The hash covers every tool's name, description and schema, so a reworded description is a changed server. That matters because a description is where a hostile server hides instructions for the model.
docs.title: What is checked

docs.text: Installed dependencies ( node_modules , site-packages ) are not hashed, and neither is anything the server downloads or reads while it runs. A locked script is trusted code. The check and the start are separate moments. A file could change between them. A remote server is pinned by its address and what it advertises, and nothing else. See above. The connection is pinned to the address that was checked. The name is resolved once, every address is judged by the URL policy, and the request goes to the first one with the name in the Host header and in TLS, so the certificate is still checked against the name. A name that resolves differently a moment later cannot send a request inward (DNS rebinding). Only one address is tried: if it is down the request fails and is transient, rather than falling back to another. A proxy named in the environment receives the address, not the name. Launchers are refused : npx , pnpx , bunx , uvx , pipx , npm , pnpm , yarn , docker , podman and env fetch or choose code that cannot be hashed here. Install the server, then lock the executable or script it really runs. A lock proves the server is the one that was approved. It does not make a server safe to approve. What a server's tools return is untrusted text like any other tool's, and the stage's tool allowlist still decides which tools a stage can call.
docs.title: What a lock does not protect, and what is refused

docs.text: A server that declares the MCP resources capability gets two tools added by this client , list_resources and read_resource . Their descriptions and schemas are fixed in this project's code and are not the server's, so a server cannot put instructions in them. They are in the tool list, which means everything above applies to them unchanged: they are pinned by the lock's tools hash, appear in ei tools list and verify , are offered to no stage unless granted by name ( ei tools grant files research list_resources read_resource ), and their results are wrapped as untrusted tool output like any other. list_resources sends resources/list and returns one line per resource (uri, then name and type), at most 200, with the rest counted. read_resource takes a uri of one line and at most 2,000 characters and sends resources/read , and returns the text of what comes back; a binary resource is noted as left out and its bytes are never passed on. A server that already has a tool named list_resources or read_resource gets neither of ours, and its own tool is called as any tool. Nothing is subscribed to , and no resource is read unless a granted stage's model asks for it by uri. A resource's content can change between reads, so unlike the tool list it is not pinned. A server that declares resources and was locked before this change no longer matches its lock , because its tool list now has two more tools: ei tools verify names them, and ei tools add --replace locks it again. This is the way a model reads a server's resources; it is not yet a way to give a run a resource as an input.
docs.title: Resources

docs.text: McpClient speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 for initialize , tools/list , tools/call and, for the two resource tools above, resources/list and resources/read , written from the protocol's published shape. It has been run against a small server written for the tests, over a real process and pipes. It has not been run against third-party MCP servers. It offers the server nothing. It announces no capabilities. A request the server sends anyway is refused with -32601 , except ping , so a server cannot ask this client to sample the model, read a root or prompt a person. Everything a server sends is untrusted and bounded. A malformed reply is an error. A tool list is cut off at 500 tools and 20 pages, and a server that sends more than 100 messages that are not the answer is cut off. A tool's answer is reduced to its text, and any other content is replaced by a note that it was left out. It speaks protocol versions 2025-06-18 , 2025-03-26 and 2024-11-05 .
docs.title: The MCP client
