It makes one tiny request to the local model and one real search request, and it does not look at the database or the broker. If the machine is fine and the stack is not, find the symptom in the table below. The rows about the stack assume you ran set -a; . examples/.env; set +a . docs.text: The worker image and the TeX toolchain ¶ BLUF: There are two images. The slim runtime image runs the API and the worker. The worker-tex image adds the TeX toolchain a book's last stage, build , needs to make the PDF and EPUB. A slim worker still writes every chapter; only build fails, naming the missing tool, and what the earlier stages wrote stays in the run. A kitchen with no oven ¶ Daniel: I started the stack, a run went through every writing stage, and then it failed at build . Everything before it looked fine. What did I do wrong? Professor Feynman: Imagine a kitchen that can chop, mix and season, but has no oven. What can it make? Daniel: Everything up to the baking. And then it stops. Professor Feynman: That is the slim worker. It does every writing stage. The build stage typesets the book with LaTeX and packs an EPUB, which needs the tools in the TeX image. Without them it fails with BUILD_FAILED and names the missing tool, and the earlier work stays in the run. Daniel: So I lose nothing, I just cannot finish. Professor Feynman: You lose nothing you wrote: every chapter is stored with the run. But a failed run is final, so you cannot run build again on it. Start a new run on the worker-tex image, or build the exported files with ei book build . One limit: the TeX image is about 2.9 GB, and only a short test book has been built in it. A full-length book has not. Daniel: Slim for writing, TeX for building, and a failed build does not cost me the chapters. The Dockerfile has two images, and docker build without a target makes the slim one. Target Command Size (measured once, not in CI) For runtime (default) docker build -t engineering-influence:local . about 1.2 GB the API and the worker, as examples/docker-compose.yml runs them worker-tex docker build --target worker-tex -t engineering-influence:tex . about 2.9 GB a worker that can build books: LuaLaTeX, latexmk, tex4ebook, pdftoppm, epubcheck, a Java runtime, zip and tidy The TeX image has the same packages the CI toolchain job installs, plus poppler-utils , zip and tidy (the CI runners already have zip , but tex4ebook needs it to pack an EPUB). Recommended TeX packages are not installed. Running it ¶ The container's filesystem is read-only. Only /tmp is writable, and the image points TeX's cache there ( HOME , TEXMFVAR and TEXMFCACHE are all /tmp ). Run it with --read-only --tmpfs /tmp , and mount the book project where the build can write it: docker run --rm --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL \ -v "$PWD/my-book:/work" -w /work engineering-influence:tex \ book build demo What was verified, and what was not ¶ Verified in the image, with the read-only filesystem and all capabilities dropped: every tool runs; ei book build produces output/demo.pdf and ei book epub produces output/demo.epub , and both pass the built-in checks (the EPUB through epubcheck); ei book covers builds the covers. The test book was one short chapter. A run's own book was built in this image too: the scripted rehearsal of the whole non-fiction plan ends in the build stage, which produced the interior PDF, the EPUB (checked by epubcheck), the ebook, paperback and hardcover covers, the listing and the release manifest. That check is tests/toolchain/test_run_builds_book.py , which the CI toolchain job runs. Not verified: a full-length book, and the two workflows that build this target ( nightly-eval.yml and the release images job), which have never run. Running a stack whose worker builds books ¶ A run's last stage, build , calls the TeX tools, so the worker that runs it needs this image. The default compose file keeps the slim one. Add the override to switch only the worker: docker compose -f examples/docker-compose.yml -f examples/docker-compose.tex.yml \ --env-file examples/.env up -d --build --wait The worker also needs EI_AUTHOR_PROFILE pointing at a profile file mounted into the container, and neither compose file provides one: without it the assembled book does not build. A slim worker still does every writing stage. Only build fails ( BUILD_FAILED ), naming the missing tool, and what the earlier stages wrote stays in the run. The TeX cache ¶ LuaTeX's font loader (luaotfload) stops with "no writeable cache path" unless TEXMFCACHE points at a directory it can use. Pointing it at /tmp works. Pointing it at a subfolder of /tmp , or at a separate tmpfs, did not. The reason is not understood, so the image uses the working setting and says so in the Dockerfile .

Target Command Size (measured once, not in CI) For runtime (default) docker build -t engineering-influence:local . about 1.2 GB the API and the worker, as examples/docker-compose.yml runs them worker-tex docker build --target worker-tex -t engineering-influence:tex . about 2.9 GB a worker that can build books: LuaLaTeX, latexmk, tex4ebook, pdftoppm, epubcheck, a Java runtime, zip and tidy The TeX image has the same packages the CI toolchain job installs, plus poppler-utils , zip and tidy (the CI runners already have zip , but tex4ebook needs it to pack an EPUB). Recommended TeX packages are not installed.
docs.title: A kitchen with no oven

docs.text: The container's filesystem is read-only. Only /tmp is writable, and the image points TeX's cache there ( HOME , TEXMFVAR and TEXMFCACHE are all /tmp ). Run it with --read-only --tmpfs /tmp , and mount the book project where the build can write it: docker run --rm --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL \ -v "$PWD/my-book:/work" -w /work engineering-influence:tex \ book build demo
docs.title: Running it

docs.text: Verified in the image, with the read-only filesystem and all capabilities dropped: every tool runs; ei book build produces output/demo.pdf and ei book epub produces output/demo.epub , and both pass the built-in checks (the EPUB through epubcheck); ei book covers builds the covers. The test book was one short chapter. A run's own book was built in this image too: the scripted rehearsal of the whole non-fiction plan ends in the build stage, which produced the interior PDF, the EPUB (checked by epubcheck), the ebook, paperback and hardcover covers, the listing and the release manifest. That check is tests/toolchain/test_run_builds_book.py , which the CI toolchain job runs. Not verified: a full-length book, and the two workflows that build this target ( nightly-eval.yml and the release images job), which have never run.
docs.title: What was verified, and what was not

docs.text: A run's last stage, build , calls the TeX tools, so the worker that runs it needs this image. The default compose file keeps the slim one. Add the override to switch only the worker: docker compose -f examples/docker-compose.yml -f examples/docker-compose.tex.yml \ --env-file examples/.env up -d --build --wait The worker also needs EI_AUTHOR_PROFILE pointing at a profile file mounted into the container, and neither compose file provides one: without it the assembled book does not build. A slim worker still does every writing stage. Only build fails ( BUILD_FAILED ), naming the missing tool, and what the earlier stages wrote stays in the run.
docs.title: Running a stack whose worker builds books

docs.text: LuaTeX's font loader (luaotfload) stops with "no writeable cache path" unless TEXMFCACHE points at a directory it can use. Pointing it at /tmp works. Pointing it at a subfolder of /tmp , or at a separate tmpfs, did not. The reason is not understood, so the image uses the working setting and says so in the Dockerfile .
docs.title: The TeX cache

docs.text: ADR 0001: Isolate vibey behind ports ¶ Status: accepted for the alpha architecture Context ¶ The pipeline needs durable jobs, leases, gates, recovery, and workflow orchestration. The target runtime is vibey-engine 0.4 ( >=0.4,<0.5 ; 4.5.0, which this ADR was first written against, was removed from PyPI). The 4.5.0 source was inspected at release commit f1cd3fe0 , and the claim below was re-checked against 0.4.0 on 2026-11-18 (no entry-point group, no handler-registration hook). The worker has a JobDispatcher that routes string job kinds to handlers, but the handler mapping is assembled inside vibey.bootstrap.build_worker and the package does not expose a third-party entry point for registering handlers or workflow definitions. Vibey's skills plugins are context assets, not worker-extension hooks. Decision ¶ Engineering-influence will depend on application-owned ports for queueing, ledger persistence, workflows, gates, runners, and skills. Vibey integration will be an infrastructure adapter, never a domain or service dependency. The first supported queue adapter will use the vibey-compatible PostgreSQL ledger/outbox and RabbitMQ transport through aio-pika when a custom worker kind cannot be registered with the installed vibey release. A future vibey release may receive a native adapter without changing the application core. Consequences ¶ Pipeline phases can use domain-specific job kinds without modifying vibey. Crash recovery and at-least-once event delivery (consumers must deduplicate) remain explicit contracts of the engineering-influence adapters. The adapter must preserve lease, retry, dead-letter, and gate semantics and must be covered by integration tests against PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ. Those tests exist in tests/integration and run in the integration CI job. They cover dead-lettering, redelivery of an unacknowledged message, retries, and a run that finishes through the stack when workers die; lease and gate semantics are covered by unit tests, because the adapters do not use vibey's leases. Native vibey worker registration remains an optimization, not an architectural prerequisite.
docs.title: ADR 0001: Isolate vibey behind ports

docs.text: ADR 0002: Audience priority and sovereign agent doctrine ¶ Status: accepted for the alpha architecture Context ¶ engineering-influence is built as an autonomous, evidence-bounded content engineering and book publishing toolchain. As part of its governance, doctrine, and developer advocacy within the broader vibey ecosystem, the system needs an explicit statement of audience prioritization and an ideological foundation regarding agent orchestration and sovereign code generation. The broader ecosystem operates with Krypton and the Vibey engine—an open-source, completely free, and censorship-free architecture created to replace proprietary agent tools (such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex). Rather than producing unverified AI "slop," the engine enforces the rigor and quality standards of a Principal Software Engineer (100% branch test coverage, append-only cryptographic ledgering, and formal architectural decision records) on an architecture geared toward sovereign Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and upcoming superintelligence. Decision ¶ Audience Ordering : All external documentation, onboarding pathways, support surfaces, and release considerations in engineering-influence adopt the following strict six-tier priority order: FOSS developers — Open-source engineers building, running, and contributing to sovereign tools without licensing gates. Freelancers — Independent creators and consultants executing fixed-scope client deliverables with Principal-grade tooling and zero vendor subscriptions. Universities and academia — Researchers, educators, and scholars seeking reproducible methodology, open papers, and verified citations. Governments and militaries — Sovereign agencies and public-sector institutions requiring deterministic provenance, local air-gapped models, and tamper-evident audit trails. Non-profit orgs — Mission-driven teams needing budget-holding, verifiable software that respects data sovereignty. Industry teams — Commercial engineering teams, platform architects, and enterprise adopters. Sovereign Engine Doctrine : The toolchain aligns with the principle that software delivery must survive transient agent failures and vendor lock-in. Code generation must satisfy Principal-grade engineering contracts rather than conversational shortcuts. All tools, SDKs, and interfaces remain free, open, and unconstrained by vendor-imposed ideological censorship. Consequences ¶ Documentation surfaces, examples, and entry-point guides must address audiences in the 1–6 sequence. Project templates and CLI workflows will prioritize local, sovereign model runners as first-class targets. Features tailored to earlier audiences (e.g., local FOSS self-hosting) take precedence over enterprise-specific integrations.

docs.text: ADR 0003: Definition of 1.0 ¶ Status: accepted Context ¶ The package is alpha ( 0.1.0a1 ). The orchestration and the KDP packaging are built, but the writing is not: the runner and gate are deterministic placeholders, nothing carries a book's brief to the worker, stage output is discarded, and no command turns an idea into files. The vibey standards define no "stable" bar, so this ADR sets one. Decision ¶ 1.0.0 ships only when every criterion below holds, with the stated evidence. # Criterion Evidence A1 ei book create --kind nonfiction "<idea>" and --kind novel "<idea>" each produce, with nobody in the loop, an interior PDF, an EPUB, an ebook cover, a paperback wrap, listing.md , publication-report.json and quality-report.json Two archived dogfood runs A2 Those files pass ei book publish --strict-release with epubcheck required and real LuaLaTeX CI toolchain job, dogfood logs A3 Both books load in Kindle Previewer and KDP's print previewer without errors Manual check, screenshots in the release PR A4 A run killed at any stage resumes to the same end state without paying for finished stages again Chaos and resume tests A5 No run exceeds its budget cap; the pre-flight estimate is within 30% of actual spend on the evaluation set Property test, evaluation report A6 Mean rubric score is at least 3.5 of 5 on every dimension and falls no more than 0.2 from the previous release Nightly paid evaluation A7 These contracts are frozen and snapshot-tested: the brief and book-config schemas, the REST OpenAPI document, the webhook catalogue, the job message, the CLI, the SDK and the MCP tools Snapshot tests, docs/COMPATIBILITY.md A8 Every quality gate in CONTRIBUTING.md passes, including 100% line and branch coverage of the core and the SDK, enforced as one global threshold CI A9 Core and SDK are published to PyPI in lockstep, and images to GHCR, with attestations Release run, gh attestation verify A10 Every documented claim matches the code, and a threat model exists Documentation and release audits The run is autonomous: it never waits for a person. A bounded revision loop that runs out keeps the best version and records the problem in quality-report.json . A budget planner reserves the cost of finishing the book before it spends on revisions, so a run always completes. Uploading to KDP stays manual, because KDP has no API. Scope at 1.0 is non-fiction and novels. The screenplay, hub, spokes and distribution stages are experimental and outside the stable contract. Consequences ¶ Each milestone toward 1.0 maps to a pre-release (alpha, beta, release candidate, see ADR 0004). The 1.0.0 release commit sets the version by hand, as every release does (ADR 0005). Conventional commits with BREAKING CHANGE: footers are still required, but they do not choose the version. Paid model runs, publishing and the KDP upload need the maintainer's explicit go-ahead.
docs.title: ADR 0003: Definition of 1.0

docs.text: ADR 0004: Versioning, compatibility and deprecation ¶ Status: accepted Context ¶ Several interfaces are public: the REST API, the webhook payloads, the job message, the CLI, the SDK, the MCP tools and the book and brief configuration files. None has a stability promise yet. Decision ¶ The package follows Semantic Versioning from 1.0.0. Before 1.0.0, minor versions may break contracts, and the changelog says so. The public contracts are those listed in criterion A7 of ADR 0003. Anything else, including internal modules, is not covered. Every contract carries a schema_version (the REST API carries it in the path, /v1/ ). A new major schema version runs beside the old one for at least one minor release. A feature scheduled for removal is deprecated for at least one minor release first: it keeps working, logs a warning once, and appears under "Deprecated" in the changelog. Pre-releases follow the plan: alpha while contracts are still moving, beta ( b ) once ei book create works end to end, release candidate ( rc ) once the contracts are frozen. The core package and the SDK share one version number and release together. Only the latest minor release receives fixes, until a support table in SECURITY.md says more. Consequences ¶ Contract changes after the freeze need a snapshot test update and a changelog entry. The release workflow keeps refusing a tag whose core and SDK versions differ.

docs.text: ADR 0005: Release flow and changelog fragments ¶ Status: accepted; points 2 and 5 are replaced by ADR 0009 Context ¶ ADR 0003 said that the vibey release flow derives versions. That is not how this repository releases. docs/RELEASING.md describes what exists and works: a person sets __version__ by hand, renames the changelog section, merges to main , and tags v<version> ; the release.yml guard refuses a tag that disagrees with the code, the changelog or the branch. The ADR 0004 pre-release tiers ( a , b , rc ) depend on that hand-set version, because a derived version cannot express them. Every pull request also edits the one ## Unreleased section of CHANGELOG.md . Concurrent pull requests conflict on it, and the conflicts are noise. Decision ¶ The version is set by hand, in the release commit. develop carries the version of the last release until the commit that prepares the next one. Documents that name the current alpha ( README.md , llms.txt , docs/GETTING_STARTED.md ) change in that same commit. This is deliberate: develop must not claim a version that has not been released. The tag guard stays authoritative. release.yml keeps refusing a tag whose version disagrees with the code, with the changelog, or with main . It also refuses a tag while unfolded fragments remain (point 3). Changes are recorded as fragments. A pull request that changes behaviour adds a file changelog.d/<short-slug>.md holding one paragraph, the text of one changelog bullet. It does not edit CHANGELOG.md . Before tagging, scripts/fold_changelog.py <version> moves every fragment into a ## <version> section, in file-name order, and deletes the fragment files. Breaking changes follow ADR 0004. The fragment says what broke and what to do. The vibey claim about deriving major versions from BREAKING CHANGE: footers is not used here: footers stay required by the conventional-commit check, but the version is still chosen by a person. Releases remain gated. Tagging, publishing to PyPI and pushing images need an explicit approval, as docs/RELEASING.md states. Nothing in this ADR automates them. Consequences ¶ Concurrent pull requests no longer conflict on the changelog. A release is one reviewable commit that sets the version, folds the fragments and updates the status text. A contributor who forgets a fragment is caught in review, not by tooling; the guard only catches fragments left behind. ADR 0003's wording is corrected to match.
docs.title: ADR 0005: Release flow and changelog fragments

docs.text: ADR 0006: Onion layers, interfaces and one class per file ¶ Status: accepted and implemented (see "As built") Context ¶ The package grew in two halves. The orchestration half ( services , controllers , repositories , infrastructure , interaction , runtime ) follows an onion, with one class per file and ABC interfaces in sibling interfaces/ folders. The packaging half ( publishing/ , 138 files, 6,386 of the 10,229 lines) is a single flat layer: 119 plain classes, models, services and adapters mixed, no interfaces, and a controller that imports 21 concrete classes. Several layers also break their own rules: composition happens in services, controllers and transports, and the architecture test forbids domain from importing errors , which is backwards for the innermost ring. The model-backed stages of ADR 0003 will add as much code again. They need the rules to be mechanical before they arrive, not after. Decision ¶ Layers, innermost first ¶ Layer Holds May import errors exception classes standard library models (was domain ) entities and value objects, enums errors , standard library contracts wire and config schemas (pydantic) errors , models , pydantic interfaces ports shared across layers standard library and other interfaces at run time; errors , models , contracts only under TYPE_CHECKING services use cases and policy the layers above, plus pure-compute libraries (numpy, markdown-it-py, defusedxml) controllers one entry point per capability the layers above, services repositories persistence, project files and sources the layers above, services.interfaces ; database and file libraries infrastructure adapters to tools, networks, images, PDFs, archives the layers above, services.interfaces ; any effectful library or process interactions (was interaction ) transports: REST, MCP, CLI, webhooks in controllers , the layers above, services.interfaces ; transport libraries runtime the composition root everything Dependencies point inward. Only runtime constructs concrete classes from more than one layer. Effectful libraries (PIL, pypdf, pdfplumber, reportlab, subprocess, zipfile, entry points, git, clocks, file reads and writes) never appear in models , contracts or services . A service that needs one depends on an interface and an adapter in infrastructure or repositories provides it. publishing/ is split across these layers. Its subpackage names ( epub , covers , typesetting , qa , release ) become folders inside the layers; its top-level modules go under publishing/ . errors is innermost. Models may import errors; the old rule that forbade it is removed. Interfaces ¶ Every folder, including every new subfolder, has an interfaces/ folder. interfaces/ packages and assets/ are exempt, and so is infrastructure/migrations/ (see "As built"). One class per file. x/foo.py defining Foo is paired with x/interfaces/foo_interface.py defining FooInterface , and Foo inherits it. An interface is an ABC with __slots__ = () that declares methods only , never fields or abstract properties. Fields would change what pydantic and dataclasses generate. Dataclasses, pydantic models, SQLModel tables and exceptions inherit their ABC interface; this was checked to leave model_fields , the OpenAPI schema and table metadata unchanged. Enums use a protocol, not an ABC. Enum and ABC have conflicting metaclasses and mypy does not catch it. An enum gets a runtime_checkable Protocol and a test that checks the enum against it. A class that already implements a top-level interface in interfaces/ satisfies the rule. The 20 *Port classes there are renamed *Interface . Interface modules import only the standard library and other interfaces at run time. Types from models , contracts and errors come in under TYPE_CHECKING with from __future__ import annotations , so signatures stay exact and mypy still checks overrides. Public API ¶ The cover-plugin API is public: entry-point group engineering_influence.covers , and the books repository imports 17 classes by their deep paths: 13 in its cover scripts, and CoverBuilder , CoverPluginLoader , PainterRegistry and ProjectLayout in its README (R0 counted only the 13; R3 corrected it). A façade engineering_influence.covers re-exports the cover classes with an __all__ ; ProjectLayout , a model, keeps a deprecated shim at its old path. The old engineering_influence.publishing.covers.* paths stay as shims that re-export the same class objects (the loader checks isinstance(plugin, CoverPlugin) ) and emit a one-time DeprecationWarning , for one minor release (ADR 0004). The entry-point group does not change. These classes keep their names even where they do not end in Interface . Method ¶ scripts/refactor/move_map.toml is the plan of record: for every class, where it lives, where it goes, its interface and why. A pull request that moves or reclassifies a class edits its entry. An architecture test keeps the map complete against the tree. scripts/refactor/inventory.py reports the facts the map is built from. Rules arrive as ratchets : tests/architecture/ratchet.json records how many violations each rule has today. A rule can only improve, and the test fails if a count rises, or falls without the file being lowered. Each restructuring PR lowers counts; the last one makes every count zero and the rules strict. Moves use git mv and a codemod that rewrites imports everywhere, including strings that name modules. No behaviour changes. Every restructuring PR must keep the test count, 100% coverage, the OpenAPI document, the CLI help, the MCP tool list and the fixture book's structural snapshot ( tests/fixtures/fixture_book/expected/snapshot.json ) unchanged. Feature work on publishing/ and the layers being moved pauses while the restructure is in flight. Consequences ¶ A reader can predict where a class lives and what it may import, and CI can check it. Roughly 240 new interface files exist. They are generated, and the ratchets stop them drifting from their classes. Test doubles become real implementations of the interfaces, which replaces the monkeypatch.setattr calls that patch production classes (33 setattr calls today, some of them on sys ). Moving every class changes every import path. The public cover-plugin paths are protected by shims; everything else is internal. As built ¶ The restructure shipped as pull requests R0 to R13 ( changelog.d/m1-r*.md has one entry for each). Four things differ from the plan above, and the plan is left as written so the difference is visible: The ratchets were retired. The plan lowered counts in tests/architecture/ratchet.json until every rule reached zero. They did, so R11 deleted the file and test_rules.py now asserts that each of nine metrics is zero everywhere and that none has been dropped. A violation fails the build; it is not recorded. The cover-plugin shims were removed in R11, with no deprecation window. publishing.covers.* and publishing.project_layout re-exported the real classes for a time, then were deleted. ADR 0004 lets a minor version before 1.0 break a contract if the changelog says so, and the R11 entry is marked Breaking . The names live on in the engineering_influence.covers facade. Test doubles replaced the patches. The plan counted 33 monkeypatch.setattr calls. R12 and R13 injected fakes through constructors, and tests/architecture/test_no_patching.py now permits only standard-library calls at the system boundary ( subprocess.run , sys.argv , sys.path , zipfile.ZipFile.testzip ) and one class a test defines. A new patch of anything else fails the build, and a boundary entry no test uses any more fails it too. Some pure helpers are still built where they are used. PublishingController builds its audit classes and EpubVerifier builds its own checks, because no test has to replace them. Anything a test replaces, and every adapter, is injected. Alembic migrations are exempt from the file rules. An Alembic script is a module of functions and constants by contract ( upgrade() , downgrade() , revision ), so infrastructure/migrations/ is excluded from the one-class-per-file, no-loose-function, interface-folder and layer-matrix checks through SCRIPT_FOLDERS in tests/architecture/architecture_metrics.py . The exemption names that folder and nothing else. The scripts are still linted, type-checked with mypy --strict and run by the tests, which also compare the schema they build with the SQLModel models, so a model change without a migration fails the build. The class that drives them, SchemaMigrator , follows every rule.

docs.text: The package grew in two halves. The orchestration half ( services , controllers , repositories , infrastructure , interaction , runtime ) follows an onion, with one class per file and ABC interfaces in sibling interfaces/ folders. The packaging half ( publishing/ , 138 files, 6,386 of the 10,229 lines) is a single flat layer: 119 plain classes, models, services and adapters mixed, no interfaces, and a controller that imports 21 concrete classes. Several layers also break their own rules: composition happens in services, controllers and transports, and the architecture test forbids domain from importing errors , which is backwards for the innermost ring. The model-backed stages of ADR 0003 will add as much code again. They need the rules to be mechanical before they arrive, not after.

docs.text: Every folder, including every new subfolder, has an interfaces/ folder. interfaces/ packages and assets/ are exempt, and so is infrastructure/migrations/ (see "As built"). One class per file. x/foo.py defining Foo is paired with x/interfaces/foo_interface.py defining FooInterface , and Foo inherits it. An interface is an ABC with __slots__ = () that declares methods only , never fields or abstract properties. Fields would change what pydantic and dataclasses generate. Dataclasses, pydantic models, SQLModel tables and exceptions inherit their ABC interface; this was checked to leave model_fields , the OpenAPI schema and table metadata unchanged. Enums use a protocol, not an ABC. Enum and ABC have conflicting metaclasses and mypy does not catch it. An enum gets a runtime_checkable Protocol and a test that checks the enum against it. A class that already implements a top-level interface in interfaces/ satisfies the rule. The 20 *Port classes there are renamed *Interface . Interface modules import only the standard library and other interfaces at run time. Types from models , contracts and errors come in under TYPE_CHECKING with from __future__ import annotations , so signatures stay exact and mypy still checks overrides.

docs.text: ADR 0007: Models are called over plain httpx, behind ModelInterface ¶ Status: accepted Context ¶ M5 needs adapters for Anthropic and for OpenAI-compatible servers (which also covers local models). The lock already contains the anthropic and openai SDKs, but only as transitive dependencies of vibey-engine , at the versions that package pins. httpx is already a direct dependency of the webhooks extra. Decision ¶ Adapters use httpx directly , not the vendor SDKs. Both APIs are one JSON POST for a completion and one for a token count. The transport is injected. An adapter takes an httpx.Client in its constructor, so tests pass one built on httpx.MockTransport and record cassettes without patching, as tests/architecture/test_no_patching.py requires. Retry classification stays ours. An adapter maps status codes onto TransientStageError (timeout, 429 without a spent-credit body, 5xx), CapacityExhaustedError (credit gone, 401/403) or an unrecoverable error, so the run machinery never sees a vendor exception. The domain types are vendor-neutral : ModelRequest , ModelResponse , ModelUsage and ProviderDescriptor , with integer micro-dollar prices that round up. Consequences ¶ The runtime dependency set does not grow, and a vibey-engine repin cannot change what the adapters send. We own request shaping, header handling, prompt-cache markers and response parsing, and must track API changes ourselves. Cassettes recorded from synthetic briefs and a paid marker for live checks keep that honest. Streaming is not used: a book stage waits for a whole response, and the run journal stores the whole response.

docs.text: ADR 0008: The model gets tools, each stage gets only the ones it names ¶ Status: proposed Context ¶ Until now a model call returns text and nothing else (ADR 0007), and the threat model counts that as a defence: a successful prompt injection can change what a chapter says, but it cannot read a file, call a service or spend money outside the run. The maintainer has decided that the model should have tools, and that web search in particular should be a tool the model calls rather than a fixed step. The scope given was web search and page fetch, an outbound MCP client, skills, plugins and marketplaces, with two conditions: a stage may use only the tools declared for it, and anything third-party runs only if it is pinned and hash-locked. That changes a security rule, the shape of the journal that makes a resumed run free, and what the project can freeze for 1.0. It deserves a reviewed design before code. Decision ¶ Tool use is part of the model port, and adapters never run tools. ModelRequest carries tool definitions (a name, a description and a JSON schema). ModelResponse can carry tool calls and a new stop reason, tool_use . Each adapter maps these onto its provider's format (content blocks for Anthropic, tool_calls and role: tool for OpenAI-compatible servers). An adapter still returns what the model said and nothing more, so the exception type stays the contract. A bounded loop runs the tools. A service ( RunToolLoop ) sits above AskModel . It caps model turns, tool calls, the time of each call, the size of each result and the run's spend (every turn reserves against the SpendGuard ). It runs a call through a ToolRunner port and feeds the result back. A loop that hits a limit ends with a blocking issue and the stage stops, as an incomplete answer does today. A tool turn is journaled whole. Every model call keeps its journal entry. Every tool call is journaled too: the tool, a canonical hash of its arguments and its result. A resumed run replays the stored result for nothing and gets the same bytes, instead of searching again against a web that has moved. The key of each later model call includes a hash of the transcript so far, so a replay is only ever of the same conversation. This also closes the double-journaling cost gap noted in M5, which matters more once calls come in loops. Each stage declares its tools; none by default. A StageRecipe lists the tools its stage may use. Only those are offered to the model and only those can run. A call to anything else is answered with "no such tool" and still counts against the call limit. Research gets web_search and fetch_url ; drafting gets none. No tool is ever discovered at run time. No stage asks a person for permission: the allowlist is the permission, and it is part of the code and config a person reviews. Whatever a tool returns is untrusted text. A result is fed back inside an <untrusted> block under a system prompt that says so, is size-capped, and cannot close its own block. Fetched pages go through HtmlTextExtractor . A fetch_url result is also recorded as a SourceRecord (address, title, hash of the text), which is what claim verification later checks against. The native tools are thin wrappers. web_search wraps SearchProviderInterface (Brave first) and returns links and titles only. fetch_url wraps SourceFetcherInterface , so it inherits the URL policy at every redirect, the size and encoding limits and the hidden-text stripping. Their keys come from the secret provider by name and never reach the model or a log. MCP is an outbound client, with servers you list. A server is declared in a lock file with a pinned command or address and version, and with a hash of the tool definitions it advertised when it was added. If a server later advertises different tools or descriptions (tool poisoning, or a changed server), the run refuses to start. Servers are reached over stdio, in a subprocess with an allow-list environment and the same time, memory and disk limits as the build tools, or over HTTP to an address the URL policy accepts, with no redirects. A server's tool is offered to a stage only if the stage names it ( server.tool ). Skills are versioned prompt packs, never code and never tools. A skill adds named prompt parts, in the same TOML shape and with the same version lock as PromptTemplate . Loading one cannot add a tool, run a command or widen a stage's allowlist. Plugins and marketplaces are install-time, human-driven, and pinned. A plugin is a bundle of MCP server definitions and skills. A marketplace is only an index of such bundles, with an address and a hash for each. A person runs ei tools add to copy an entry into the lock file, which records the pinned version and the SHA-256 of the bundle; the change is reviewed like any other commit. Nothing updates itself, and a run never contacts a marketplace. This is how the request for marketplaces fits the condition that third-party code must be pinned and hash-locked: a marketplace is where a person finds something to pin, not a source a run trusts. ACP is not a tool source. The Agent Client Protocol lets an editor or client drive this agent. It is the inbound surface already planned for M8, with its own consent rules for spend. It gives the model no tools and is built separately. Consequences ¶ The threat model's "the model has no tools" is replaced by decisions 2, 4 and 5, and the document is updated as each lands. Until a tool exists the model has none. A prompt injection in a search result or page can now try to make the model call a tool. The defences are the per-stage allowlist (a drafting stage has nothing to call), the loop's limits, the spend reservation, the untrusted wrapping, and the fact that the native tools can only read public pages through the URL policy. An MCP server widens this and is the reason it is pinned, hash-locked, resource-limited and named per stage. The journal format changes (decision 3). Existing journal rows stay readable; a run started before the change replays as before. 1.0 freezes less if less ships: the tool-lock file format, the tool schema the model sees and the ei tools commands become contracts once released. Skills, plugins and marketplaces are the parts most likely to want change, so they land last and may ship as experimental. Two costs: a model call that reaches for a tool takes more turns than one that does not, and a stage with tools is harder to reproduce exactly than one without, which is what the journal replay is for. Slices ¶ Tool use in the model port and both adapters, with cassettes for tool turns. RunToolLoop , the tool journal and replay, the ToolRunner port and the per-stage allowlist. web_search and fetch_url as tools; the research stage uses them. The tool lock file and ei tools add ; the MCP client over stdio, then HTTP. Skills as prompt packs. Plugins and marketplace indexes, install-time only. Open questions ¶ How strong a sandbox a stdio MCP server needs beyond the environment allow-list and resource limits, on macOS and on Linux. Whether a tool may carry its own secret, and how that is named in the lock file without the value ever being in it. Whether a stage's tool allowlist lives with its recipe in code or in the lock file, or both with the lock file able to narrow but never widen the code's list. This ADR leans to the last. Amendments from slice 4 ¶ Recorded on 2026-11-22 while building slice 4 ( TOOL_LOCK.md ). What the lock pins (decision 7). The maintainer chose to hash the files, not only the tool definitions: the lock records the SHA-256 of a stdio server's executable and of every script among its arguments, plus the server's reported name and version and a hash of the tools it advertises. A launcher that fetches code on each run ( npx , uvx , docker and the like) is refused, because what it would run cannot be hashed. Installed dependencies are not covered, and this is stated rather than hidden. Names. A tool from a server is offered to the model as <server>__<tool> , because the providers accept only letters, digits, - and _ ; recipes and the lock use the same form, not server.tool . A tool's secret (open question 2). The lock names the environment variables a server is given, never their values. Values come from the environment at start. Slicing. Slice 4 is built as 4a (lock models, file format, MCP client over an abstract transport, verifier), 4b (a stdio transport under the build tools' limits, and ei tools ), 4c (wiring the registry and the start-up check) and 4d (HTTP). Running a server (4b). A stdio server runs in its own process group with a bare environment and a throwaway home, under time, memory and disk limits, and is stopped by killing the group before the leader is reaped. It is not sandboxed. ei tools add runs the server, so it refuses a launcher, a missing executable or a relative script before starting anything, and ei tools verify never starts a server whose files have changed. Where a stage's permission for a locked tool lives (4c; the third open question). In the lock file, chosen by the maintainer: a per-server [server.grants] table naming, for each stage, exactly which of the server's tools it may call, with no wildcards. Recipes in code still name the built-in tools; the stage's offered tools are the recipe's plus the lock's grants. It is reviewed in the same commit as the server. A run reads a lock only when EI_TOOL_LOCK names it , so a stray file in the working directory starts no server, and a tool's journal key includes the tool's revision (for a locked tool, the hash of the server's tools) so a replaced server's old answers are not replayed. Remote servers (4d). HTTP follows decision 7 and the slices above, with these choices. The transport is Streamable HTTP, one POST per message, the answer as JSON or as events read within the same request, and no stream of the client's own. A remote entry locks the address and what the server advertises; its code cannot be hashed, and the weaker pin is stated in the docs and the ei tools add output rather than hidden. The address goes through the existing public-https URL policy before every request, with no redirects, so a server on this machine or network is reached over stdio, not HTTP ; a loosening for local development is a separate decision. Credentials are a named variable ( bearer_env ), never part of the address, and the lock refuses a user, query or fragment so a secret cannot be committed in a URL. Other auth schemes (OAuth, custom headers) are not built. Outbound connections are pinned to the checked address (after 4d). A security review of the remote transport found what the docs had listed as a gap: the policy resolved a name when asked and the client resolved it again when it connected. PublicHttpsUrlPinner now resolves once, has the policy judge every address, and hands the caller the vetted address with the name for the Host header and for TLS, so the certificate is still checked against the name. fetch_url and the remote transport use it; only one address is tried, and fetch_url sends Connection: close so a connection verified for one name is not reused for another that shares its address. Signed webhook delivery was not changed. Amendments from slice 5 ¶ Recorded on 2026-11-22 while building slice 5 ( SKILLS.md ). A skill is one file of text, with a part for each stage it speaks to (decision 8). The ADR said "named prompt parts, in the same TOML shape as PromptTemplate ". A template's parts are the pieces of one prompt ( system , user ) with blanks to fill; a skill's parts are which stage the text is for . A skill has no blanks, so there is nothing to fill and no value to smuggle into; it has no untrusted list, because all of it is text a person chose; and any key it should not have ( command , tools , url ) is refused by name. The version lock is a hash, in its own lock file. A shipped template is pinned by a fingerprint in a test fixture. A skill is installed by a person, so it is pinned by the SHA-256 of its file's bytes in ei-skills.lock.toml , which a run reads only when EI_SKILL_LOCK names it. It is a separate file from the tool lock so either can be used alone; plugins (slice 6) will copy entries into both. ei skills add keeps a copy of the file in a skills/ folder beside the lock, so what is committed is what is hashed, and the lock needs no paths. Permission is per stage and explicit, as for tools. A new skill is enabled for no stage. ei skills enable NAME STAGE checks the file against its hash and refuses a stage the skill has no text for; at most four skills may be enabled for one stage; locking a skill again clears its stages, because new text has not been approved for anything. Where the text goes (a decision the ADR left open). At the end of the user part of the stage's prompt, in a delimited block under a fixed frame (the skill_guidance template), never in the system part. It is not wrapped as <untrusted> : unlike a page, it is meant to instruct, and the person approved it. The trade-off is stated plainly in SKILLS.md : a skill that was hostile when it was locked is trusted as locked. A copy of the block's tags inside a skill is defused. What a person approved is what a model sees. Text that renders as nothing or reorders what is shown (control characters, zero-width and bidirectional marks, line and paragraph separators, private-use and unassigned code points) is refused when the skill is read, and each part is capped, so a skill cannot hide an instruction from the review the lock exists for. The journal key (decision 3) names the skills. A stage with skills sends <template>@<n>+skill_guidance@<n>:<digest> , the digest covering each skill's name, version and hash, so a resumed run replays an answer only for the same text. A stage with no skill enabled sends exactly the prompt and version it always did, so existing journals are unaffected. The check happens once, at start, before anything else. Skills enabled for some stage are read and hashed when the stage executor is built, before any tool server is started or any model is called; the text is then held for the life of the process, so every stage of a run sees the same text. A skill that is installed but enabled for no stage is not read. What a skill still cannot do. It adds no tool, changes no stage's allowlist, output cap or system prompt, and cannot raise a budget: those are decided in code, in the tool lock and in the spend guard. Amendments from slice 6a ¶ Recorded on 2026-11-22 while building the first part of slice 6 ( PLUGINS.md ). Slice 6 is split as slice 4 was: 6a plugins installed from a file on disk, 6b marketplace indexes and fetching. Installing a plugin runs and contacts nothing (decision 9). The ADR said a person runs ei tools add to copy an entry into the lock. The installer therefore does not run a bundle's servers: a bundle is text from someone else, and ei tools add is the step that starts a server (or contacts one) and pins what it reports. The installer locks the bundle's skills (each enabled for no stage) and prints the exact ei tools add command for each server, shell-quoted, for a person to review and run. A bundle cannot decide what a model may do. There is no key for a grant, for a stage to enable a skill for, or for anything else; any unknown key is refused. A server definition is held to the same rules the tool lock uses (an absolute command that is not a launcher, an https address with no secret in it), so a plugin cannot describe a server the lock would refuse. One file, one hash. A plugin is a single TOML file with [[server]] and [[skill]] tables, so one SHA-256 pins everything a person reviewed. Skills in it are read by the same strict parser as a skill file, and are written into the skill lock as skill files, so they are ordinary skills afterwards. A third lock file, which a run never reads. ei-plugins.lock.toml records the bundle's hash, the servers it described and the hash each skill was locked under, so ei plugins verify can check the bundle that was reviewed and ei plugins remove can undo the install. What a run may do stays in the tool lock and the skill lock; no new thing is added to the run's trust surface. No replace. A plugin that is installed, or whose skills are already locked, is refused before anything is written. Installing a newer version is remove then add , because replacing text a person approved is a decision, not a side effect. remove deletes only skills that are still exactly what the plugin installed. An install either completes or leaves nothing. The bundle's copy is written first, and a failure while locking a later skill removes the copy and the skills already locked. Amendments from slice 6b ¶ Recorded on 2026-11-22 while building the second part of slice 6 ( PLUGINS.md ). A marketplace is only an index, and a download is a separate step from an install (decision 9). An index is a TOML file of plugin names, versions, descriptions, addresses and SHA-256 hashes, with no other key. ei plugins fetch INDEX NAME downloads one plugin file, checks its hash against the index's before reading it as anything , checks that it is the plugin and version the index named, and saves it; it installs nothing. A person reads it with ei plugins show and installs it with ei plugins add , which stays an offline step on a local file. This keeps the one network-facing command narrow: it can produce a file, and cannot change a lock. A run never contacts a marketplace. Only search and fetch , run by a person, can use a network, and add , show , verify and remove never do. The download is held to the rules every other outbound connection here is. It goes through the same pinned-address URL policy as fetch_url and the remote tool transport (https, a public address checked each time, the connection made to the address that was checked with the name in TLS), follows no redirect, sends no cookie or credential, accepts no compression and is bounded to 512 KiB and 30 seconds. An address in an index is held to the lock's rules for a remote server (no user, password, query string or fragment). An index is not trusted more than its host. Indexes and plugin files are not signed, so the hash only proves that the bytes are the ones the index described. Vouching for a publisher (signatures, a key to trust) is a decision this slice does not make; the defence is that a person reads the file and that installing enables nothing. The core install still works without httpx . The downloader is built on first use, and a missing dependency becomes a message that names the runtime extra; a local index file needs no network code at all. Amendments from M6.5: SKILL.md import and reference sections (2026-11-22) ¶ A skill may carry reference sections ( [reference] , "title" = "text" ), read on request. This is the one place a skill changes what a stage is offered, and it adds exactly one built-in, read-only tool: read_skill . It is offered to a stage only when a reference skill is enabled for that stage, and the guidance says so ( Guidance.tools ), so the prompt never points at a tool the model was not given. It can return the text of a section of a skill the lock approved, hash-checked at start, and nothing else: no file, no address, no other state. The stage's prompt is the permission. The tool is shared, so each call is checked against what the stage's own prompt lists, through the same refuses hook fetch_url uses. A skill enabled for one stage cannot be read from another. A section's text is returned as the tool's result, which the runner wraps as untrusted, and a section is never longer than the runner's result limit, so it is never cut. A stored result carries a digest of every reference section as its revision, so a changed skill is not answered from an old result. Skills from the wild: ei skills import reads a SKILL.md (frontmatter name and description , markdown body cut at its ## headings) into an ordinary skill file for review. It sets aside every other frontmatter key ( allowed-tools , domains ), because a skill grants nothing, and it never locks, enables or overwrites. --reference keeps the sections for read_skill ; without it they become stage text and must fit a part (8,000 characters) or be chosen with --section . The skill guidance template is version 2, because the frame gained the reference note. Amendments from M6.5: Claude Code plugin folder import (2026-11-22) ¶ ei plugins import FOLDER reads a plugin folder's .claude-plugin/plugin.json , .mcp.json and skills/*/SKILL.md , and writes an ordinary bundle for review. It opens only those files, follows no link, runs nothing, and never replaces a file. The bytes are parsed again before they are written. Nothing widens. Skills become reference skills enabled for no stage. A server is kept only when the tool lock's own rules accept it (an absolute, non-launcher command, or an https address with no secret in it); ${...} placeholders are not expanded; environment values and headers are not copied, only environment names and a Bearer ${NAME} token as bearer_env . Commands, agents, hooks, output styles, monitors and .lsp.json are named and set aside, never read or run. Every skipped piece is printed with its reason. Decision 9 is unchanged: importing, like installing, starts nothing, contacts nothing, grants nothing and enables nothing. ei plugins search FILE.json lists a Claude Code marketplace.json (four fields read per plugin, all other keys ignored; sources classified as path , github , url or other and printed, never followed). It fetches, clones and installs nothing, because a marketplace names folders and repositories rather than hashable files; a path source in a local marketplace prints the ei plugins import command for it. The import is where the bundle is read and checked. Pinning a source by commit and hash-checking a fetched folder is not built. Amendments from M6.5: MCP resources (2026-11-23) ¶ Resources are reached as two tools the client adds , list_resources and read_resource , when a server declares the resources capability and has no tool of those names. Their descriptions and schemas are fixed in this project's code, not the server's. Because they are in the tool list they are pinned by the tools hash, granted to a stage only by name, offered to no stage by default, and returned as untrusted tool output. No new lock field, grant kind or code path in the runner. A resource is read only on request , by a stage the lock grants it, by the uri the model names: text only (a binary resource is noted as left out), a uri of one line and at most 2,000 characters, a listing of at most 200 entries. docs.title: ADR 0008: The model gets tools, each stage gets only the ones it names

docs.text: Status: proposed
docs.title: ADR 0008: The model gets tools, each stage gets only the ones it names

docs.text: Until now a model call returns text and nothing else (ADR 0007), and the threat model counts that as a defence: a successful prompt injection can change what a chapter says, but it cannot read a file, call a service or spend money outside the run. The maintainer has decided that the model should have tools, and that web search in particular should be a tool the model calls rather than a fixed step. The scope given was web search and page fetch, an outbound MCP client, skills, plugins and marketplaces, with two conditions: a stage may use only the tools declared for it, and anything third-party runs only if it is pinned and hash-locked. That changes a security rule, the shape of the journal that makes a resumed run free, and what the project can freeze for 1.0. It deserves a reviewed design before code.
docs.title: Context

docs.text: Tool use is part of the model port, and adapters never run tools. ModelRequest carries tool definitions (a name, a description and a JSON schema). ModelResponse can carry tool calls and a new stop reason, tool_use . Each adapter maps these onto its provider's format (content blocks for Anthropic, tool_calls and role: tool for OpenAI-compatible servers). An adapter still returns what the model said and nothing more, so the exception type stays the contract. A bounded loop runs the tools. A service ( RunToolLoop ) sits above AskModel . It caps model turns, tool calls, the time of each call, the size of each result and the run's spend (every turn reserves against the SpendGuard ). It runs a call through a ToolRunner port and feeds the result back. A loop that hits a limit ends with a blocking issue and the stage stops, as an incomplete answer does today. A tool turn is journaled whole. Every model call keeps its journal entry. Every tool call is journaled too: the tool, a canonical hash of its arguments and its result. A resumed run replays the stored result for nothing and gets the same bytes, instead of searching again against a web that has moved. The key of each later model call includes a hash of the transcript so far, so a replay is only ever of the same conversation. This also closes the double-journaling cost gap noted in M5, which matters more once calls come in loops. Each stage declares its tools; none by default. A StageRecipe lists the tools its stage may use. Only those are offered to the model and only those can run. A call to anything else is answered with "no such tool" and still counts against the call limit. Research gets web_search and fetch_url ; drafting gets none. No tool is ever discovered at run time. No stage asks a person for permission: the allowlist is the permission, and it is part of the code and config a person reviews. Whatever a tool returns is untrusted text. A result is fed back inside an <untrusted> block under a system prompt that says so, is size-capped, and cannot close its own block. Fetched pages go through HtmlTextExtractor . A fetch_url result is also recorded as a SourceRecord (address, title, hash of the text), which is what claim verification later checks against. The native tools are thin wrappers. web_search wraps SearchProviderInterface (Brave first) and returns links and titles only. fetch_url wraps SourceFetcherInterface , so it inherits the URL policy at every redirect, the size and encoding limits and the hidden-text stripping. Their keys come from the secret provider by name and never reach the model or a log. MCP is an outbound client, with servers you list. A server is declared in a lock file with a pinned command or address and version, and with a hash of the tool definitions it advertised when it was added. If a server later advertises different tools or descriptions (tool poisoning, or a changed server), the run refuses to start. Servers are reached over stdio, in a subprocess with an allow-list environment and the same time, memory and disk limits as the build tools, or over HTTP to an address the URL policy accepts, with no redirects. A server's tool is offered to a stage only if the stage names it ( server.tool ). Skills are versioned prompt packs, never code and never tools. A skill adds named prompt parts, in the same TOML shape and with the same version lock as PromptTemplate . Loading one cannot add a tool, run a command or widen a stage's allowlist. Plugins and marketplaces are install-time, human-driven, and pinned. A plugin is a bundle of MCP server definitions and skills. A marketplace is only an index of such bundles, with an address and a hash for each. A person runs ei tools add to copy an entry into the lock file, which records the pinned version and the SHA-256 of the bundle; the change is reviewed like any other commit. Nothing updates itself, and a run never contacts a marketplace. This is how the request for marketplaces fits the condition that third-party code must be pinned and hash-locked: a marketplace is where a person finds something to pin, not a source a run trusts. ACP is not a tool source. The Agent Client Protocol lets an editor or client drive this agent. It is the inbound surface already planned for M8, with its own consent rules for spend. It gives the model no tools and is built separately.
docs.title: Decision

docs.text: The threat model's "the model has no tools" is replaced by decisions 2, 4 and 5, and the document is updated as each lands. Until a tool exists the model has none. A prompt injection in a search result or page can now try to make the model call a tool. The defences are the per-stage allowlist (a drafting stage has nothing to call), the loop's limits, the spend reservation, the untrusted wrapping, and the fact that the native tools can only read public pages through the URL policy. An MCP server widens this and is the reason it is pinned, hash-locked, resource-limited and named per stage. The journal format changes (decision 3). Existing journal rows stay readable; a run started before the change replays as before. 1.0 freezes less if less ships: the tool-lock file format, the tool schema the model sees and the ei tools commands become contracts once released. Skills, plugins and marketplaces are the parts most likely to want change, so they land last and may ship as experimental. Two costs: a model call that reaches for a tool takes more turns than one that does not, and a stage with tools is harder to reproduce exactly than one without, which is what the journal replay is for.
docs.title: Consequences

docs.text: Tool use in the model port and both adapters, with cassettes for tool turns. RunToolLoop , the tool journal and replay, the ToolRunner port and the per-stage allowlist. web_search and fetch_url as tools; the research stage uses them. The tool lock file and ei tools add ; the MCP client over stdio, then HTTP. Skills as prompt packs. Plugins and marketplace indexes, install-time only.
docs.title: Slices

docs.text: How strong a sandbox a stdio MCP server needs beyond the environment allow-list and resource limits, on macOS and on Linux. Whether a tool may carry its own secret, and how that is named in the lock file without the value ever being in it. Whether a stage's tool allowlist lives with its recipe in code or in the lock file, or both with the lock file able to narrow but never widen the code's list. This ADR leans to the last.
docs.title: Open questions

docs.text: Recorded on 2026-11-22 while building slice 4 ( TOOL_LOCK.md ). What the lock pins (decision 7). The maintainer chose to hash the files, not only the tool definitions: the lock records the SHA-256 of a stdio server's executable and of every script among its arguments, plus the server's reported name and version and a hash of the tools it advertises. A launcher that fetches code on each run ( npx , uvx , docker and the like) is refused, because what it would run cannot be hashed. Installed dependencies are not covered, and this is stated rather than hidden. Names. A tool from a server is offered to the model as <server>__<tool> , because the providers accept only letters, digits, - and _ ; recipes and the lock use the same form, not server.tool . A tool's secret (open question 2). The lock names the environment variables a server is given, never their values. Values come from the environment at start. Slicing. Slice 4 is built as 4a (lock models, file format, MCP client over an abstract transport, verifier), 4b (a stdio transport under the build tools' limits, and ei tools ), 4c (wiring the registry and the start-up check) and 4d (HTTP). Running a server (4b). A stdio server runs in its own process group with a bare environment and a throwaway home, under time, memory and disk limits, and is stopped by killing the group before the leader is reaped. It is not sandboxed. ei tools add runs the server, so it refuses a launcher, a missing executable or a relative script before starting anything, and ei tools verify never starts a server whose files have changed. Where a stage's permission for a locked tool lives (4c; the third open question). In the lock file, chosen by the maintainer: a per-server [server.grants] table naming, for each stage, exactly which of the server's tools it may call, with no wildcards. Recipes in code still name the built-in tools; the stage's offered tools are the recipe's plus the lock's grants. It is reviewed in the same commit as the server. A run reads a lock only when EI_TOOL_LOCK names it , so a stray file in the working directory starts no server, and a tool's journal key includes the tool's revision (for a locked tool, the hash of the server's tools) so a replaced server's old answers are not replayed. Remote servers (4d). HTTP follows decision 7 and the slices above, with these choices. The transport is Streamable HTTP, one POST per message, the answer as JSON or as events read within the same request, and no stream of the client's own. A remote entry locks the address and what the server advertises; its code cannot be hashed, and the weaker pin is stated in the docs and the ei tools add output rather than hidden. The address goes through the existing public-https URL policy before every request, with no redirects, so a server on this machine or network is reached over stdio, not HTTP ; a loosening for local development is a separate decision. Credentials are a named variable ( bearer_env ), never part of the address, and the lock refuses a user, query or fragment so a secret cannot be committed in a URL. Other auth schemes (OAuth, custom headers) are not built. Outbound connections are pinned to the checked address (after 4d). A security review of the remote transport found what the docs had listed as a gap: the policy resolved a name when asked and the client resolved it again when it connected. PublicHttpsUrlPinner now resolves once, has the policy judge every address, and hands the caller the vetted address with the name for the Host header and for TLS, so the certificate is still checked against the name. fetch_url and the remote transport use it; only one address is tried, and fetch_url sends Connection: close so a connection verified for one name is not reused for another that shares its address. Signed webhook delivery was not changed.

docs.text: Recorded on 2026-11-22 while building slice 5 ( SKILLS.md ). A skill is one file of text, with a part for each stage it speaks to (decision 8). The ADR said "named prompt parts, in the same TOML shape as PromptTemplate ". A template's parts are the pieces of one prompt ( system , user ) with blanks to fill; a skill's parts are which stage the text is for . A skill has no blanks, so there is nothing to fill and no value to smuggle into; it has no untrusted list, because all of it is text a person chose; and any key it should not have ( command , tools , url ) is refused by name. The version lock is a hash, in its own lock file. A shipped template is pinned by a fingerprint in a test fixture. A skill is installed by a person, so it is pinned by the SHA-256 of its file's bytes in ei-skills.lock.toml , which a run reads only when EI_SKILL_LOCK names it. It is a separate file from the tool lock so either can be used alone; plugins (slice 6) will copy entries into both. ei skills add keeps a copy of the file in a skills/ folder beside the lock, so what is committed is what is hashed, and the lock needs no paths. Permission is per stage and explicit, as for tools. A new skill is enabled for no stage. ei skills enable NAME STAGE checks the file against its hash and refuses a stage the skill has no text for; at most four skills may be enabled for one stage; locking a skill again clears its stages, because new text has not been approved for anything. Where the text goes (a decision the ADR left open). At the end of the user part of the stage's prompt, in a delimited block under a fixed frame (the skill_guidance template), never in the system part. It is not wrapped as <untrusted> : unlike a page, it is meant to instruct, and the person approved it. The trade-off is stated plainly in SKILLS.md : a skill that was hostile when it was locked is trusted as locked. A copy of the block's tags inside a skill is defused. What a person approved is what a model sees. Text that renders as nothing or reorders what is shown (control characters, zero-width and bidirectional marks, line and paragraph separators, private-use and unassigned code points) is refused when the skill is read, and each part is capped, so a skill cannot hide an instruction from the review the lock exists for. The journal key (decision 3) names the skills. A stage with skills sends <template>@<n>+skill_guidance@<n>:<digest> , the digest covering each skill's name, version and hash, so a resumed run replays an answer only for the same text. A stage with no skill enabled sends exactly the prompt and version it always did, so existing journals are unaffected. The check happens once, at start, before anything else. Skills enabled for some stage are read and hashed when the stage executor is built, before any tool server is started or any model is called; the text is then held for the life of the process, so every stage of a run sees the same text. A skill that is installed but enabled for no stage is not read. What a skill still cannot do. It adds no tool, changes no stage's allowlist, output cap or system prompt, and cannot raise a budget: those are decided in code, in the tool lock and in the spend guard.
docs.title: Amendments from slice 5

docs.text: Recorded on 2026-11-22 while building the first part of slice 6 ( PLUGINS.md ). Slice 6 is split as slice 4 was: 6a plugins installed from a file on disk, 6b marketplace indexes and fetching. Installing a plugin runs and contacts nothing (decision 9). The ADR said a person runs ei tools add to copy an entry into the lock. The installer therefore does not run a bundle's servers: a bundle is text from someone else, and ei tools add is the step that starts a server (or contacts one) and pins what it reports. The installer locks the bundle's skills (each enabled for no stage) and prints the exact ei tools add command for each server, shell-quoted, for a person to review and run. A bundle cannot decide what a model may do. There is no key for a grant, for a stage to enable a skill for, or for anything else; any unknown key is refused. A server definition is held to the same rules the tool lock uses (an absolute command that is not a launcher, an https address with no secret in it), so a plugin cannot describe a server the lock would refuse. One file, one hash. A plugin is a single TOML file with [[server]] and [[skill]] tables, so one SHA-256 pins everything a person reviewed. Skills in it are read by the same strict parser as a skill file, and are written into the skill lock as skill files, so they are ordinary skills afterwards. A third lock file, which a run never reads. ei-plugins.lock.toml records the bundle's hash, the servers it described and the hash each skill was locked under, so ei plugins verify can check the bundle that was reviewed and ei plugins remove can undo the install. What a run may do stays in the tool lock and the skill lock; no new thing is added to the run's trust surface. No replace. A plugin that is installed, or whose skills are already locked, is refused before anything is written. Installing a newer version is remove then add , because replacing text a person approved is a decision, not a side effect. remove deletes only skills that are still exactly what the plugin installed. An install either completes or leaves nothing. The bundle's copy is written first, and a failure while locking a later skill removes the copy and the skills already locked.
docs.title: Amendments from slice 6a

docs.text: Recorded on 2026-11-22 while building the second part of slice 6 ( PLUGINS.md ). A marketplace is only an index, and a download is a separate step from an install (decision 9). An index is a TOML file of plugin names, versions, descriptions, addresses and SHA-256 hashes, with no other key. ei plugins fetch INDEX NAME downloads one plugin file, checks its hash against the index's before reading it as anything , checks that it is the plugin and version the index named, and saves it; it installs nothing. A person reads it with ei plugins show and installs it with ei plugins add , which stays an offline step on a local file. This keeps the one network-facing command narrow: it can produce a file, and cannot change a lock. A run never contacts a marketplace. Only search and fetch , run by a person, can use a network, and add , show , verify and remove never do. The download is held to the rules every other outbound connection here is. It goes through the same pinned-address URL policy as fetch_url and the remote tool transport (https, a public address checked each time, the connection made to the address that was checked with the name in TLS), follows no redirect, sends no cookie or credential, accepts no compression and is bounded to 512 KiB and 30 seconds. An address in an index is held to the lock's rules for a remote server (no user, password, query string or fragment). An index is not trusted more than its host. Indexes and plugin files are not signed, so the hash only proves that the bytes are the ones the index described. Vouching for a publisher (signatures, a key to trust) is a decision this slice does not make; the defence is that a person reads the file and that installing enables nothing. The core install still works without httpx . The downloader is built on first use, and a missing dependency becomes a message that names the runtime extra; a local index file needs no network code at all.

docs.text: ADR 0009: Publishing follows the branch: develop to TestPyPI, main to PyPI ¶ Status: accepted Context ¶ ADR 0005 set a release as a tag, v<version> , pushed by a person from main , with the version set by hand and the guard refusing a tag that disagrees with the code, the changelog or the branch. It also said that tagging and publishing "need an explicit approval" and that nothing in that ADR automates them. The maintainer has decided that a merge to develop should upload to TestPyPI and a merge to main should upload to PyPI. Decision ¶ The trigger is a push to develop or main , not a tag. release.yml runs on those two branches and by hand. A tag push does nothing, and a run from any other branch is refused by the guard. develop uploads development builds to TestPyPI. A package index never accepts a version twice, and develop carries one version until the next release, so each build is stamped <version>.dev<run number> . The stamping is done to a copy of the commit by scripts/stamp_dev_version.py , so the checkout, the lock file and the tests see the real version. main is the release. A merge to main runs the guard (a plain release version, a changelog section for exactly that version, no unfolded fragments, the commit on main ) and the full tests, creates the tag v<version> and a GitHub release at the built commit, and uploads to PyPI. The version is still set by hand in the release commit (ADR 0005, point 1) and the fragments are still folded before it (point 3). main should receive releases only. The approval is the environment, not the tag. Each upload runs from its own GitHub environment with required reviewers, and each index has a repository variable that switches it on ( PUBLISH_TO_TESTPYPI , PUBLISH_TO_PYPI ). Both are off by default. This replaces ADR 0005's point 5 for uploads: a person still approves each one, but the approval comes from the environment when the merge happens, not from the act of tagging. The core and the SDK are separate jobs and environments , because PyPI tells pending trusted publishers apart by owner, repository, workflow and environment (see docs/RELEASING.md ). A release also publishes the two images to GHCR (added for criterion A9 of ADR 0003). The images job runs after the GitHub release, from its own ghcr environment and behind PUBLISH_IMAGES , which is off by default. It builds with the plain docker command and attests each image by digest, so it adds no third-party action. A version tag is never written over an image built from another commit, which is the same rule the git tag follows. Consequences ¶ A release is one merge, so the guard has to be strict: a merge to main without a version bump fails (the changelog has no section, or PyPI refuses a duplicate) and should be fixed forward. Every merge to develop can upload. If the testpypi environments require reviewers, each merge waits for an approval; the maintainer chooses whether that is wanted. A development version sorts before the release it is named for, so while develop carries an already released version, its builds sort below that release. A failure between the core and SDK uploads can publish one and not the other. A PyPI version can never be reused, so it is repaired with the next version. The tag now comes from the workflow, so the workflow must not trust one it did not make: it looks the tag up, accepts one that already names the built commit, and stops on one that names another or on any lookup it cannot read. The tag now comes from the workflow. Nothing reads a tag any more, so a person tagging by hand has no effect, and a release that failed after the GitHub release was created is repeated by running the workflow again, which finds the release and carries on. ADR 0005's points 2 (the tag guard) and 5 (releases remain gated) are replaced by points 1, 3 and 4 above. Its points on fragments, hand-set versions and breaking changes stand.

Each upload runs from its own GitHub environment with required reviewers, and each index has a repository variable that switches it on ( PUBLISH_TO_TESTPYPI , PUBLISH_TO_PYPI ). Both are off by default. This replaces ADR 0005's point 5 for uploads: a person still approves each one, but the approval comes from the environment when the merge happens, not from the act of tagging. A release also publishes the two images to GHCR (added for criterion A9 of ADR 0003). The images job runs after the GitHub release, from its own ghcr environment and behind PUBLISH_IMAGES , which is off by default. It builds with the plain docker command and attests each image by digest, so it adds no third-party action. A version tag is never written over an image built from another commit, which is the same rule the git tag follows.

docs.text: A release is one merge, so the guard has to be strict: a merge to main without a version bump fails (the changelog has no section, or PyPI refuses a duplicate) and should be fixed forward. Every merge to develop can upload. If the testpypi environments require reviewers, each merge waits for an approval; the maintainer chooses whether that is wanted. A development version sorts before the release it is named for, so while develop carries an already released version, its builds sort below that release. A failure between the core and SDK uploads can publish one and not the other. A PyPI version can never be reused, so it is repaired with the next version. The tag now comes from the workflow, so the workflow must not trust one it did not make: it looks the tag up, accepts one that already names the built commit, and stops on one that names another or on any lookup it cannot read. The tag now comes from the workflow. Nothing reads a tag any more, so a person tagging by hand has no effect, and a release that failed after the GitHub release was created is repeated by running the workflow again, which finds the release and carries on. ADR 0005's points 2 (the tag guard) and 5 (releases remain gated) are replaced by points 1, 3 and 4 above. Its points on fragments, hand-set versions and breaking changes stand.
