docs.text: ADR 0010: Chapters are drafted in order, inside one stage ¶ Status: proposed Context ¶ The plan for the non-fiction stages (M6) asks for per-chapter drafting as a fan-out with an atomic join counter and a concurrency cap , and also for a rolling summary and a fact tracker carried across chapters . Those two do not fit together: a summary of the chapters before this one needs those chapters to exist, so chapters drafted at the same time cannot be given each other's summaries. The machinery that exists points the same way: A StagePlan is a fixed, ordered tuple of distinct stage names, stored with the run when it starts, before the outline exists and so before the number of chapters is known. AdvanceRun walks it one stage at a time and makes duplicate deliveries safe with compare-and-swap. The M5 ContextAssembler was built for drafting in order: it fits the style, the grounding, the beats, as many of the newest prior-chapter summaries as will fit, and the tail of the previous chapter into a token budget. Every model call is journaled by a key made from the request, so a call that is repeated with the same request is replayed for nothing. On 2026-11-22 the maintainer chose to draft the chapters in order, in one stage , and to leave parallel fan-out for after 1.0. Decision ¶ A non-fiction plan gets one draft stage after outline . It does not change how runs work: no sub-stages, no plan that grows, no new queue message and no join table. The stage takes the outline's chapters in order, in a single execution. The outline is a contract. The stage_outline template tells the model to write each chapter as ## Chapter N: Title , then Purpose: , Beats: and Claims to source: (bullets) and Leads to: . An OutlineParser reads that strictly into an Outline of ChapterOutline s (at most 50 chapters, numbered 1, 2, 3 with no gaps, one-line bounded texts), and a check run when the outline stage finishes refuses an answer it cannot read, before it is stored. A malformed outline therefore stops the run at the outline, not one stage later after drafting has been paid for. A model's preamble before the first heading and a closing paragraph after a blank line are ignored; hidden and control characters are removed. Each chapter is drafted from what came before it. For chapter n the context assembler is given the book's style (from the positioning), the grounding (the outline and the research notes), the chapter's beats, the summaries of chapters 1 to n −1 and the tail of chapter n −1. One model call, with no tools, drafts the chapter; a second summarizes it. They are stored as chapter_NN.md and summary_NN.md (two digits). Everything that came out of a model or off the web goes into a later prompt inside an <untrusted> block, as every other stage does. A chapter is done when both of its files exist, and a repeated execution skips done chapters. A stage that fails or is redelivered part-way through starts over at the first chapter that is not done. Because a repeated model call is replayed from the journal for nothing, even a chapter that is redrafted costs nothing if its request is unchanged. Spend is the same as for every other stage. Each call reserves against the run's budget through the stage's SpendGuard and is journaled, so a stage with 30 chapters cannot pass the cap and its cost survives a crash. The stage's own artifact is draft.md , an index of the chapters drafted and their lengths, so that the stage leaves the same kind of trace as the others and later stages can name one input. Not decided here ¶ The fact tracker, structural and line revision, copy edit, front and back matter, assembly into books/<slug>.toml and claim verification are separate slices, each recorded by an amendment when it is built. Parallel drafting. If it is wanted after 1.0, a join counter would slot in as follows: the draft stage would enqueue one run.draft_chapter message per chapter and finish when an atomic counter row reaches the chapter count. It is not built because chapters drafted at the same time cannot see each other's summaries, so continuity would rest on the outline alone, and because it adds a queue message, a table and a worker-sharing rule for the spend guard (which today is per process) for a speed-up that a first book does not need. Consequences ¶ The plan's fan-out, join counter and concurrency cap are dropped for 1.0. That is a deliberate change to the plan, recorded here. A book takes as long as its chapters take in a row. The stage is long-running, so it must stay within the queue's redelivery window; the next slice records how long, and a person can resume a run that was stopped. The outline's format is now a contract between two stages: changing the stage_outline template or the parser means changing both, with a version bump and a new fixture. A run whose outline stage produced a malformed outline fails with OUTLINE_INVALID , and, because the journal replays the same request, trying the same stage again with the same prompt gives the same answer. The remedy is to change what the outline stage is asked (for example with a skill) and start a new run. Amendment: the drafting stage as built (2026-11-22) ¶ DraftStageExecutor does the stage, and StageExecutorRouter sends draft to it and every other stage to ModelStageExecutor . The plan names draft after outline , but there is no recipe for it, because it is not one prompt. What the code does where this decision left room: A chapter written but not summarized is summarized from its stored text, never redrafted. "Done" is both files, but the two calls are separate, so a stage that fails between them resumes at the summary alone. How long a chapter is. The brief's target_words shared across the chapters, or 2,500 words when there is none, never under 300 or over 6,000. The output cap is that many words as tokens (1.6 a word) plus 400, never more than the model allows. The input budget is the model's window less the output cap, less a 512-token margin, less an estimate for any skills enabled for the stage. A window too small for that stops the stage before the first call ( STAGE_MODEL_TOO_SMALL ). The instruction holds numbers only. The only plain text in the draft prompt says which chapter of how many and about how many words; the voice, the grounding, the beats, the summaries and the tail are untrusted blocks, as the context assembler lays them out. A call that does not finish stores nothing for that chapter and fails the stage ( STAGE_ANSWER_UNUSABLE , with the model's own reasons); the chapters before it stay, and the next delivery starts at that chapter. The summary of a chapter is a short note (400 tokens at most) from stage_summary ; the draft prompt gets each one on one line as Chapter k: ... , oldest dropped first when the window is short. Not yet checked: that a chapter keeps to its beats or its length. That belongs to revision. Nothing here has run against a live model. Amendment: the assemble stage (2026-11-22) ¶ A non-fiction plan now ends with assemble , which makes no model call. AssembleStageExecutor reads outline.md and the chapter_NN.md files and writes, in the run's artifacts, the project layout BookLoader reads: manuscript/src/chapter_NN.md and manuscript/books/<slug>.toml , plus assemble.md listing them. A property test holds the contract: whatever a model wrote, the stage either refuses with MANUSCRIPT_TEXT_REFUSED or writes a manuscript that BookLoader loads in strict mode and the forbidden-content check passes. Dashes are rewritten, unfinished work is refused. The typesetter refuses an em or en dash in non-fiction, and a model's prose is full of them, so a dash between digits becomes a hyphen and any other dash becomes a comma (or nothing at the start or end of a line or before punctuation). A marker such as [TODO] , or the word Draft , is refused with the chapter and line, because deleting it would hide an unfinished chapter. The rewrite is a plain edit; the copy edit stage is where the sentences get reworked. The outline's title heads the chapter. A heading the model put at the top of its answer is dropped, and any other level-1 heading in the body becomes level 2. Nothing is written until every chapter has been cleaned , so a refused chapter leaves no half manuscript. The config holds only what is known: the kind, the title (the brief's hint, or its idea's first line), src , the trim size when the brief set one, and one part, Part One , holding every chapter. It has no author, publisher, edition, year or bio. Those are the author's, so the book loads but does not build until they are added. Setting them, and real parts, front and back matter belong to the front/back matter and metadata slice. Amendment: the listing and the author's details (2026-11-22) ¶ A non-fiction plan now has a metadata stage after outline (before drafting, because it needs only the brief, the positioning and the outline), and assemble reads its result. metadata is one prompt , so it has a recipe and goes through the same executor as the earlier stages. It writes the title, subtitle, description, seven keywords and one to three categories in a fixed format. MetadataParser reads it strictly and NonfictionOutputChecks refuses an unreadable one before it is stored ( METADATA_INVALID ). BookMetadata holds the release contract's rules (an 80 word description of at most 4,000 characters, seven distinct keywords, one to three browse paths of two levels or more), so a listing that is built cannot fail the contract for its shape. The author's details are not a stage. They are the author's, so they come from a file the person names with EI_AUTHOR_PROFILE ( AuthorProfile , read by TomlAuthorProfileLoader ), never from a model and never into a prompt. The assemble stage writes them into the config with the listing, with the release contract's [release] keywords and categories. A book assembled with a profile passes the release contract's metadata and category checks (a test runs them). Without one, it loads but does not build. Front and back matter are not Markdown files. The title page, copyright page, dedication and about-the-author page are made by the typesetter from the config, so no stage writes them. Pricing and the cover are still the author's to supply. The title is the listing's , which is the title the brief asked for when it gave one, and the config's file name is its slug. Amendment: the audit stage (2026-11-22) ¶ A non-fiction plan now ends with audit , which makes no model call. AuditStageExecutor reads the manuscript/ files, gives them to a ManuscriptAuditorInterface as a project, and stores what comes back under audit/ ( manuscript-audit.json , release-readiness.json , publication-report.json ) with a summary in audit.md . It runs the publishing pipeline's own audit-only gates , the manuscript audit and the release readiness check, so there is one definition of a book that is ready. They need no TeX toolchain and no cover. TempProjectManuscriptAuditor lays the files out as a project in a private temporary folder, runs PublishPipeline.publish(..., audit_only=True) , reads the reports back and removes the folder; nothing of the book is left on disk. The publishing libraries are imported only when an audit runs. Errors stop the run, warnings do not. The reports are stored first, so a failed book can be read, then the run stops with AUDIT_FAILED and every error. A book with no prices passes with a warning for each, because prices are the author's. Measured, not assumed: an assembled book passes the real audit. Without an author profile the only extra finding is missing-author (a warning); with one, the findings are the missing prices and their date and source. A runtime test runs the real gates on a book that the assemble stage made. Not done: the PDF and EPUB build and the cover, which need the TeX toolchain, the cover design settings and cover art that are the author's. They are the next slice. Amendment: the editing passes (2026-11-22) ¶ A non-fiction plan now has three editing stages between draft and assemble : revise_structure , revise_lines and copy_edit , each a RevisionStageExecutor run with one of the passes in NonfictionRevisionPasses . Each is one call with no tools for each chapter, in order. Each pass reads what the one before wrote. The first reads chapter_NN.md ; the files are structure_NN.md , lines_NN.md and copy_NN.md ; and assemble now reads copy_NN.md . Each pass is told only what it needs: structure sees the whole outline, a line on every other chapter and this chapter's plan; lines sees the voice; copy sees nothing but the chapter. They have their own templates rather than the drafting assembler, whose system text says "write the chapter" and has no place for text to be revised. A revision is kept only if it is plausible. An answer that did not finish stops the stage, as in drafting. One that did finish but is blank, or whose length in words is outside the pass's bounds of the chapter's (a fifth for structure, a tenth for lines, a twentieth for copy), is not stored and the chapter passes through unchanged . A retry would replay the same answer, so stopping would only fail the run again. The stage reports each unchanged chapter as a tolerated issue ( revision-unchanged ), worked out from the stored files so a redelivery says the same, and <stage>.md lists every chapter's length before and after. This is a guard against an answer that is not an edit, not a judgment of whether an edit is good. The window is checked, not assumed. A chapter whose prompt (estimated at three characters a token) and answer would not fit the model's window stops the stage before the call ( STAGE_MODEL_TOO_SMALL ); nothing is cut to make it fit. Cost: every pass is one call per chapter, so a book with n chapters now makes about 5 n model calls after the outline (a draft, a summary and three edits for each chapter). Every call reserves against the run's budget, and a run whose cap cannot cover the next call stops there. Not known: whether the edits improve the prose. Nothing here has run against a live model, and the length bounds only catch an answer that is plainly not an edit.

docs.text: ADR 0011: Run inputs are untrusted text carried inside the brief ¶ Status: proposed Context ¶ A run's only input is the brief's one idea . A person who has notes, an excerpt, a draft or reference text has no way to give it to the run, and the plan (M6.5) asks for pasted text and files. Nothing started a run when this was written ( ei book create was M8; it now exists), so whatever is decided here has to hold for every surface that will: the CLI, the API, MCP and the SDK. Anything a person hands over may have been written by someone else (a page they copied, a file they were sent). It has to reach a model as evidence, never as instructions , and it must not be able to widen what a stage may call. Decision ¶ An input is a RunInput : a name (lowercase letters, digits, dots, hyphens, underscores; at most 60), plain text, and an origin ( pasted or file ). A line break and a tab are allowed; every other control, format, private-use or invisible character is refused , never cleaned, by the rule a skill's text is held to. The text is at most 50,000 characters and is never cut. Inputs live in the brief ( BookBrief.inputs ): at most 8, each name once, 200,000 characters in all. They are stored with the run (the run's JSON gains brief.inputs ), so a run carries what it was given, a resumed run sees the same text, and a run stored before this existed loads with none. Brief v1 gains an optional inputs list: an additive change that leaves every existing brief reading the same, as the contract promised for later compatible versions. Files are read here only as plain text ( .txt , .md , .markdown , UTF-8, at most 256 KiB, no link followed). A leading byte-order mark is dropped and line endings are made \n ; a file with a hidden character is refused. PDF and HTML files need an extractor and are not read yet. Every input is untrusted. It will reach a prompt only inside an <untrusted> block, like the brief and the research. It grants nothing: no input can name a tool, enable a skill or change a budget, and the stages' tool grants are unchanged. docs.text: An input is a RunInput : a name (lowercase letters, digits, dots, hyphens, underscores; at most 60), plain text, and an origin ( pasted or file ). A line break and a tab are allowed; every other control, format, private-use or invisible character is refused , never cleaned, by the rule a skill's text is held to. The text is at most 50,000 characters and is never cut. Inputs live in the brief ( BookBrief.inputs ): at most 8, each name once, 200,000 characters in all. They are stored with the run (the run's JSON gains brief.inputs ), so a run carries what it was given, a resumed run sees the same text, and a run stored before this existed loads with none. Brief v1 gains an optional inputs list: an additive change that leaves every existing brief reading the same, as the contract promised for later compatible versions. Files are read here only as plain text ( .txt , .md , .markdown , UTF-8, at most 256 KiB, no link followed). A leading byte-order mark is dropped and line endings are made \n ; a file with a hidden character is refused. PDF and HTML files need an extractor and are not read yet. Every input is untrusted. It will reach a prompt only inside an <untrusted> block, like the brief and the research.
